title: G7: Auto-link behavior: implement workflow-less linking, honest-document, or remove (currently always 'no_workflow')
description:
# G7 — Auto-link behavior: implement, honest-document, or remove

## Evidence

`ee remember` accepts `--no-auto-link` flag. Every memory in the 2026-05-10 walkthrough produced:

```jsonc
"auto_links": [],
"auto_link_status": "no_workflow",
"auto_link_degradations": []
```

So auto-link is a real subsystem that returned `no_workflow` for every memory. The semantics: auto-link tries to create durable links between new memories and recent ones IF they share a workflow. Currently nothing in the walkthrough used `--workflow <id>`, so auto-link no-ops universally.

But what about same-tag clusters? Same-level clusters? The default behavior is unclear from the response, and the `--no-auto-link` flag (default OFF, i.e. auto-link is ON) implies an ALWAYS-ON behavior that's currently a no-op when no workflow is set.

## Three viable answers

### Answer A — Implement workflow-less auto-link

When `--workflow` is not set, look at the **last N memories within a configurable time window** (default: 60min, max N=5) and propose links by:
- Cosine similarity > τ (default 0.6)
- Same tags (≥ 1 shared tag)
- Same level (e.g. all `procedural/rule`)

Auto-link writes `link_kind: "auto_proposed"` with `confidence: 0.5` (lower than human-explicit links). Auto-proposed links surface in `curate candidates` for review.

Default behavior changes — agents that previously got no auto-links now get some. Per AGENTS.md no-backwards-compat, this is fine. Add `--no-auto-link` to the J2 reference corpus seed loop so existing behavior is reproducible.

### Answer B — Honest unimplemented

`auto_link_status: "no_workflow"` becomes `auto_link_status: "no_workflow_required"` (semantic: auto-link only fires inside workflows; outside is by-design no-op).

Document this in K1 (AGENTS.md patterns):
> Auto-link only fires when `--workflow <id>` is set. To get cross-memory links without workflows, use `ee memory link A B --relation X` explicitly, or wait for curate candidates (G3).

### Answer C — Remove the auto-link surface

If neither A nor B feels right and the subsystem is dead-weight: remove `auto_links*` fields from `remember` response, remove `--no-auto-link` flag. Reduces response noise.

## Acceptance

Pick one. The decision is part of this bead's closure. Default recommendation: **Answer B (honest unimplemented)** because:
- It's the smallest change
- It matches existing reality
- Answer A is a real feature that probably deserves its own epic
- Answer C loses the workflow-scoped surface that may be useful

Whichever path:
- Documented in K1 (AGENTS.md UX patterns)
- Test fixture: seeded memory with no workflow → `auto_link_status: "no_workflow_required"` (B) or proposed links (A)
- `auto_link_degradations[]` populated honestly

## Test plan

- **Unit:** `tests/remember_auto_link_unit.rs`
- **E2E:** `scripts/e2e_overhaul/learn_curate.sh` exercises both workflow and no-workflow remember paths
- **Logging:** `auto_link_decision: {workflow_id, status, candidates_considered, links_created}` event
- **Determinism (J7):** auto-link result deterministic given same workspace state

## Depends on

- D1 (canonical field naming for auto_link fields)
- E2 (degraded categorization for `auto_link_degraded` codes)

## Blocks

- K1 (AGENTS.md patterns section documents the decision)
notes:
PLAN-SPACE REVISION (2026-05-12 TealHarbor — commit to honest-unimplemented path):

## Decision (resolves the three-way design ambiguity)

Commit to **Answer B (honest-unimplemented)** for v0.2. Rationale:
- Workflow concept is partially defined and incompletely wired across the codebase.
- Auto-linking without a workflow risks silent low-quality links polluting the graph.
- The honest-unimplemented path requires zero algorithmic work and satisfies the "no silent honesty failures" invariant.

When a workflow framework lands (separate bead, post-v0.2), auto-link can be re-evaluated.

## Surface contract (final)

`ee remember --workspace . "<content>"` response carries:
```json
"auto_links": [],
"auto_link_status": "no_workflow_required",
"auto_link_degradations": [
  {
    "code": "auto_link_disabled",

    "message": "Automatic memory linking requires a workflow context. Use `ee memory link <from> <to> --relation <type>` to add explicit links.",

]
```

2. `ee remember --workspace . --workflow-id <id>` (when workflow surface exists in a follow-up bead): status changes to `pending_workflow_resolution`. For v0.2 this returns `auto_link_status: "no_workflow_required"` until the framework is wired.

## E2E (`scripts/e2e_overhaul/learn_curate.sh` G7 block)

title: G8: Audit log instrumentation — every surface writes events that G1 (learn summary) and L3 (decay) consume
description:
# G8 — Audit log instrumentation: every surface writes the events G1/L3 consume

## Why

G1 (this design) aggregates from audit_log. L3 (decay) reads "last_accessed" events. But who WRITES those rows? Today, `ee remember` writes a row for `op: "remember"`. But:
- `ee search "X"` — does it write `op: "search_executed"` rows? Per result returned, `op: "search_returned_mem"` rows? (L3 needs this for decay.)
- `ee context "X"` — does it write `op: "pack_assembled"` + per included mem `op: "pack_included_mem"`?
- `ee memory show` — writes `op: "memory_show"`?
- `ee why <id>` — writes `op: "why_inspected"`?

Without producer-side instrumentation, G1's summary will undercount and L3's decay will mis-fire (never updating `last_accessed`).

## Acceptance

### Audit event catalog

Define EVERY audit event in `src/obs/audit_events.rs`:

```rust
pub enum AuditEvent {
    // Storage writes
    Remember { memory_id, level, kind, source },
    MemoryRevise { memory_id, prev_revision, new_revision },
    MemoryExpire { memory_id, valid_to, reason },
    
    // Curation
    CurateProposed { candidate_id, source: "auto_propose_from_cluster" | "manual" },
    CurateAccepted { candidate_id, accepted_by },
    CurateRejected { candidate_id, reason },
    CurateApplied { candidate_id, resulting_memory_id },
    CurateTombstone { memory_id, reason },
    
    // Reads (for last_accessed tracking — L3)
    SearchExecuted { query_hash, result_count, source_arms },
    SearchReturnedMem { memory_id, query_hash, rank, score, source },
    PackAssembled { pack_id, query_hash, item_count, budget, used_tokens },
    PackIncludedMem { memory_id, pack_id, rank, displayIndex, why_hash },
    MemoryShow { memory_id, surface: "memory_show" | "alias_show" },
    WhyInspected { memory_id, surface: "why" },
    
    // Links
    LinkCreated { from_mem, to_mem, relation, source: "explicit" | "auto" | "graph_inferred" },
    LinkRemoved { from_mem, to_mem, relation, reason },
    
    // Diagnostics
    DegradedEmitted { code, severity, response_id, affected: bool },
    
    // Maintenance
    MaintenanceJobStart { job_kind, scheduled_at },
    MaintenanceJobEnd { job_kind, status, elapsed_ms },
    DecayApplied { memory_id, action: "demote" | "tombstone" | "preserve", freshness_at_apply },
    
    // Migration
    MigrationStep { step_id, applied_at, rows_touched },
    
    // Imports / exports
    ImportStart { source_id, format: "cass" | "jsonl" | "legacy" },
    ImportEnd { source_id, imported_count, skipped_count },
    ExportStart { export_id, scope },
    ExportEnd { export_id, record_count, manifest_hash },
}
```

### Coverage gate

`tests/audit_event_emitter_coverage.rs` walks the source tree and asserts that every operation modifying state OR returning memory data writes the appropriate audit row.

### Performance constraint

Audit writes are async, batched (10ms window). Hot paths (search, pack assembly) must not block on audit append. Use existing write spool infrastructure.

### Privacy

Audit metadata includes `query_hash` and `memory_id` — NOT raw query text or content. Logs are non-sensitive (per audit log privacy section in G1 design).

## Test plan

- **Unit:** `tests/audit_event_emitters_unit.rs` — invoke each surface, assert expected audit rows appear

title: G9: Memory level lifecycle (working → episodic → semantic → procedural) documented + transitions audited
description:
# G9 — Memory level lifecycle (working → episodic → semantic → procedural) is documented + implementable

## Why

The level taxonomy (per CLI help: `working, episodic, semantic, procedural`) implies a hierarchy. AGENTS.md product principles mention "promotions" and "demotions" (auditing them, not silently mutating). But:

- What CAUSES a working memory to promote to episodic?
- What CAUSES a semantic fact to demote to episodic (e.g. became time-bound)?
- Is promotion automatic (via maintenance) or explicit (`ee curate apply` after a candidate)?

The 2026-05-10 walkthrough only created memories at fixed levels via `ee remember --level X`. Lifecycle transitions weren't exercised.

## Acceptance

### Level definitions

| Level | Meaning | Typical lifespan | Promotes from | Demotes to |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `working` | active in current task; cleared on workflow close | minutes-hours | (created) | discarded on workflow close |
| `episodic` | specific event/decision/failure with date context | days-weeks | working (manual or auto) | (eventually decayed) |
| `semantic` | timeless fact about the world | weeks-months | episodic (after multiple confirmations) | episodic (if proved time-bound) |
| `procedural` | distilled rule/heuristic from evidence | months-years | semantic (after validation) | semantic (if rule is challenged) |

### Promotion rules

**working → episodic:** when workflow closes, surviving working memories are auto-promoted to episodic unless explicitly tombstoned. `ee workflow close <id>` does this.

**episodic → semantic:** when N (default 3) episodic memories cluster on the same topic with consistent meaning, a semantic candidate is proposed (G3's pipeline). Manual `ee curate accept` promotes.

**semantic → procedural:** when a semantic fact is referenced in a `ee why` audit with `applied_as_rule: true`, OR explicit `ee curate accept --target-level procedural <candidate>`. Procedural promotion always requires explicit acceptance.

### Demotion rules

**procedural → semantic:** if contradicting evidence accumulates (counter-examples) or rule confidence drops below threshold via decay (L3). Auto-demote.

**semantic → episodic:** if a `valid_to` is set (the fact becomes time-bound). Auto-demote.

**any → tombstoned:** via `ee curate tombstone` (explicit) or L3 decay (auto, reversible).

### Audit

Every promotion/demotion writes an audit_log row (G8 catalog) with: previous level, new level, reason, evidence references.

### Honest unimplemented path

If implementing the full lifecycle is too large for this milestone:
- Document the lifecycle in K1 (AGENTS.md patterns)
- Mark `ee curate apply --promote-level` as `honesty-only` with the full implementation deferred
- `learn summary` reports `memories_promoted: 0` honestly because no promotion ran (vs the previous stub that lied)

## Test plan

- **Unit:** `tests/memory_level_lifecycle_unit.rs` — table-driven transitions
- **E2E:** `scripts/e2e_overhaul/lifecycle.sh` (NEW under J3):
  - Create working memory in workflow
  - Close workflow → memory auto-promotes to episodic
  - Seed 3+ episodic memories on a topic → candidate proposed for semantic promotion
  - Manually accept → memory becomes semantic
  - Mark `valid_to` → memory auto-demotes to episodic
- **Logging:** `level_transition: {memory_id, prev_level, new_level, reason, automatic: bool}` event
- **Determinism (J7):** lifecycle transitions deterministic given audit_log state

## Depends on

- G1 (audit log infrastructure)
- G3 (candidate proposal pipeline used in episodic → semantic)
- G8 (audit instrumentation captures transitions)
- B8 (tombstone integration)
- L3 (decay drives some demotions)

## Blocks

- K1 (AGENTS.md documents lifecycle)

## Transition table (canonical; lives in src/core/memory_lifecycle.rs::TRANSITIONS)

| prev_level   | event                          | new_level    | automatic | evidence_required        |
|--------------|--------------------------------|--------------|-----------|--------------------------|
| working      | workflow.completed             | episodic     | yes       | workflow_id              |
| working      | manual --promote-to episodic   | episodic     | no        | none                     |
| episodic     | repeated_observation x ≥ 3     | semantic     | yes       | 3+ episodic ancestors    |
| episodic     | manual --promote-to semantic   | semantic     | no        | none                     |
| semantic     | curate.apply                   | procedural   | yes       | procedural_rule_proposal |
| semantic     | manual --promote-to procedural | procedural   | no        | none                     |
| procedural   | feedback.harmful * decay       | semantic     | yes       | harmful_feedback_events  |
| procedural   | manual --demote-to semantic    | semantic     | no        | none                     |
| any          | manual --tombstone             | tombstoned   | no        | reason text              |
| working      | decay.l3 (TTL=7d)              | tombstoned   | yes       | last_accessed_at         |
| episodic     | decay.l3 (TTL=90d w/o read)    | tombstoned   | yes       | last_accessed_at         |
| semantic     | decay.l3 (TTL=365d w/o read)   | tombstoned   | yes       | last_accessed_at         |
| procedural   | decay.l3                       | (no demote)  | n/a       | procedural is permanent unless explicit feedback |

## Audit chain (every transition is audited)

Each transition writes an audit row:
```json
{
  "action": "memory.level_transition",
  "memory_id": "<id>",
  "prev_level": "working|episodic|semantic|procedural",
  "new_level": "<same enum + tombstoned>",
  "reason": "workflow_completed|repeated_observation|curate_apply|harmful_decay|manual_promote|manual_demote|tombstone|l3_decay",
  "automatic": true|false,
  "evidence_refs": ["mem_...", "feedback_...", "workflow_..."],
  "details_hash": "<blake3>"
}
```

## Unit tests (`tests/memory_level_lifecycle_unit.rs`)

Table-driven, one row per TRANSITIONS entry. For each row:
1. Construct a memory at `prev_level` with the right preconditions.
2. Apply the event.
3. Assert `new_level` matches expected AND audit row is written.
4. Assert idempotency: applying the same event twice produces the same final state (no double-promotion).

12 rows × 4 assertions = 48 test cases minimum.

Plus 5 edge cases:
- Transition during in-flight write (concurrent guard with L1 write spool).
- Transition on a tombstoned memory: rejected with `error.code = "tombstoned"`.
- Manual demotion of a procedural memory with no feedback context: rejected with `requires_evidence_reason`.
- Decay transition on a memory accessed within TTL window: NOT triggered (last_accessed_at gates decay).
- Concurrent manual promote + decay arriving for same memory: one wins, audit chain shows both attempts with last-write-wins semantics.

## E2E (`scripts/e2e_overhaul/learn_curate.sh` G9 block)

1. Workflow-driven promotion: open workflow → ee remember at working level → close workflow → assert promotion to episodic.
2. Curate-driven promotion: ee learn agenda → curate apply → assert procedural creation.
3. Harmful-feedback demotion: ee outcome <procedural_id> --signal harmful (3x) → assert demotion to semantic.
4. Decay-driven tombstoning: synthesize a working memory with last_accessed_at 14 days ago → run `ee maintenance run l3-decay` → assert tombstoned.

## Logging event

```json
{
  "schema": "ee.test_event.v1",
  "kind": "level_transition",
  "memory_id": "<id>",
  "prev_level": "...",
  "new_level": "...",
  "reason": "<enum>",
  "automatic": true|false,
  "evidence_refs": [...],
  "elapsed_ms": <float>,
  "audit_row_id": "<id>"
}
```

## Failure-mode fixtures (J6)

- `tests/fixtures/failure_modes/level_transition_tombstoned_rejected.json`
- `tests/fixtures/failure_modes/level_transition_requires_evidence.json`
- `tests/fixtures/failure_modes/level_transition_concurrent_conflict.json`

## Acceptance gate

- All 48 unit-test rows pass + 5 edge cases.
- E2E exercises all 4 transition paths.
- Audit chain row present for every transition (no silent demotion).
- J6 fixtures land + validator passes.

title: Output rendering: minimal markdown escapes, contiguous numbering, tested renderer
description:
# EPIC H — Output rendering

## The problem (with evidence)

`ee context "prepare release v0.2.0" --format markdown` output:

```
# Context Pack: prepare release v0\.2\.0

**Profile:** balanced | **Budget:** 310/1500 tokens
...
### 1. mem\_01KR9VVVWSE8SBH9RR7M376NEG (17 tokens)

\`\`\`
Run cargo fmt --check before cutting any release tag; CI rejects unformatted code.
\`\`\`
```

Two structural problems and one content problem:

**H1 — Over-escaped output.** Every `.` after a digit is escaped to `\.`. Every backtick in inline code is `\``. Every `_` in IDs is `\_`. CommonMark does NOT require this escaping in body text — version numbers and identifiers do not need escapes; only delimiter chars at the *start* of a potential markdown construct do. The current renderer is implementing "escape everything that could possibly be special" rather than "escape what the spec requires for this context".

**H2 — No tested CommonMark renderer.** Custom escaping rolled by hand. A round-trip test against `pulldown_cmark` would catch this in 5 lines.

**H3 — Non-monotonic numbering.** After MMR filtering drops items 2, 3, 5, 6, the rendered list shows `### 1.` then `### 4.` then `### 7.`. Reads like data was deleted. The `rank` field in JSON should preserve original rank, but in markdown the numbering should be 1..N over what was actually emitted.

Compound effect: the markdown body is what an agent prepends to its LLM prompt. Over-escaped text feeds the LLM noise (`v0\.2\.0` is two tokens worse than `v0.2.0`). Non-monotonic numbering makes the LLM think it's seeing a partial extract.

## Why agent-first

The markdown render IS the prompt fragment. An LLM tokenizer will treat `v0\.2\.0` and `v0.2.0` as different sequences. Beyond token cost, the visual noise reduces the LLM's confidence in the structure.

## Design considerations

- **Spec-minimal escape policy:** escape characters ONLY when they would otherwise be interpreted as a markdown construct in the current context. Body text: no escaping needed except for literal backticks inside inline code (which should use a longer-backtick fence anyway). Use `pulldown_cmark` round-trip as the oracle: render → parse → re-render, output is stable when escapes are minimal.
- **Renderer choice:** swap the hand-rolled renderer for one that takes a structured pack tree and emits markdown. Candidates:
  - Build it on `pulldown_cmark` events
  - Use `markdown-rs` if it's lighter
  - Continue hand-rolled but with the spec-minimal rule enforced by tests
- **Renumber post-filter:** in the rendered markdown, items are 1..N in the order they appear. JSON keeps `rank` as the original. Add `displayIndex: N` in JSON for callers that want to correlate the two.

## Tasks under this epic

- H1: Spec-minimal markdown escape policy (P2)
- H2: Round-trip test against `pulldown_cmark` (P3)
- H3: Renumber items 1..N in markdown render (depends on A3 / why-text rewrite for clean output) (P3)

## Dependencies

- H1 independent
- H2 depends on H1 (test catches new policy)
- H3 partially depends on A1 (item list canonicalization) — only need A1's structure decision, not its full implementation

## Acceptance gate

- Re-running `ee context "prepare release v0.2.0" --format markdown` produces `# Context Pack: prepare release v0.2.0` (no escapes).
- `pulldown_cmark::Parser::new(rendered).into_iter()` does not produce escape characters as text events.
- Item numbering in markdown is contiguous 1..N.
- Goldens under `tests/snapshots/markdown_render_clean.snap`.

## Out of scope

- Theming, ANSI color, terminal-specific rendering. Markdown should be plain CommonMark — host environments style it themselves.

title: H1: Spec-minimal markdown escape policy (current escapes 'v0\.2\.0' and 'mem\_01KR...' unnecessarily)
description:
# H1 — Spec-minimal markdown escape policy

## Evidence

`ee context "prepare release v0.2.0" --format markdown` produces:

```
# Context Pack: prepare release v0\.2\.0
### 1. mem\_01KR9VVVWSE8SBH9RR7M376NEG (17 tokens)
**Why:** Deterministic retrieval explanation for query \`prepare release v0\.2\.0\`...
```

Every `.` is escaped (`v0\.2\.0`), every `_` inside an ID is escaped (`mem\_01KR9V...`), every backtick is escaped (`\``). CommonMark does NOT require escaping `.` after a digit or `_` inside a word — those are not markdown constructs in those contexts.

Cost: ~30 extra escape characters per pack item × 13 items = ~400 extra characters of pure noise per pack. The LLM tokenizer sees `v0\.2\.0` as a different sequence than `v0.2.0`.

## Acceptance

Replace the current escape policy with the CommonMark minimal:

| Character | Escape when... | Don't escape otherwise |
|---|---|---|
| `\` | Always | — |
| `` ` `` | Inside paragraph text (potential code-span start) | Inside fenced code block |
| `*`, `_` | Adjacent to a word boundary in body text (potential emphasis) | Inside identifiers like `mem_01ABC` where surrounding chars are alphanumeric |
| `#` | At start of line (potential heading) | Mid-line |
| `[`, `]` | Potential link/footnote | Always-safe in body text otherwise |
| `<` | Potential HTML tag/autolink | When not followed by a tag-shape |
| `.`, `(`, `)`, `!`, `>` | Almost never (only in specific list/quote contexts) | Default: no escape |

Strategy: implement a context-aware escaper that walks the markdown tree and emits escapes only where the parser would otherwise interpret the character as syntax.

## Design considerations

- **Round-trip oracle:** the test for "correct" is: render → parse with `pulldown_cmark` → re-render → output equals input. If a character can be omitted from escape without changing the parse, omit it.
- **Don't try to be cute about precedence rules.** CommonMark has documented escape requirements; follow them literally.
- **Special case for IDs:** `mem_01KR9V...` is one token to a tokenizer. Escaping `_` to `\_` splits it. Body text containing identifiers should pass through without escaping the underscore.

## Depends on

- nothing internal

## Blocks

- H2 (test infrastructure tests this)
- H3 (renumbering reads from the new renderer)
- D2 (JSON↔MD parity needs clean MD)
- A4 (pack.text quality depends on H1)

## Acceptance gate

`tests/markdown_render_minimal_escapes.rs` table-driven test:
- 50 input pack samples
- For each, render → parse with pulldown_cmark → verify no escape characters appear as text events
- Verify byte-for-byte stability under round-trip

Goldens under `tests/snapshots/markdown_render_clean.snap`.

## Token-cost target

A 13-item pack's rendered markdown drops by ~400 characters (~100 tokens for the LLM). Modest but pure savings.

# Design refinement — identifier-context detection

The escape policy needs to recognize when a character is inside an "identifier context" vs body text. Identifier context = a sequence of `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+` characters with no adjacent markdown construct triggers. In identifier context, NO escapes are applied even to chars like `_` that would otherwise need it.

## Identifier detection regex

```regex
\b[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_-]*\b
```

When a span matches, the renderer emits the span as-is. Examples:
- `mem_01KR9V` — identifier; no escape on `_`
- `v0.1.0` — multiple identifier-ish segments separated by `.`; the dots are literal in body text per the spec-minimal policy
- `policy.detector` — same — dots in body text are not list markers unless followed by space

## Context-aware escape rules

| Char | In identifier | In body text | At line start | Inside emphasis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `_` | no escape | escape only if adjacent to whitespace and likely to start emphasis | escape | escape outer pair |
| `.` | no escape | no escape (unless after digit at line start, which would be ordered-list marker) | escape if `\d+\.` | no escape |
| `#` | no escape | no escape | escape (heading start) | no escape |
| `` ` `` | escape (could split code span) | escape (could start code span) | escape | escape |
| `\` | escape always | escape always | escape always | escape always |
| `*` | escape (could start emphasis) | escape adjacent to word boundary | escape | escape outer pair |
| `[` `]` | no escape | escape if followed by `(` (potential link) | escape if start | no escape |

## Implementation

Single function `escape_in_context(text: &str, context: NodeContext) -> String` driven by the table. NodeContext enum: `Body`, `Heading`, `ListItem`, `Blockquote`, `TableCell`, `InlineCode`, `CodeBlock`.

## Test additions

- `tests/markdown_escape_table_driven.rs` — every cell in the table above has at least one fixture
- `tests/markdown_escape_identifier_context.rs` — known-identifier strings round-trip without escapes
close_reason: Rewrote src/output/markdown.rs::escape_text with context-aware policy: ASCII letters/digits + dots + underscores pass through unescaped in body text (CommonMark intra-word rule); list/heading markers only escape at line start; brackets always escape (link safety); backticks always escape (code span safety); HTML chars become entities. 20 new H1 tests pass + 11 existing escape tests still pass. Two adversarial-content tests updated to reflect new minimal escapes (security boundary still met). E2E: 'ee context prepare release v0.2.0 --format markdown' now emits '# Context Pack: prepare release v0.2.0' and 'mem_01KR9V...' identifiers unescaped.

title: H2: Round-trip test against pulldown_cmark as the oracle — fails CI on escape drift
description:
# H2 — Round-trip test against `pulldown_cmark` (or equivalent) as the oracle

## Why

Hand-rolled markdown escape policies drift. CI needs a fast, mechanical check that the rendered output is correctly escaped under the CommonMark spec.

## Acceptance

`tests/markdown_render_roundtrip.rs`:

```rust
fn roundtrip_stable(input_tree: PackTree) -> bool {
    let rendered = render_markdown(&input_tree);
    let parsed = parse_with_pulldown_cmark(&rendered);
    let re_rendered = render_from_parsed(&parsed);
    rendered == re_rendered
}
```

Apply to 100+ generated fixtures (pack outputs across multiple workspaces, sizes, languages). Run in CI.

Additionally: assert no escape character (`\\`) appears in `Text(...)` events from pulldown_cmark — escapes should only appear adjacent to constructs that require them.

## Design considerations

- **`pulldown_cmark` is already a likely indirect dep.** Adding it as a dev-dep is cheap.
- **Don't ship pulldown_cmark in the main binary.** It's a test-only dependency.
- **CI inclusion:** add to `scripts/verify.sh` between the unit and golden test stages.

## Depends on

- H1 (policy must exist to test)

## Blocks

- nothing internal

## Out of scope

- Swapping `ee`'s markdown emitter to use pulldown_cmark for rendering. We're using it as an oracle, not as the renderer.

title: H3: Markdown renderer reads new short why field (A3 changes data; H3 ensures renderer follows)
description:
# H3 — Per-item `why` rewrite in markdown (depends on A3 source-of-truth)

## Why

This bead exists so the rendering layer has explicit responsibility for emitting the new short `why` field. A3 changes the data; H3 ensures the markdown renderer reads the new field.

## Acceptance

After A3 ships, the rendered markdown for a pack item looks like:

```markdown
### 1. mem_01KR9VVVWSE8SBH9RR7M376NEG (17 tokens)

```
Run cargo fmt --check before cutting any release tag; CI rejects unformatted code.
```

**Why:** matched 'release v0.2.0' via semantic-fast (relevance 0.149); diversity slot: cargo rules

**Trust:** `human_explicit` / `authoritative`

**Provenance:** `ee-mem://mem_01KR9VVVWSE8SBH9RR7M376NEG`
```

Not:
```markdown
**Why:** Deterministic retrieval explanation for query `prepare release v0.2.0`: source=memory search_source=semantic_fast; score_components=[relevance=unit_score(search_hit.score) with search_hit.score=0.1491, utility=unit_score(memory.utility) with memory.utility=0.5000]; formula=unit_score(field)=clamp(field, 0.0, 1.0) for finite fields, otherwise 0.0; inputs are stored memory/link fields and the explicit search hit, not agent reasoning.
```

## Design considerations

- **Renderer reads `items[].why`** (post-A3, the 1-line form). No transformation in the renderer.
- **Algorithm meta** (the formula) is no longer per-item — render it once at the bottom of the pack as a `## Algorithm` section or HTML comment.

## Depends on

- A3 (data source)
- H1 (clean escapes)
- A7 (renumbering — both touch the same renderer)

## Blocks

- nothing internal
close_reason: Already satisfied by A3 (commit 95614a6): the markdown renderer in src/output/mod.rs reads item.why directly via markdown::escape_text(&item.why), so rewriting the why-text in A3 immediately propagated to the rendered output. E2E verified: '**Why:** matched ...query... via ...source... (relevance ..., utility ...)' renders in markdown for every pack item. No additional renderer work required for H3.

title: Agent triad design spike: ee pack / ee note / ee why as canonical agent surface
description:
# EPIC I — Agent triad (design spike)

## What this explores

Could ee's agent-facing surface collapse to **three commands**?

```bash
ee pack "<task>"    # context pack, ready-to-prepend
ee note "<text>"    # remember; auto-tag + auto-link
ee why <id>         # full provenance + scoring
```

Everything else (init, doctor, status, learn, curate, graph, import, export, memory list/show/link/tags, capabilities, hooks…) stays available but moves to a "support commands" namespace that humans and tooling reach for but agents rarely do.

## Why explore this

The walkthrough surfaced ~40 commands in `ee --help`. An agent picks at most 5 of them in a typical workflow. The other 35 are noise in the agent's tool-selection prompt. If the agent triad covers the common path, the cognitive load drops dramatically.

`ee pack` = the merged `context` + `search` (search is implicit; pack runs the search).
`ee note` = `remember` with smart defaults (level/kind inferred from content + sentinel words; tags auto-suggested; auto-link to last accessed memories within workflow).
`ee why` = `why` + `memory show` + `memory history` + `memory link list` (everything an agent needs to *audit* a memory in one shot).

## Why this is a spike, not a feature

The other 8 epics (A–H) are concrete, well-scoped fixes. This is a redesign of the CLI namespace. Before committing:
1. Prototype `ee pack` and `ee note` as thin wrappers calling the existing core.
2. Run them through the same 2026-05-10 walkthrough.
3. Decide: does the triad cover ≥ 90% of agent calls? If yes, promote to a real epic. If no, keep the verbose surface and just polish the agent shortcuts (F2).

## Tasks under this epic

- I1: Prototype `ee pack` / `ee note` / `ee why` as thin wrappers; agent-run them against the 2026-05-10 corpus (P3)
- I2: Compatibility plan: which verbose commands stay, which alias under triad, which deprecate (P3)

## Dependencies

- I1 effectively depends on F2 (top-level aliases) being clear about argument-shape routing
- I2 depends on I1 outcome

## Acceptance gate

The spike outputs a written recommendation (could be a follow-up bead description, or a comment on this one): "promote to feature epic" vs "drop, fold the useful bits into F2/A".

## Out of scope

- Actually deprecating the verbose surface. That's a separate, larger conversation. This spike answers "is it worth doing at all?"
notes: Closed 2026-05-13: I1/I2/I3 are closed. Spike outcome artifact reports promote_to_epic with coverage=1.0, sloc_reduction=0.4007, inference_precision=1.0, inference_recall=1.0, pack_hash_parity=true, discoverability_pass=true. Follow-up implementation epic filed as bd-17c65.15.
close_reason: Design spike complete: triad outcome promoted and follow-up epic bd-17c65.15 filed.

title: I1: Prototype ee pack / ee note / ee why as thin wrappers; verify against 2026-05-10 corpus
description:
# I1 — Prototype `ee pack` / `ee note` / `ee why` as thin wrappers; verify against 2026-05-10 corpus

## Why

The CLI currently has 40+ commands. An agent uses 5 in a typical session. Could the agent-facing API be three commands, with the other 35 demoted to "support" surfaces?

This bead is a SPIKE — design exploration to decide if the triad is worth promoting to a real feature epic.

## Acceptance

Three thin wrapper commands shipped behind a `--experimental-triad` flag (or hidden subcommand `ee triad`):

**`ee pack "<task>"`** = current `ee context` with smart defaults:
- Reads workspace config for token budget, profile
- Renders both JSON and markdown by default (`pack.text` always present per A4)
- Implicitly runs search; no separate `ee search` needed for the common path

**`ee note "<text>"`** = current `ee remember` with smart inference:
- Level inferred from content: imperative + "must"/"always"/"never" → procedural/rule; past tense + specific date → episodic/event; descriptive noun phrase → semantic/fact; problem statement → episodic/failure
- Tags auto-suggested from content (TF-IDF against existing tags); user can accept/override
- Auto-link to last accessed memory within current workflow

**`ee why <id>`** = current `ee why` PLUS:
- `memory show` data (storage facts)
- `memory history` data (audit timeline)
- `memory link list` for the ID (relationships)

All three wrappers call into the existing core APIs; no new core logic.

## Design considerations

- **Smart inference must be optional.** `ee note --level <x>` overrides inference. Same for tags. The wrapper must never *silently* change semantic meaning.
- **Track inference accuracy:** wrapper logs (in audit) the inference decision so we can measure how often users override. > 30% override rate means the inference is wrong; refine or drop.
- **Don't replace; ADD.** During the spike, all existing commands keep working. The triad is opt-in.
- **Test against the 2026-05-10 corpus.** Re-run the walking-skeleton walkthrough using only `ee init`, `ee note`, `ee pack`, `ee why`. Measure: does the triad cover the common path? If yes (≥ 90% of agent calls fit), promote to feature epic. If no, keep verbose surface and just polish F2 aliases.

## Output of the spike

A written recommendation appended to this bead's description (via `br update`):
- "Promote to feature epic: triad covers X% of agent calls; promote with these refinements: ..."
- OR "Drop: triad doesn't cover X case; the gains aren't worth the redirect cost. Fold the inference helpers into ee remember as flags."

## Depends on

- F2 (argument-shape routing concept; triad is a related pattern)
- All A epic tasks (pack render must already be agent-clean)

## Blocks

- I2 (compatibility plan reads from this spike's output)

## Spike result — 2026-05-13

Promote to feature epic: triad covers 100% of the measured common path with `ee note`, `ee pack`, and `ee why`. The retained spike artifact is `tests/logs/active/triad_spike_outcome.json` and reports outcome `promote_to_epic`, coverage `1.0`, slocReduction `0.35`, inferencePrecision `1.0`, inferenceRecall `1.0`, packItemCount `9`, and no missing triad surface. Evidence also confirms `why` includes storage, links, and history.
design:
# Design refinement — spike outcome artifact

After running the spike, `scripts/e2e_overhaul/agent_triad.sh` MUST write `tests/logs/active/triad_spike_outcome.json` per the I3 schema. I2 reads this file as input.

## Decision routing

```
if coverage >= 0.90 AND sloc_reduction <= 0.60 AND inference_precision >= 0.80 AND inference_recall >= 0.80:
    outcome = "promote_to_epic"
elif coverage < 0.70 OR inference_precision < 0.60:
    outcome = "drop_triad"
else:
    outcome = "iterate"
```

`iterate` means: refine the wrappers based on observed failures, re-measure within this same bead, do not promote to a new epic yet.

## Wrapper implementation surface

`src/cli/triad.rs` (new file) with three command structs: `Pack`, `Note`, `Why`. Each constructs the appropriate verbose-command argument tree and dispatches into existing core APIs. NO new core logic.

## Hidden feature flag

Triad commands gated behind `--experimental-triad` flag or `EE_EXPERIMENTAL_TRIAD=1` env var (added to F5 registry) during the spike. Off by default. If I1 promotes, the flag becomes a no-op alias for "always on" and a deprecation warning is added if anyone tries to disable.

## What we do NOT measure

- **Performance:** triad wrappers add < 1ms of dispatch overhead; not worth measuring.
- **Token cost of error envelopes:** unchanged — wrappers call the same error paths.

## Anti-goals

- Making `ee note` use AI to infer level/kind. Inference is rule-based pattern matching; ee never calls an LLM internally.
- Making `ee pack` differ semantically from `ee context`. Wrapper must be byte-thin.
- Hiding the verbose commands. They stay; the triad is additive.

close_reason: Completed triad spike: e2e driver produced promote_to_epic outcome with 100% measured coverage; focused triad parser/inference tests passed.

title: I2: Compatibility plan — which verbose commands stay, alias, or deprecate after triad lands
description:
# I2 — Compatibility plan: which verbose commands stay, alias, or deprecate

## Why

If I1 spike concludes "promote to feature epic", we need a plan for the existing 40+ commands. Some should stay as alternatives (debug, audit), some should alias to triad subcommands, some should deprecate.

## Acceptance

A document `docs/triad_compat_plan.md` listing every existing command in one of three columns:

| Command | Disposition |
|---|---|
| `ee context "<q>"` | aliased: alias for `ee pack` |
| `ee remember "<t>"` | aliased: alias for `ee note` (no inference applied to preserve current contract) |
| `ee search "<q>"` | kept: explicit fine-grained search remains useful |
| `ee why <id>` | merged: same shape, just adds adjacent data |
| `ee memory show <id>` | kept: detail view |
| `ee doctor` | kept: debug surface |
| `ee init` | kept: setup |
| ... | ... |

For each "aliased" entry: when the alias is invoked, emit `degraded.deprecated_alias` with a pointer to the new triad command.

## Design considerations

- **No deletion in this milestone.** AGENTS.md "no backwards compatibility" applies to APIs, but for CLI surfaces a soft-deprecation period is reasonable: keep old commands, surface the deprecation, let users migrate.
- **Deprecation timeline:** N+2 milestones from now. If users complain, extend.

## Depends on

- I1 (spike outcome)

## Blocks

- nothing internal
notes: Completed 2026-05-13: added docs/triad_compat_plan.md with dispositions for every current top-level command and explicit deprecated_alias behavior for context/remember. Added tests/triad_compat_plan_contract.rs so future top-level commands must be represented in the plan.
close_reason: Added triad compatibility plan and contract test covering all top-level commands.

title: I3: Quantitative success criteria for the agent triad spike (coverage, inference accuracy, decision rule)
description:
# I3 — Quantitative success criteria for the agent triad spike

## Why

I1 outputs a "promote vs drop" recommendation but doesn't define what numbers justify the decision. Without quantitative criteria, the spike risks becoming a vibes-based opinion. Define the metrics up front.

## Acceptance

The spike (I1) must measure and report:

### Coverage metrics

- **Agent-call coverage:** fraction of typical-session ee invocations that the triad can satisfy. Target: ≥ 90%.
- **Common-path SLoC reduction:** average characters typed across a typical session, triad vs verbose. Target: triad ≤ 60% of verbose.

### Correctness metrics

- **Inference accuracy on `ee note`:** when the wrapper infers level/kind from content, how often does the inference match what a human would have specified explicitly?
  - Measure against a labeled fixture (`tests/fixtures/note_inference_cases.jsonl`, 100+ examples).
  - Target: precision ≥ 80%, recall ≥ 80%.
- **Pack quality preservation:** for the 2026-05-10 corpus, `ee pack "<query>"` and `ee context "<query>"` produce packs with the same `pack.hash`. (They should — the wrapper is thin.) If they diverge, that's a bug.

### Cognitive load metrics (qualitative, structured)

- **Discoverability:** a fresh agent invocation, given only `ee --help` output, should be able to use `ee note`, `ee pack`, `ee why` correctly within 3 sample tasks. Measure by re-running the 2026-05-10 walkthrough with the triad-only constraint.

### Decision rule

After running the spike, the recommendation is one of:

```jsonc
{
  "outcome": "promote_to_epic" | "drop_triad" | "iterate",
  "metrics": {
    "coverage": 0.95,
    "sloc_reduction": 0.55,
    "inference_precision": 0.82,
    "inference_recall": 0.78,
    "pack_hash_parity": true,
    "discoverability_pass": true
  },
  "promote_conditions_met": ["coverage >= 0.90", "sloc_reduction <= 0.60", …],
  "promote_conditions_missed": [],
  "next_actions": "..."
}
```

`promote_to_epic` iff all coverage/correctness targets met. `drop_triad` iff coverage < 70% OR inference accuracy < 60%. `iterate` otherwise (refine the wrapper, re-measure).

## Design considerations

- **Pre-commit to the metric.** Don't move the goalposts after measuring. If the numbers don't meet the bar, the answer is drop or iterate, not "well, qualitatively it felt better".
- **Compare apples-to-apples:** the verbose-baseline session uses the SAME tasks as the triad-baseline; only the command vocabulary changes.

## Depends on

- I1 (spike must run to produce the numbers)

## Blocks

- I2 (compatibility plan reads from the I3 outcome)

## Test plan

- **Unit:** `tests/agent_triad_inference_acc.rs` against the labeled inference fixture
- **E2E:** `scripts/e2e_overhaul/agent_triad.sh` runs the 2026-05-10 walkthrough twice (verbose, triad), logs every command call, computes coverage/sloc metrics
- **Logging:** per-call `{command_kind, verbose_or_triad, sloc, succeeded}` event; spike outcome written to `tests/logs/active/triad_spike_outcome.json`
notes: Completed 2026-05-13: added tests/fixtures/note_inference_cases.jsonl with 104 labeled cases and tests/agent_triad_inference_acc.rs. Updated scripts/e2e_overhaul/agent_triad.sh to compute coverage, typed-character reduction, pack-hash parity, discoverability, promote condition lists, and per-call metric events. Latest retained artifact tests/logs/active/triad_spike_outcome.json reports outcome=promote_to_epic, coverage=1.0, sloc_reduction=0.4007, inference_precision=1.0, inference_recall=1.0, pack_hash_parity=true, discoverability_pass=true.

title: [process] Closure linter: forbid abstention-as-implementation closures
description:
## Background

Counterpart to the bead-taxonomy bead. The taxonomy is policy; this is enforcement. Without enforcement, `honesty-only` vs `implements-surface:<name>` is just a naming convention that the swarm can ignore.

## What this bead does

Adds a CI check (a Rust binary in `tools/` or a shell script in `scripts/`) that runs on every PR and on push to main:

1. Walks every bead closed in the last N commits (or every bead with status=closed if running in audit mode).
2. For each `implements-surface:<name>` bead:
   - Reject the closure if `close_reason` matches the regex: `(abstain|unavailable|degraded|stub|placeholder|removed simulation|honest empty|conservative abstention)`.
   - Reject the closure if a `<NAME>_UNAVAILABLE_CODE` constant still exists in src/cli/mod.rs for the named surface.
   - Reject the closure if no golden snapshot exists at `tests/golden/<surface>.snap`.
3. For each `honesty-only` bead:
   - Require a sibling `implements-surface:<same-name>` bead exists in the open queue (not closed, not deleted).
4. Report a summary table: bead ID, label, surface, blocking reason.

## Why this is wave-0 and blocks everything

This is the structural fix that prevents the dishonest-closure pattern from recurring. Every implements-surface bead in CLOSE_THE_GAP_PLAN depends on this gate being live before the bead can be claimed.

## Wiring

Add as the first stage of `scripts/verify.sh` (after forbidden-deps audit) so it runs locally before commit. Add to GitHub Actions on every PR. Failure exits non-zero with a JSON report at .closure-lint-report.json.
close_reason: Implemented closure linter enforcement for abstention closures, unavailable constants, golden snapshots, verify wiring, and PR/main CI.

title: [guard] Prevent future verification baseline drift from becoming invisible
description:
Background: once the baseline is green, the project needs a lightweight guardrail so future agents cannot normalize red gates as permanent background noise. This should complement, not replace, existing closure-lint and verify.sh gates.

Scope:
- Add or update the smallest project-local guard that detects when known verification debt is being carried without an open Bead. Options include a docs/testing-strategy section plus a contract test, a verify.sh status summary check, or a br/bv hygiene check that asserts all failing gates named in docs have open blockers.
- The guard must be deterministic, local-first, and avoid network or paid API dependencies.
- It must not create noisy false positives for intentionally ignored or feature-gated tests; document any accepted exclusions.

Acceptance:
- A regression test or script check fails when a known red gate is documented without an open blocker, and passes for the final green baseline.
- docs/testing-strategy.md or an equivalent project doc explains the rule and how agents should file blockers.
- ./scripts/verify.sh or a focused test invokes the guard in a way that future CI can enforce.
- The close reason includes an example failure and the passing command.

title: [perf] Index status check on every search adds latency
description:
**File:** src/core/search.rs:848, src/core/search.rs:900-921

**Bottleneck:** Every `run_search` call executes `search_degradations` which calls `get_index_status`:

```rust
let degraded = search_degradations(options, &index_dir);  // line 848
```

This performs file I/O to check index staleness against database generation, even when the index is known to be fresh.

**Impact:** Adds 1-5ms per search call depending on I/O. With p50 target of 38ms, this is ~5-13% overhead.

**Fix options:**
1. **Cache index status:** Store generation check result with short TTL (e.g., 1 second)
2. **Lazy check:** Only check staleness if results are empty or on explicit flag
3. **Background refresh:** Move staleness detection to a background job that updates a flag

**Benchmark baseline:** Search p50 38ms, p99 110ms per plan §28.

**Note:** The degradation info is useful for diagnostics but not critical for search correctness. Consider making it opt-in via `--check-staleness` flag.
close_reason: Implemented short-TTL process-local cache for search index status checks in fa2f708c; focused RCH regression core::search::tests::search_degradations_reuse_index_status_within_ttl passed, rustfmt --check and git diff --check passed on src/core/search.rs.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Plan §12.2 specifies the SQL transition:
```
UPDATE memories SET level = 'EPISODIC', ttl_seconds = NULL, expires_at = NULL, updated_at = ?
WHERE workflow_id = ? AND level = 'WORKING' AND (access_count >= 2 OR importance >= 0.5);
```
The trigger is either explicit `ee workflow close <id>` or TTL expiry. Searched src/cli/mod.rs: no Command::Workflow, no WorkflowCommand, no fn handle_workflow_close. Searched src/core/: no level == Working transition logic that fires on workflow boundary.

Concrete impact: every `ee remember --level working` row stays WORKING forever or expires via TTL. The only path to Episodic today is to write `--level episodic` directly, bypassing the lifecycle entirely. Walking-skeleton North Star scenarios 1, 3, 4 implicitly assume Episodic memories accumulate over time from working sessions — they cannot.

Fix scope:
1. Add Command::Workflow with subcommands: Close { workflow_id, --json }, List, Show
2. handle_workflow_close: lock workspace → execute the §12.2 UPDATE → audit_log entry per affected row → return promoted_count + expired_count
3. Wire into ee remember --workflow <id> (separate bead rboz)
4. Add deterministic e2e test: remember(--level working --workflow X) → workflow close X → memory show should report level=Episodic
5. Optional: extend ee status --json to surface open workflow count and oldest-open-since

title: EE-125: Implement document builder for sessions
description:
Source plan item: EE-125 from the `Search` backlog.

Task: Implement document builder for sessions

Background and intent:
Build the Frankensearch-backed retrieval path with lexical fallback, canonical documents, indexing jobs, search command output, and score explanations.

Why this matters:
This bead contributes to the overarching goal of making `ee` a dependable local memory substrate for coding agents: useful before work, auditable after work, and safe under degraded conditions. The work should be implemented in the smallest coherent slice that fully satisfies the public contract implied by the title.

Dependency context:
Original plan dependencies: EE-122, EE-103. These are also represented as br dependency edges where the referenced bead exists.

Non-negotiable constraints:
Global implementation invariants for this task:
- Keep the CLI local-first, deterministic, and agent-native; stdout is data, stderr is diagnostics.
- Preserve the no-Tokio and no-rusqlite constraint unless a later ADR explicitly changes the architecture.
- Use SQLModel Rust plus FrankenSQLite for durable data; do not introduce a second storage stack.
- Use Asupersync for async edges and cancellation/budget behavior; do not smuggle in a Tokio executor.
- Keep JSON as the canonical public contract. TOON, Markdown, diagrams, and MCP are renderers or adapters over the same domain data.
- Mutating commands need dry-run/idempotency/audit behavior unless the task explicitly says otherwise.
- Add focused tests proportional to risk: unit tests for domain logic, contract/golden tests for public output, and integration/evaluation tests for cross-subsystem behavior.

## Acceptance Criteria

Detailed closure criteria are stored in this bead's structured acceptance_criteria field. Treat those criteria as part of this bead's implementation contract, including the comprehensive testing and logging requirements.
design:

- Command output must use the stable `ee.response.v1` envelope, preserve stdout/stderr isolation, and provide useful degraded-state metadata.

Implementation guidance:
- Read the surrounding modules and existing project conventions before editing.
- Prefer the planned crate boundaries from the comprehensive plan: CLI wiring in `ee-cli`, reusable domain/services in `ee-core`, models in `ee-models`, persistence in `ee-db`, output rendering in `ee-output`, and adapters in their own optional crates.
- Keep public contracts stable and versioned. Any data structure that leaves the process through CLI/MCP/hook/export should have a schema and at least one golden fixture.
- If a dependency or upstream Franken project is not ready, implement the smallest honest diagnostic/degraded path rather than faking behavior.
- Document any architectural exception with an ADR-oriented note and a verification hook.

title: [MEDIUM] recorder tail_recording_from_store passes u32::MAX to SQL LIMIT, ignoring caller --limit
description:
Repro:
  src/core/recorder.rs::tail_recording_from_store calls
  `conn.list_recorder_events_filtered(query_run_id, options.since.as_deref(),
   query_source, u32::MAX)` regardless of the caller-supplied
  `options.limit`. The caller's limit is only applied later in
  `tail_recording_from_events`, after every matching row in the
  recorder_events table has been fetched into memory.

  In a long-running recorder with N events that match the (run_id,
  since, source) filter, `ee recorder tail --limit 100` reads N rows
  from disk + N StoredRecorderEvent allocations + N
  RecorderEventSummary allocations, then truncates to 100.

Expected: the SQL `LIMIT` ?-binding tracks the caller's `--limit` flag
(plus a small head-room for filter terms applied client-side), so a
`--limit 100` call reads ~100 rows.

Actual: the SQL `LIMIT` is hard-coded to `u32::MAX` (~4.29 × 10^9).
For a workspace with millions of recorder events the call materializes
millions of rows for a "show me the latest 100" request.

Evidence-line:
  src/core/recorder.rs:1389-1395 (tail_recording_from_store, the
    `u32::MAX` constant)
  src/core/recorder.rs:1404-1416 (tail_recording_from_events,
    where options.limit is finally applied)
  src/db/mod.rs::list_recorder_events_filtered respects the limit;
    only the caller fails to pass it.

Suggested fix:
  - When the caller has client-side filter terms beyond run_id /
    since / source, fetch limit * SOME_HEADROOM (say 4×limit, capped
    at 10,000) so client-side filtering still has enough rows.
  - When there are no extra filter terms, pass `options.limit` straight
    through to the SQL LIMIT.
  - Add a test that asserts a 10,000-row recorder run with `--limit 50`
    reads at most ~250 rows from disk (use a small instrumented hook
    around list_recorder_events_filtered to count).

Severity: MEDIUM. CLI use is small today, but the recorder is one of
the surfaces designed to scale to millions of agent events. This
regression bites under exactly the load the surface is meant to handle.
close_reason: fixed

title: [release] Author install.sh per installer-workmanship spec
description:
## Background
README front-matter promises: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Dicklesworthstone/eidetic_engine_cli/main/install.sh | bash. The file does not exist in the repo. The single most user-facing promise is broken at face value.

## What ships
POSIX-shell install.sh at repo root, idempotent, following the installer-workmanship skill conventions:
1. Detects host OS + architecture (uname -s/-m), maps to one of: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, x86_64-unknown-linux-musl, aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-apple-darwin, x86_64-apple-darwin, x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.
2. Discovers latest release tag via GitHub API (with curl OR wget fallback) or accepts EE_VERSION env override.
3. Downloads ee-<target>.tar.xz + .sha256 + .sigstore.json from the release.
4. Verifies SHA256 (mandatory), verifies Sigstore bundle if cosign present (warns if not).
5. Extracts to ~/.local/bin/ee (or  if set), chmod +x, runs ee --version + ee doctor to confirm.
6. Prints PATH-export instructions if ~/.local/bin not in PATH.
7. Exits non-zero with clear message on any failure; never leaves partial state.

## Acceptance
- Running install.sh on a clean machine yields a working ee --version.
- Tampered tarball detected via SHA mismatch; install aborts.
- Idempotent: re-running upgrades or no-ops cleanly.
- Shellcheck passes.
- Smoke test in CI runs install.sh against a mock release server.
- Closure linter passes.
close_reason: Implemented: install.sh with platform detection, SHA256/Sigstore verification, idempotent install to ~/.local/bin

title: [idea-wizard] Epic: Deterministic pack-quality sentinel and behavioral drift gates
description:
Background:
Existing work already provides context pack quality metrics, deterministic eval fixtures, pack replay ledgers, pack diff, freshness reporting, and performance gates. What is still missing is a behavioral drift sentinel that answers a sharper question: for canonical agent tasks, did the pack select the evidence we expect, omit the evidence we expect, preserve provenance/redaction/degradation posture, and stay useful under lexical-only or stale-derived-asset conditions?

This epic is plan-space only until current pack replay/freshness work closes. It must build on existing `ee eval`, `ee context`, `ee pack`, pack replay ledgers, and fixture schemas. It must not invent a second evaluator, second retrieval stack, or subjective LLM judge.

Intended UX:
- `ee eval run --pack-quality --json [--scenario <id>]` or an equivalent eval-namespaced read-only surface runs deterministic pack-quality checks.
- The output is a stable `ee.eval.pack_quality_report.v1` response containing fixture IDs, command invocations, expected/actual selected memory IDs, omitted evidence, provenance density, degradation deltas, redaction status, pack hashes, ledger hashes, pass/fail status, and first-failure diagnosis.
- The report is suitable for CI and support-bundle inclusion, but the command itself remains read-only and local-first.

Out of scope:
- No LLM-as-judge scoring.
- No replacement for existing per-pack quality metrics.
- No custom retrieval or ranking algorithm.
- No daemon, web UI, or cloud service.

## Success Criteria

- A deterministic pack-quality sentinel can be run from the eval command family without daemon mode, network access, or hidden mutation.
- Canonical fixture tasks detect selected-memory drift, omitted critical evidence, degradation posture changes, redaction leaks, missing/malformed ledgers, and stale derived assets with stable machine-readable first-failure details.
- Reports reuse existing context/pack/eval/ledger services and include reproduction commands, pack hashes, ledger hashes, fixture IDs, and scenario IDs.
- Contract, golden, unit, and logged no-mock E2E coverage prove stdout discipline, deterministic ordering, redaction safety, and degraded-mode honesty.
- Documentation explains how this sentinel differs from per-pack quality metrics, pack diff, performance benchmarks, and support bundles.

title: Meta-doc: docs/volatile_field_registry.md — single source for J7 strip-field semantics
description:
# Meta-doc: volatile field registry

## Why

Multiple beads reference \"J7 _strip_fields\" for determinism comparisons:
- D6 (renderers; bd-17c65.4.6)
- D8 (parity matrix; bd-17c65.4.9)
- M3 (handoff round-trip; bd-17c65.13.4)
- N15.4 (lab replay; bd-17c65.14.15.5)
- S7 (swarm scale; bd-1zb7k.8)
- bd-xzuma (pack hash; via the J7 unit test it composes with)

Each bead currently restates the strip list ad-hoc. If the list changes in one bead's notes, the others drift. This bead pins ONE registry that every bead references.

## Acceptance

### File: docs/volatile_field_registry.md

Markdown table (canonical):

| Field path                        | Reason for volatility                     | Introduced in version | Notes                                |
|-----------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|-----------------------|--------------------------------------|
| generatedAt / generated_at        | wall-clock timestamp                       | v0.1                  | RFC 3339                              |
| last_accessed / last_accessed_at  | per-read update                            | v0.1                  | G8 audit trigger                      |
| last_used_at                      | per-read update                            | v0.1                  | same                                  |
| audit_ts                          | per-write timestamp                        | v0.1                  | audit chain                           |
| elapsedMs / elapsed_ms            | wall-clock elapsed                         | v0.1                  | perf-only                             |
| startedAt / started_at            | wall-clock start                           | v0.1                  | maintenance jobs                      |
| endedAt / ended_at                | wall-clock end                             | v0.1                  | maintenance jobs                      |
| ts / timestamp                    | generic wall-clock                         | v0.1                  | log envelopes                         |
| ee_binary_hash                    | per-build artifact hash                    | v0.1                  | included in status only               |
| databasePath / workspacePath      | absolute path (machine-dependent)          | v0.1                  | canonicalized but still env-dependent |
| indexDir                          | absolute path                              | v0.1                  | same                                  |

### File: src/obs/volatile_fields.rs

```rust
/// Canonical list of fields that legitimately vary between invocations
/// against the same workspace state. The J7 determinism harness strips
/// these before computing comparison hashes. Bead bd-NEW.
pub const VOLATILE_FIELD_NAMES: &[&str] = &[
    \"generatedAt\", \"generated_at\",
    \"last_accessed\", \"last_accessed_at\", \"last_used_at\",
    \"audit_ts\",
    \"elapsedMs\", \"elapsed_ms\",
    \"startedAt\", \"started_at\",
    \"endedAt\", \"ended_at\",
    \"ts\", \"timestamp\",
    \"ee_binary_hash\",
    \"databasePath\", \"workspacePath\", \"indexDir\",
];

pub fn strip_volatile_fields(value: &mut serde_json::Value) { ... }
```

scripts/e2e_overhaul/determinism.sh uses the same list via a sourced bash variable.

### Test: tests/volatile_field_registry_consistency_test.rs

Asserts that:
1. The Rust constant `VOLATILE_FIELD_NAMES` matches the bash list literal in `scripts/e2e_overhaul/determinism.sh`.
2. The markdown table at `docs/volatile_field_registry.md` mentions every field name in the Rust constant.
3. No bead body mentions a field that ISN'T in the registry (grep test against tests/fixtures/failure_modes/, etc.).

If a new field is added to the registry, ALL THREE must update in lockstep.

### Logging event

The strip step itself emits one event per invocation:
```json
{
  \"schema\": \"ee.test_event.v1\",
  \"kind\": \"volatile_strip\",
  \"fields_stripped_count\": <usize>,
  \"fields_stripped\": [\"generatedAt\", ...],
  \"input_bytes\": <usize>,
  \"output_bytes\": <usize>
}
```

## Depends on

- J7 determinism harness (bd-17c65.10.7) — closed.

## Blocks

title: Epic: Swarm-scale responsiveness and resource-governance roadmap
description:
## Background
The project vision is a local-first memory substrate for coding agents, and the user explicitly wants it to be compelling for massive agent swarms on machines with 256GB+ RAM and 64+ CPU cores. The current backlog already covers the walking skeleton, implements-surface gaps, daemon, release, and baseline performance budgets. This epic captures the next layer: proving and improving behavior when many agent harnesses read context, write outcomes, import evidence, and rebuild derived indexes concurrently.

## Idea-wizard rationale
Phase 2 generated 30 possible improvements and winnowed to the strongest theme: swarm-scale responsiveness with resource governance. Phase 3 kept complementary ideas around benchmark fixtures, hotset prewarming, write coalescing, explainable profiling, and failure evidence. Phase 4 overlap check found related but narrower beads (`eidetic_engine_cli-htjd`, `eidetic_engine_cli-59dp`, `eidetic_engine_cli-9s0q`, recorder/support-bundle surfaces), so this epic is deliberately framed as an integration track that depends on those foundations instead of duplicating them.

## Goals
- Provide reproducible swarm-scale workloads that exercise many readers, serialized writers, index rebuilds, graph refreshes, and pack generation.
- Make latency and memory behavior explainable enough for agents to diagnose regressions without a profiler first.
- Keep the product boundary intact: `ee` remains a CLI-first memory substrate, not an agent harness or scheduler.
- Use Frankensearch, FrankenSQLite/SQLModel, FrankenNetworkX, and Asupersync correctly rather than adding custom search, DB, graph, or runtime stacks.

## Non-goals
- No daemon requirement for ordinary commands.
- No custom BM25/vector/RRF implementation.
- No web UI or central orchestration service.
- No replacement for Agent Mail, Beads, Codex, Claude Code, or other harnesses.

## Closure evidence
This epic closes only when its child beads provide scale fixtures, benchmark gates, cache/write-governance implementation beads, and logged E2E coverage with clear resource metrics. Closure requires `bv --robot-insights` showing no dependency cycles and the relevant Cargo/script gates passing through `rch`.
close_reason: All child beads closed: ADR (fcq1.8), workload model (fcq1.1), benchmark harness (fcq1.2), cache/prewarm (fcq1.3), write spool (fcq1.4), explain-plan (fcq1.5), E2E contention suite (fcq1.6), support bundle (fcq1.7), plus oxt2 Appendix C parity scenario. Swarm-scale responsiveness and resource-governance roadmap complete.

title: EE-CURATE-TTL-001: Add curation candidate TTL, auto-disposition, and backlog health in ee status
description:
Make the curation candidate queue an active system instead of a write-only backlog: TTL, auto-disposition, and a backlog health metric in `ee status`.

Background:
F7 (systems-thinking) and F4 (failure mode) flagged that the curation pipeline as drafted in the bead set has a structural attractor: agents propose candidates faster than humans review them, the queue grows without bound, semantic and procedural memory layers starve of new high-confidence rules, and the user eventually stops trusting the curation surface. EE-180 (curation_candidates table), EE-181 (candidate validation), EE-183/184/185 (`ee curate candidates/validate/apply`), EE-301 (review queue states), and EE-302 (accept/reject/snooze/merge) collectively implement the surface but assume an active human reviewer. Nothing in the bead set defines what happens to a candidate that has been pending for 14, 30, or 90 days; nothing surfaces the backlog health to the agent in `ee status`; nothing triggers the steward to escalate.

Intended scope:
This bead adds three things on top of the existing curation surface, not a parallel one:
- A configurable TTL per candidate state (proposed, validated, snoozed) with deterministic auto-disposition rules: proposed candidates older than TTL with no outcome events auto-snooze; validated candidates older than TTL with high evidence auto-promote (configurable, default off); harmful-flagged candidates older than TTL escalate.
- A `ee status --json` `curation_health` block: counts per state, oldest pending age, mean review latency, escalations open, and the next deterministic action the steward will take.
- A `ee curate disposition --json` command that explains every auto-disposition decision (dry-run by default) and produces an audit entry on apply.

It does not change the basic propose/validate/apply lifecycle. It closes the loop so the curation backlog never silently rots.

Why this matters:
The premise of EE is that procedural memory grows in trustworthiness over time. The curation backlog is the single chokepoint between agent assertion and durable memory. If it is unbounded, the system trends toward "everything is an agent_assertion" and the value of trust classes erodes. F7 modeled this as a positive feedback loop with an obvious dead-loop attractor; this bead breaks the loop with a deterministic, auditable steward action.

Dependency intent:
This bead must wait for the curation candidate schema and validation surfaces, the review queue state/command surface, the trust taxonomy ADR and enum, the config parser/merge layer, `ee status --json`, the steward worker, the operation/audit log path, and the multi-agent concurrent-writer contract. That dependency shape is deliberate: TTL disposition is a high-leverage quality layer, but it should not force earlier curation tasks to guess about trust semantics, policy storage, audit durability, or lock behavior.

## Acceptance Criteria

Detailed closure criteria are stored in this bead's structured acceptance_criteria field. Treat those criteria as part of this bead's implementation contract, including the TTL policy, curation_health status block, disposition command, audit behavior, frozen-time tests, property tests, concurrency fixture, and e2e logging requirements.
design:
Recommended design:
- Implement the TTL policy as a small typed table (state, action, threshold_seconds, requires_evidence, requires_no_harmful_within) so changes are configuration, not code. Seed default rows in the migration.
- Reuse the existing audit_log shape; do not invent a parallel audit. Add a `event_kind = curation_disposition` discriminator with the policy_id and the deterministic rule fingerprint.
- Run the disposition pass as part of the existing steward worker (Epic: Steward) so it composes with cancellation, budgets, and the optional daemon. In CLI-only mode, run it on `ee curate disposition --apply` and on `ee maintenance` if that umbrella exists.
- Make the curation_health block in `ee status --json` versioned (`schema: ee.status.v<N>`) so consumers can pin. Keep the field present but empty on a fresh workspace; do not omit it.
- Auto-promote stays disabled by default behind config flag `curation.auto_promote = false`. The bead must ship the gate and the disabled default; users opt in. A deterministic experiment harness (EE-USR-004 path) can flip it later.
- Harmful escalation surfaces through the existing `degraded` array; do not invent a new error path. The escalation clears when the human runs `ee curate apply <id>` or `ee curate reject <id>` and the audit cites the original escalation event.
- Composition: depends on EE-180 (table) and EE-181 (validation); depends on EE-201 (steward module) and EE-260 (trust class enum) so dispositions can produce the right trust transitions. Blocks the future Epic: Steward closure gate.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

Acceptance criteria:
- The curation_candidates schema gains TTL-relevant fields (state_entered_at, last_action_at, ttl_policy_id) without breaking existing rows; migration is idempotent and reversible.
- A new ttl_policy table (or config-resident table) stores per-state TTLs and per-state auto-disposition actions. Defaults: proposed=14d->snoozed, validated=30d->prompt-promote, snoozed=90d->retire-with-audit, harmful=7d->escalate. All defaults are overridable via config and visible through `ee config show --json`.
- The steward gets a deterministic curation_disposition job that runs on schedule and on `ee curate disposition --apply`. Every state transition emits an audit log entry citing the candidate id, prior state, new state, ttl_policy_id, ttl_elapsed_ms, evidence_count, and the deterministic rule that fired.
- `ee status --json` includes a stable curation_health block: per-state counts, oldest pending age in days, mean review latency in days, open escalations, and the next deterministic action with its scheduled time.
- `ee curate disposition --json --dry-run` (default) lists every disposition decision with the rule applied, the evidence evaluated, and the planned audit entry. `--apply` runs the deterministic transitions and emits stable JSON for each.
- Auto-promote is gated: it only fires when (a) the candidate has at least N=2 helpful outcomes from distinct sessions, (b) no harmful outcome inside the decay window, (c) the deterministic specificity check passes (links to EE-CURATE-SPEC-001 if added). Otherwise auto-promote becomes auto-prompt (a read-only notice on next `ee status`).
- Harmful candidates older than the harmful TTL escalate by surfacing a stable `degraded` array entry on every `ee status` and a non-zero exit on `ee doctor`. Escalations clear when the human resolves them.
- All TTL math uses deterministic UTC timestamps and is testable with frozen time.

Testing and logging requirements:
- Unit tests cover deterministic TTL evaluation under frozen time, per-state policy lookup, edge cases at boundary (TTL minus 1s, TTL exactly, TTL plus 1s), missing fields, and migration of legacy rows without TTL data.
- Integration tests using a real ee binary seed candidates at known ages, run `ee curate disposition --json --dry-run`, assert the planned transitions, run `--apply`, assert audit log shape, then run a second dry-run to assert idempotency (no further transitions).
- Property tests assert that auto-promote never bypasses the dual-outcome and decay-window gates and that auto-snooze never deletes evidence.
- Adversarial fixtures cover: candidates aged into the future (clock drift), candidates with corrupt or missing audit history, escalations on a candidate whose underlying memory has been retired, and concurrent dispositions by two writers (must compose with EE-CONC-001 advisory lock).
- E2E logs capture command, cwd/workspace, sanitized environment, elapsed time, exit code, stdout/stderr artifact paths, audit log diff, schema validation status, and a first-failure diagnosis.
- Stdout assertions prove only machine data leaves stdout for `ee status --json`, `ee curate disposition --json`, and `ee config show --json`.
- Closeout evidence cites integration fixture IDs, the audit log delta, the policy table contents, and the verification commands a future agent would run.
notes: Closes the F7 dead-loop attractor: unbounded curation backlog erodes the value of trust classes. Three-bead system (TTL + status block + disposition command) chosen over a single big change because each piece has a separate test surface and a separate release point. Default policy (14d/30d/90d/7d) chosen to match the README decay half-life of 60d.

title: EE-145: Implement redundancy control
description:
Source plan item: EE-145 from the `Context Packing` backlog.

Task: Implement redundancy control

Background and intent:
Make ee context the primary product surface: small, deterministic, explainable packs with sections, quotas, redundancy control, provenance, audit hashes, and why support.

Why this matters:
This bead contributes to the overarching goal of making `ee` a dependable local memory substrate for coding agents: useful before work, auditable after work, and safe under degraded conditions. The work should be implemented in the smallest coherent slice that fully satisfies the public contract implied by the title.

Dependency context:
Original plan dependencies: EE-144. These are also represented as br dependency edges where the referenced bead exists.

Non-negotiable constraints:
Global implementation invariants for this task:
- Keep the CLI local-first, deterministic, and agent-native; stdout is data, stderr is diagnostics.
- Preserve the no-Tokio and no-rusqlite constraint unless a later ADR explicitly changes the architecture.
- Use SQLModel Rust plus FrankenSQLite for durable data; do not introduce a second storage stack.
- Use Asupersync for async edges and cancellation/budget behavior; do not smuggle in a Tokio executor.
- Keep JSON as the canonical public contract. TOON, Markdown, diagrams, and MCP are renderers or adapters over the same domain data.
- Mutating commands need dry-run/idempotency/audit behavior unless the task explicitly says otherwise.
- Add focused tests proportional to risk: unit tests for domain logic, contract/golden tests for public output, and integration/evaluation tests for cross-subsystem behavior.

## Acceptance Criteria

Detailed closure criteria are stored in this bead's structured acceptance_criteria field. Treat those criteria as part of this bead's implementation contract, including the comprehensive testing and logging requirements.
design:
Suggested design approach:
- Command output must use the stable `ee.response.v1` envelope, preserve stdout/stderr isolation, and provide useful degraded-state metadata.

Implementation guidance:
- Read the surrounding modules and existing project conventions before editing.
- Prefer the planned crate boundaries from the comprehensive plan: CLI wiring in `ee-cli`, reusable domain/services in `ee-core`, models in `ee-models`, persistence in `ee-db`, output rendering in `ee-output`, and adapters in their own optional crates.
- Keep public contracts stable and versioned. Any data structure that leaves the process through CLI/MCP/hook/export should have a schema and at least one golden fixture.
- If a dependency or upstream Franken project is not ready, implement the smallest honest diagnostic/degraded path rather than faking behavior.
- Document any architectural exception with an ADR-oriented note and a verification hook.
acceptance_criteria:

title: [perf-forensics][schema] Normalize performance artifact summaries
description:
## Background

The compare surface must consume multiple existing artifact families without parsing raw logs or secret-bearing data. A normalized summary schema keeps the comparison core deterministic and testable.

## Scope

Define `ee.perf.artifact_summary.v1` and related Rust domain types for redaction-safe summaries of benchmark reports, support-bundle manifests, explain-performance reports, profile evidence, cache reports, write queue reports, and swarm contention reports.

## Acceptance criteria

- Summary records include source path or artifact ID, source kind, source schema, content hash, profile, fixture tier, command family, metric map, degraded codes, redaction posture, and provenance for copied fields.
- Unsupported artifact kinds and schema versions produce stable degraded summaries rather than panics.
- Raw logs, raw memory text, query text, command output, host paths, and secrets are not copied into summaries.
- Deterministic ordering is defined for metrics, degradations, and provenance entries.
- Unit tests cover every accepted artifact class with synthetic inputs, missing optional fields, stale schema, tampered hash, and redaction uncertainty.
- Contract/golden fixture(s) freeze the summary JSON shape.

## Testing and logging

Use exact golden comparisons for deterministic fields and explicit volatility classification for timing/resource values. If the public schema registry is touched, add/update schema advertisement coverage. All Cargo verification must run through RCH.
