Added dependency shape: derived-asset store depends on freshness DAG; zero-copy output is related to schema consistency; optional explanation circuit breaker is related to current perf explain-latency work; verification normalizer is related to RCH clean-tree verification. Rejected duplicates already covered by existing beads: shard fan-out, read pool, L2 cache, EQL plan cache, audit MPSC lane, workspace hygiene, symbol graph, RCH topology, RCH clean-tree mode, swarm next-action planner, single-flight, hotset prewarm, QoS lanes, and broad graph feature work. Remaining children must stay additive and must not become replacement epics for those surfaces.

title: zero-copy response envelope renderer for hot agent JSON surfaces
description: Problem: high-frequency agent surfaces such as context, search, status, health, why, workspace hygiene, and perf commands often build serde_json Value trees before serialization. In 64-agent swarms this allocates and copies deterministic boilerplate for every call even when schemas and static fields are unchanged. Scope: add a typed response-envelope writer path that preserves ee.response.v2 and ee.error.v2 field order, supports compact and pretty modes where applicable, precomputes static schema fragments safely, and falls back to existing serde_json rendering for uncommon surfaces during rollout. Do not change public JSON semantics or bypass redaction. Distinguish from pack densification: this is output serialization machinery, not pack selection or pack shape. Required tests: golden parity for representative success and error envelopes, property coverage for stable field order, allocation or byte-count benchmark through RCH-only proof, and an e2e script with ee.test_event.v1 logs proving identical bytes for old and new renderers on fixed fixtures. Acceptance: selected hot surfaces produce byte-identical JSON or an explicitly version-bumped schema, allocation count or serialized latency is measurably lower, and the feature can be disabled by config or env registry without touching repo-local Cargo config.

title: content-addressed derived-asset store with safe cross-workspace reuse
description: Problem: graph snapshots, index manifests, algorithm witnesses, pack-cache entries, and restored backup-derived assets are rebuildable but large. Multiple workspaces and agents can produce identical or near-identical derived assets, yet current surfaces treat each workspace path as its own storage island. Scope: design and implement a content-addressed derived-asset store keyed by schema version, source manifest hash, config hash, binary capability hash, and asset body hash. Reuse must be read-only by default, with refcount or lease metadata, copy fallback where hardlinks are unsafe, and no automatic deletion. Distinguish from L2 pack cache and shard fan-out: this stores validated derived artifacts across workspaces, not live DB writes or single-command result caches. Required tests: unit tests for deterministic keys, contract tests for refcount and no-delete behavior, e2e using two temporary workspaces proving safe reuse without data leakage, backup and restore parity checks, and failure-mode fixtures for hash mismatch and schema mismatch. Acceptance: ee status or support bundle can report derived-asset reuse statistics, corrupted or stale assets fail closed and rebuild locally, and cleanup output only proposes safe human-reviewed actions.

title: derived-asset freshness DAG and invalidation planner
description: Problem: derived assets currently need scattered stale checks across search indexes, graph snapshots, algorithm result caches, pack caches, backups, and support bundles. Under swarm load this creates redundant rebuilds, false stale warnings, and hard-to-debug freshness gaps. Scope: introduce a deterministic derived-asset freshness DAG that maps each asset to source tables, config sections, binary feature flags, workspace identity, and input manifests. Commands ask the planner whether an asset is fresh, stale, missing, incompatible, or rebuild-needed, and receive stable repair actions. Distinguish from content-addressed storage: this bead defines the invalidation truth table and diagnostics, while reuse/storage is a separate child. Required tests: pure unit cases for dependency hashing, migration/config changes, feature-flag changes, and clock-independent ordering; contract tests for degraded codes and repair actions; e2e with generated DB mutations proving only affected assets invalidate; golden support-bundle output. Acceptance: at least search index, graph snapshot, and pack-cache freshness checks are routed through the planner, response degraded entries become more precise, and same DB plus config produces byte-identical freshness reports.

title: optional explanation latency circuit breaker for context and why
description: Problem: agent-facing context and why calls must stay responsive, but optional explanation work such as graph DNA, expensive neighborhood analysis, and provenance enrichment can dominate tail latency during bursts. Existing QoS and burst-admission beads protect broad lanes, but the command itself still needs a per-response way to spend budget on mandatory pack content before optional explanation detail. Scope: add a deterministic optional-work budget policy for context and why that classifies explanation components as required, useful, or deferrable. When budget is tight, the command returns the primary answer with structured degraded entries and a replayable follow-up command for omitted explanation detail. No daemon requirement and no silent mutation. Required tests: unit tests for budget classification and stable component order, golden context and why responses with omitted optional detail, e2e with synthetic slow graph fixtures, and perf evidence through RCH once topology is healthy. Acceptance: primary pack or why content is never delayed behind optional explanation beyond configured p95 budget, degradation is honest and actionable, and identical inputs plus budget produce byte-identical omission decisions.

title: verification evidence normalizer for RCH CI and closeout artifacts
description: Problem: agents paste RCH proof summaries, CI job output, verify script tails, command hashes, and caveats into Beads and Agent Mail in many shapes. Existing RCH and closeout work improves individual sources, but consumers still need to interpret heterogeneous proof evidence. Scope: add an ee verification evidence normalization surface that ingests existing RCH proof JSON, verify script logs, GitHub Actions job summaries, and static-check records into a single ee.verification_evidence.v1 envelope. The normalizer must be read-only, never run Cargo locally, preserve command hashes and source tree identity, classify environment blockers separately from code failures, and emit Beads-ready compact summaries without shell-dangerous command substitution text. Required tests: fixture parsers for RCH version-skew, path-dependency mismatch, CI success, CI failure, local static-only proof, and malformed logs; golden output; e2e with fake files; no network dependency in tests. Acceptance: completion-audit and support-bundle consumers can reference one evidence schema, Beads closeout comments can be generated from the normalized summary, and proof gaps are explicit rather than flattened into success or failure.

comments.text:
TopazPuma withdrawing claim on bd-1nxz4.5 at 2026-05-19T04:25Z without committing — duplication risk discovered, requires reframing.

## What I found

The repo already has a substantial verification-evidence ledger in `src/models/verification.rs` plus parsers in `src/core/verify.rs` and `src/core/swarm_next_action.rs`. Specifically:

- `pub const VERIFICATION_EVIDENCE_SCHEMA_V1: &str = "ee.verification.evidence.v1";` (note the **dot** between verification and evidence) at `src/models/verification.rs:15`.
- A rich `VerificationEvidenceRecord` type with `verification_id`, `gate_name`, `status` (VerificationStatus: Passed, Failed, Blocked, Interrupted, FallbackDetected, Unknown), `environment`, `offload` (VerificationOffload with RCH/required_remote/fallback_detected), `output_summary`, `artifacts`, and `producer` metadata.
- Sibling schemas: `ee.verification.run.v1`, `ee.verification.reuse_advisory.v1`, `ee.verification.broker_view.v1`, `ee.verification.closeout_capsule.v1`, `ee.verification.compile_blocker_cache.v1`, `ee.verification.compile_blocker_lookup.v1`.
- Tests covering this surface: `tests/verification_evidence_schema_unit.rs` (817 lines), `tests/verification_closure_guidance_unit.rs`, `tests/verification_ledger_lookup_unit.rs`.
- A `verifier_evidence_from_json(value: &Value)` parser in `src/core/swarm_next_action.rs:236` that already extracts first-error evidence from `ee.rch.verify.v1` proof JSON.

The bd-1nxz4.5 acceptance text asks for a single `ee.verification_evidence.v1` envelope (note the **underscore**), distinct schema id from the existing `ee.verification.evidence.v1` ledger. Building it as a parallel parser would create two `VERIFICATION_EVIDENCE_SCHEMA_V1` constants pointing at near-identical schema names, with overlapping intent (normalizing RCH/CI/verify-script proof) and only slightly different structure.

## What I built locally (uncommitted)

NEW files exist on disk in my checkout but were NOT committed:
- `src/obs/verification_evidence.rs` (with VerificationEvidence type, EvidenceSource/EvidenceStatus enums, parse_rch_verify, compact_summary, 13 inline tests).
- `docs/schemas/ee.verification_evidence.v1.json`.
- `tests/verification_evidence_parsers.rs` (8 fixture-driven tests).
- `tests/fixtures/verification_evidence/{rch_remote_pass,rch_path_dep_version_skew,rch_topology_refusal,rch_remote_compile_error,malformed_wrong_schema}.json`.

`src/obs/mod.rs` was restored to its pre-slice state. None of these are staged or committed.

Static checks did pass on the implementation (rustfmt, jq, git diff --check), and the design follows the swarm's narrow-additive slice pattern. The work is preserved on my checkout for whoever continues this bead.

## Recommended reframing options

1. **Integrate, don't duplicate**: redefine bd-1nxz4.5 as "extend `src/models/verification.rs` with parsers for RCH/CI/verify-script/static-check sources that emit existing `VerificationEvidenceRecord` rows." The schema name stays `ee.verification.evidence.v1`. My local code becomes a starting point but should be rewritten to map RCH proof JSON into the existing `VerificationEvidenceInput` shape with proper `VerificationStatus` (Blocked/Failed/Passed/FallbackDetected) and `VerificationOffload` population.
2. **Cleanly separate**: rename my schema to something that does not look like a near-duplicate (e.g. `ee.verification.proof_summary.v1`) and document distinguishability. Risk: still adds parallel constants and parsers without clearly subsuming the existing layer.
3. **Withdraw entirely**: the existing infrastructure plus `verifier_evidence_from_json` already covers most of what the bead asks for. The remaining gap (CI/GH Actions parsing, verify-script tail parsing, static-check ingestion, Beads-ready compact summary) can land directly as small additions to `src/models/verification.rs` under a new bead with a narrower title.

I am leaving bd-1nxz4.5 open with this comment so the bead owner (WildGlen / Jeff Emanuel) can pick a direction. No remote mutation, no file deletion, no destructive git action was performed; bd-2mey5 commits 8e5d7a0b, b879d11e, ec8e6c7f from earlier this swarm cycle are untouched.

— TopazPuma

title: [LOW] normalize_alias accepts multi-dot strings; looks_like_path then misroutes them to path resolution
description:
## Surface
Workspace alias / path classification (audit cycle 7, surface 4)

## Finding
src/core/workspace.rs:670-691 normalize_alias allows aliases that contain ASCII alphanumeric + '-', '_', '.' and rejects only the exact strings '.' and '..'. So:
- `...` (three dots) — accepted
- `..foo` — accepted
- `.bar.` — accepted
- `foo..` — accepted

src/core/workspace.rs:709-718 looks_like_path classifies a target string as a path (not alias) when it starts with '.', '~', or contains '/' or '\\'. So an alias accepted by normalize_alias like `..foo` is later treated by looks_like_path as a PATH (because it starts with '.').

That mismatch means a registered alias `..foo` becomes unreachable through the normal resolve path: `ee --workspace ..foo` is routed to path resolution, never alias lookup.

## Path traversal angle (cleared)
This is NOT a CVE-grade path traversal:
- ee never uses an alias as a filesystem path component — aliases are stored only as registry keys.
- Workspace paths come from --workspace flag or EE_WORKSPACE env, both user-controlled.
- normalize_lexical (src/core/workspace.rs:734) correctly handles `..` components when canonicalize() fails: components pop the path, and dangling `..` only persist when the input was a relative path that legitimately wants to escape its base. No user-controlled input is then concatenated with a privileged path.

## Why it matters
1. UX bug: if a user registers `ee workspace alias --as ..foo` (accepted), `ee --workspace ..foo ...` resolves to a relative-path interpretation rather than the alias. Confusing.
2. Documentation correctness: the alias doc says aliases 'are stable identifiers', but the looks_like_path classifier silently overrides them.

## Fix options
A) Tighten normalize_alias to reject any alias that starts with '.': add `if alias.starts_with('.') { return Err(...) }` after the existing checks. Mirror in test alias_validation_rejects_paths (src/core/workspace.rs:785).
B) Symmetric fix on looks_like_path: only classify as path when it contains a path separator OR matches a registry-relative pattern; defer to alias lookup first when both could apply.
C) Document the constraint and add a test asserting that an alias starting with '.' produces a friendly error rather than silent misrouting.

Option A is preferred — small, defensive, aligns with the existing exact '.' / '..' rejection.

## Severity
LOW because:
- Internal-only — no privilege escalation, no data leak, no path traversal.
- Caught at registration time via friendly error if the user collides with a path-like name.
- Workaround obvious once the issue is observed (rename the alias).
close_reason: Completed: normalize_alias now rejects aliases that start with '.', while preserving internal dots such as client.api and foo... Existing alias validation tests now cover '.', '..', '...', '..foo', '.bar.', client.api, and foo... Verification: rustfmt --edition 2024 --check src/core/workspace.rs; git diff --check -- src/core/workspace.rs; RCH cargo test --lib workspace::tests::alias -- --nocapture passed 3/3; RCH cargo check --all-targets reached Cargo Finished with existing e2e_swarm_contention_recovery warnings before RCH artifact retrieval stall; cargo fmt --check and RCH cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings still fail on unrelated baseline/dirty files outside src/core/workspace.rs.

title: [LOW] pack/mod.rs and curate/mod.rs serde_json::to_string fallback to "{}" silently corrupts schema on impossible error
close_reason: Fixed: pack/curate to_json helpers no longer fall back to {}; RateDistortionReport, SectionBudgetReport, QuarantinedFeedback, ProtectedRuleStatus, TraumaGuardEvaluation, and FeedbackHealthSummary now return explicit ee.error.v1 serialization_failed JSON on serializer failure. Added failing-serializer tests and retained success-path JSON tests. comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Affected sites (all introduced in zudw/tof3/dkuo/6rmv hardening pushes):
- src/pack/mod.rs RateDistortionReport::to_json — ends with serde_json::to_string(&json_repr).unwrap_or_else(|_| "{}".to_owned())
- src/pack/mod.rs SectionBudgetReport::to_json — same pattern
- src/curate/mod.rs FeedbackHealthSummary::to_json — same pattern (introduced by 6rmv)
- src/curate/mod.rs QuarantinedFeedback::to_json — same pattern (1f8f7e8)
- src/curate/mod.rs ProtectedRuleStatus::to_json — same pattern (0b70784)

The structs being serialized contain only String, u32, u64, f64, Option<String>, and bool — none of which can fail to serialize via serde_json. The unwrap_or_else fallback is dead code, but if a future refactor adds a non-Serializable field (e.g. a custom type with a fallible Serialize impl), the to_json output silently degrades to '{}' — a wire-shape that downstream parsers will accept as a valid empty object and proceed with NO indication that the schema invariant was violated.

Fix: replace .unwrap_or_else(|_| "{}".to_owned()) with .expect("<TypeName> JSON must serialize"). This preserves no-panic behavior for the today-known-impossible case (because the assertion holds) while making schema regressions audible. Alternative: make to_json return Result<String, serde_json::Error> and force callers to handle.

title: SECURITY: generated hooks execute ee through PATH and allow hook-time binary hijack
description: HIGH. The generated hook script is #!/bin/sh and executes ee hooks run {hook_type} "$@" (src/hooks/installer.rs:223, src/hooks/installer.rs:233). It does not pin the installed binary path or verify argv[0]. Hooks commonly run inside project and agent environments where PATH may be attacker-controlled. A malicious ee earlier on PATH gains arbitrary code execution whenever the installed hook fires. Expected fix: generate hooks with an absolute canonical ee binary path captured at install time or a secure launcher, quote it, and test that PATH-prepended fake binaries are not invoked.

title: Swarm-X: extreme swarm responsiveness on 256GB+ / 64+-core hosts
description:
# Swarm-X — Extreme swarm responsiveness epic

Goal: take `ee context` and the swarm-write path from "fast" to "world-class" on hosts with 256GB+ RAM and 64+ cores, where dozens of agents fan out the same query within seconds and need byte-stable, low-latency responses.

This epic was filed via the `/idea-wizard` skill on 2026-05-15 by StormyCove against the explicit user goal: "taking full advantage of 256gb+ of RAM and 64+ cpu cores".

## Top 5 (P1 children, each child gets its own bead under this epic)

1. **stream-pack** (swarmx.1): chunked `ee context` output. First usable item ≤10ms via SSE/NDJSON; pack hash committed on stream close so the determinism contract still holds. `--stream` flag on `ee context`; falls back to batch when stdout is not a TTY. Surface: `src/cli/mod.rs`, `src/core/context.rs`, `src/output/mod.rs`. Output contract bumped to `ee.pack.v2.streaming` with one frame per memory + a trailing frame containing the final pack hash and selection ledger.
2. **xagent-pack-singleflight** (swarmx.2): extend `ee.singleflight.key.v1` (already shipped) with a workspace-scoped RAM cache. Same `(query, profile, snapshot_gen, max_tokens)` digest on two panes within ~5s shares one assembled pack. LRU + content-hash invalidation on memory writes. 256GB host holds ~10⁵ cached packs hot.
3. **prewarm-from-beads** (swarmx.3): opt-in steward job that runs `ee context "<bead-title>\n\n<bead-description>"` in background for the top-N `br ready` beads and stages results in the singleflight cache. Bounded by `--prewarm-budget-ms` per bead.
4. **numa-mmap-graph-snapshot** (swarmx.4): pin graph snapshot blobs in RAM via `mmap+MAP_POPULATE+mbind` to the NUMA node of the requesting CPU. PPR/HITS hot loops stay node-local. Falls back transparently on non-NUMA hosts.
5. **per-agent-context-profile** (swarmx.5): durable per-`agent_name` table of `(memory_id, outcome_signal)` feedback weights; capped (≤0.05) contribution to retrieval score so a misbehaving agent cannot dominate. After ~50 outcomes the agent's packs are measurably more relevant; degrades gracefully when feedback is sparse.

## Next 10 (P2 children, filed after the top 5 land)

6. wal-group-commit, 7. adaptive-pack-budget, 8. zstd-pack-dict, 9. tiered-hot-warm-cold-storage, 10. bloom-precheck, 11. rcu-read-snapshots, 12. arena-pack-assembly, 13. hash-cons-memory, 14. crossagent-key-singleflight (subsumed by swarmx.2 if scope merges), 15. pack-dna-pipelined.

## Dependency edges (proposed)

- swarmx.4 (NUMA) is a prerequisite for swarmx.11 (RCU) — both touch the read path.
- swarmx.1 (stream-pack) enables swarmx.7 (adaptive-pack-budget) because streaming exposes "first usable item" latency for the classifier to optimize.
- swarmx.2 (xagent-pack-singleflight) ↔ swarmx.14 (crossagent-key) — merge if scope overlaps.

## Tests/acceptance pattern (shared across all children)

Every swarmx.* child must include:

- Unit tests: pure-function pieces (cache eviction policy, NUMA hint resolver, classifier scoring) covered with `#[cfg(test)]` modules.
- Integration: real DB + index + graph snapshot, multi-thread/multi-agent harness.
- e2e: `scripts/e2e_overhaul/sx_<name>.sh` driving the surface end-to-end with structured tracing fields per `docs/observability/tracing_field_convention.md`.
- Bench: criterion group in `benches/sx_<name>.rs` with a baseline pinned in `benches/baselines/swarmx-v0.1.json`.
- Determinism: extend `tests/cross_platform_determinism.rs` (bd-3usjw.25) with hash rows for any new algorithm output.
- Failure-mode fixture: `tests/fixtures/failure_modes/swarmx_<name>_*.json` per degraded code.
- Backward compat: each new flag is additive; legacy invocation byte-identical to today's output.

## How this epic relates to existing beads

- Cooperates with `bd-oja31` (SRR1: ee daemon --hot-mode RAM-pinned ANN) — swarmx.4 NUMA mmap is the graph-side counterpart to oja31's ANN side.
- Subsumes parts of `bd-1zb7k.17.3` (IW3: Context hotset prewarm) → swarmx.3 is the same concept with concrete budgets.
- Complements `bd-2seqp` (MVCC fork-on-context-pack) and `bd-2lsxf` (SRR3: wait-free MPSC + WAL group commit). swarmx.6 may be a duplicate of bd-2lsxf — merge if so.

This epic is OPEN, not in_progress. Children stay deferred until idea-wizard Phase 6 review confirms scope and dependencies.

— StormyCove, idea-wizard pass 2026-05-15

title: swarmx.1 — ee context --stream: chunked context-pack emission
description:
## swarmx.1 — `ee context --stream`: chunked context-pack emission

### Why

Today every `ee context` invocation is a single batch JSON response. On a 256GB / 64-core swarm host where 8-12 agents may fan out the same task within seconds, even a 95ms p50 → 240ms p99 (current `mac-m3-pro` baseline) means the first agent waits a full pack cycle before any item is usable. Streaming first-usable-item ≤10ms changes the agent experience from "wait then act" to "act as items arrive, refine continuously".

### What the surface does

```
ee context "<task>" --stream --format json [other-flags]
```

Emits NDJSON to stdout (one JSON object per line):

```json
{"schema":"ee.pack.stream.v1","kind":"header","packId":"...","query":"...","ts":"..."}
{"schema":"ee.pack.stream.v1","kind":"item","seq":0,"memoryId":"...","content":"...","score":...,"why":"..."}
{"schema":"ee.pack.stream.v1","kind":"item","seq":1,...}
...
{"schema":"ee.pack.stream.v1","kind":"trailer","packHash":"blake3:...","totalItems":N,"selectionLedger":{...},"degraded":[...]}
```

- Header frame committed before any heavy compute (e.g., before graph snapshot warm or PPR runs) so an agent can begin allocating buffers.
- Item frames stream as the pack assembler emits them. Top-of-pack (highest-score items) arrive first.
- Trailer frame carries the byte-stable `packHash` (must match a non-stream invocation byte-for-byte given the same DB+indexes+config+query+seed) and the selection ledger needed for `ee pack replay`.

### Determinism contract

- `packHash` in the trailer MUST equal the `packHash` from `ee context --no-stream` for the same `(workspace, db_gen, index_gen, config, query, seed, max_tokens, profile)`. The streamed item ordering MUST equal the non-streaming item ordering. Tests: golden snapshot of one streamed run + assertion that batch hash equals streamed trailer hash for the same fixture.
- Stream emission is buffered with explicit `flush()` after every frame to defeat pipe buffering in shell pipelines.

### Falls back to batch when

- stdout is not a TTY AND no explicit `--stream` is passed.
- `--format` is not `json` or `ndjson` (markdown/toon/human are non-streaming).
- `--explain` AND `packDna` is requested (Pack DNA frame requires the full selection; for that combo, stream items but block the trailer until DNA computes — agents see items first, DNA at the end).

### File surface

| Path | Change |
|---|---|
| `src/cli/mod.rs` | `ContextArgs` gains `stream: bool`, wired into `handle_context`. |
| `src/core/context.rs` | `run_context_pack` gains a streaming variant returning `impl Stream<Item = StreamFrame>` (under Asupersync's `&Cx`, NOT Tokio); the existing batch fn becomes a thin wrapper that drains the stream and assembles the pack. |
| `src/output/streaming.rs` | NEW. NDJSON frame writer with explicit flush. Lives alongside existing `src/output/mod.rs` renderers. |
| `src/output/mod.rs` | Renderer enum gains `StreamingNdjson` variant; legacy renderers untouched. |
| `tests/context_stream.rs` | NEW. Integration test: same fixture, both modes, assert byte-stable hashes match. |
| `tests/snapshots/context_stream.snap` | NEW. Golden snapshot of one streamed run (header + items + trailer concatenated). |
| `scripts/e2e_overhaul/sx1_stream.sh` | NEW. Runs `ee context --stream`, asserts header arrives before first item, item ordering monotone by score, trailer present and hash matches non-stream. |
| `benches/context_stream.rs` | NEW. Criterion: `time_to_first_item` (header→item[0]) and `time_to_last_item` (header→trailer). |
| `docs/schemas/ee.pack.stream.v1.json` | NEW. Frame schema. |
| `docs/agent-ux/streaming-context.md` | NEW. Agent harness integration guide (when to use, how to consume). |

### Acceptance

- Header frame emitted ≤10ms after process start (measured by `time_to_first_item` bench).
- Trailer `packHash` byte-identical to batch `packHash` for 5+ fixture queries.
- `ee context --stream` exit code 0 on success; non-zero with structured error frame on failure (no half-streamed corruption).
- Unit: 5 cases (header order, item order monotone, trailer ordering, flush semantics, error mid-stream).
- Integration: 3 cases (small pack, large pack with PPR, degraded mode with stale graph snapshot).
- e2e: `scripts/e2e_overhaul/sx1_stream.sh` driving real `ee` binary with byte-stable header→trailer flow.
- Bench: criterion baseline pinned in `benches/baselines/swarmx-v0.1.json`.
- Tracing: structured fields `workspace_id`, `request_id`, `bead_id=bd-1prrl.1` (or whatever child id this gets), `surface=context_stream`, `phase` in {input, dependency_check, dispatch, item_emit, trailer}, `elapsed_ms`, `degraded_codes`.
- Failure-mode fixture: `tests/fixtures/failure_modes/context_stream_partial_emission.json` documenting the "client disconnect mid-stream" path; degraded code emitted by trailer.

### Out-of-scope

- HTTP / SSE wire protocol (the `serve` adapter can wrap NDJSON later; not in this bead).
- Backpressure beyond stdout pipe — assume consumer reads at line rate.
- Streaming `ee why` / `ee search` — pack-only for now.

### Dependencies

- Parent: bd-1prrl.
- Blocked by: nothing in the current open queue (the streaming path is purely additive).
- Likely consumer: swarmx.7 (adaptive-pack-budget) wants `time_to_first_item` from the bench.

### Risks / open questions

1. `--stream` + `--ppr-weight` interplay: PPR runs over the full seed set before any item is rankable. Stream the header immediately, then run PPR, then stream items. Header→item[0] latency in PPR mode ≈ PPR runtime (currently bounded by bd-3usjw.49's 50ms p50 target on 14k memories).
2. `--stream` + `--explain` + `packDna`: Pack DNA computes from the final selection; trailer must wait. Document this in the agent-ux guide.
3. Cancellation: Asupersync `&Cx` cancellation midstream — trailer with `degraded: ["cancelled_mid_stream"]` and partial item ledger so `ee pack replay` can reconstruct what was emitted.

title: swarmx.5 — per-agent context profile learning (capped feedback bias)
description:
## swarmx.5 — per-agent context profile learning

### Why

Different agents have different judgment styles, knowledge gaps, and tool preferences. The same memory may be "essential" for one agent and "noise" for another. Today the retrieval scorer treats every agent identically. With per-agent feedback weights, the scorer learns over ~50 outcomes which memories each agent finds load-bearing vs harmful and biases retrieval accordingly — without giving any single agent enough leverage to dominate the pack.

### What the surface does

- New `agent_context_profiles` table: `(workspace_id, agent_name, memory_id, helpful_count, harmful_count, ignored_count, last_seen_at, weight_cached)`.
- Every `ee outcome <memory_id> --signal helpful|harmful` call writes a row keyed on the calling agent's name (from `agent-mail/identity` or `EE_AGENT_NAME` env). The pre-existing memory utility/confidence delta is unchanged; the profile row is ADDITIVE.
- At pack time, the scorer reads the calling agent's profile rows and applies a capped weight: `agent_bias(v) = clamp(0.05 * (log(1 + helpful) - log(1 + harmful)) / log(1 + ignored + 1), -0.05, +0.05)`. The cap of ±0.05 guarantees no single agent's history can move a memory more than ±5% relative to the base score.
- Cold-start: when an agent has <10 outcome events for the workspace, `agent_bias = 0` (no contribution); the pack assembler reports `agent_profile.cold_start` in the explain block.
- Profile decay: the half-life on `helpful_count`/`harmful_count` is the same as the procedural-rule decay (default 365 days, configurable via `[curation.agent_profile.half_life_days]`).

### Surface

- `ee remember`/`ee outcome` honor `EE_AGENT_NAME` (already in env registry) and `agent-mail/identity` files.
- `ee context --explain --json` adds an `agentProfile` block when bias is non-zero:
  ```json
  "agentProfile": {
    "agentName": "StormyCove",
    "observedOutcomes": 73,
    "biasMagnitude": 0.031,
    "memoryBiasApplied": 12,
    "coldStart": false
  }
  ```
- `ee why <memory-id> --json` adds the per-agent helpful/harmful counts to the existing `retrieval` block.
- New audit event `agent_profile.update` when outcomes change a row.

### File surface

| Path | Change |
|---|---|
| `migrations/<NNNN>_agent_context_profiles.sql` | NEW. Table + indexes (workspace_id, agent_name) and (workspace_id, memory_id) for fast read in pack. |
| `src/db/mod.rs` | NEW CRUD methods `insert_agent_profile_event`, `agent_profile_for_pack(workspace_id, agent_name)`. |
| `src/core/outcome.rs` | When recording outcome, also insert/update profile row. |
| `src/core/context.rs` | Pack scorer reads profile rows for the calling agent and applies bias. |
| `src/core/why.rs` | Surface per-agent counts in the why explanation. |
| `src/output/mod.rs` | `agentProfile` block renderer. |
| `docs/schemas/ee.context.agent_profile.v1.json` | NEW. Schema for the bias block. |
| `tests/agent_profile_unit.rs` | NEW. Unit tests for bias calc, cap, cold-start, decay. |
| `tests/agent_profile_e2e.rs` | NEW. Multi-agent integration test: agent A says memory M is helpful 20×, agent B says harmful 20×; same query from A vs B returns visibly different ranking; no other agent affected. |
| `scripts/e2e_overhaul/sx5_agent_profile.sh` | NEW. Real `ee` binary drives the multi-agent scenario end to end. |
| `tests/snapshots/agent_profile.snap` | NEW. Golden snapshot. |
| `tests/fixtures/failure_modes/agent_profile_cold_start.json` | NEW. Documents the cold-start sentinel. |

### Acceptance

- Profile bias caps at ±0.05; unit test asserts no input (any combination of helpful/harmful/ignored counts) can produce |bias| > 0.05.
- Cold-start path returns no bias and emits the documented sentinel.
- E2e: two agents see measurably different rankings for the same memory after asymmetric outcome history; a third agent sees the unbiased ranking.
- Audit row written on every profile change with chain-hash continuity (per bd-3usjw.61 audit_row_obligation).
- Same query + same agent + same DB → byte-identical pack hash (determinism preserved).
- Bench: profile read adds ≤2ms p50 on the 1k-memory fixture (single-row index lookup).

### Privacy & trust constraints

- Profile rows are workspace-scoped; no cross-workspace leakage.
- `ee support bundle` redacts `agent_name` to a hash by default; raw names only when the caller passes `--redact none`.
- `[trust.prompt_injection_guard]` still applies — a flagged memory cannot enter the profile (the outcome write rejects with `policy_denied`).

### Dependencies

- Parent: bd-1prrl.
- Blocked by: nothing in the open queue (additive table + new code paths).
- Likely consumer: swarmx.7 (adaptive-pack-budget) may use profile bias signal to widen budget for agents whose recent outcomes show pack-too-narrow rejections.

### Risks / open questions

1. **Sybil**: an agent that repeatedly cycles through different `agent_name` values can fragment its own profile but cannot dominate any single profile. Cross-workspace and cross-agent caps already bound the influence. Accept.
2. **Profile staleness across compactions**: when a workspace is restored from backup, profile rows restore too (they're in the durable DB). When `ee curate apply` merges two memories, profile rows on the source memory transfer to the target. Add a unit test.
3. **Profile cold-start for new agents**: the 10-outcome threshold is configurable. Document the trade-off in `docs/agent-ux/per-agent-profile.md` (NEW).

— StormyCove (idea-wizard Phase 5)

title: swarmx.4 — NUMA-aware mmap'd graph snapshot pinning
description:
## swarmx.4 — NUMA-aware mmap'd graph snapshot pinning

### Why

On hosts with 256GB+ RAM and 64+ cores (typically 2-socket Xeon/EPYC with 2× NUMA nodes), graph algorithm hot loops (PPR, HITS, k-truss) iterate over node-and-edge data that can be 100MB+ for a 100k-memory workspace. Without NUMA hints, the kernel scatters those pages across both nodes; when a worker thread on socket 0 touches a page resident on socket 1's memory controller, latency goes from ~80ns to ~160ns. For an algorithm doing 10⁸ random accesses, that's the difference between ~8s and ~16s wall-clock.

Pinning the snapshot blob to the NUMA node of the requesting CPU recovers ~50% of the latency budget without changing any algorithm code.

### What the surface does

- Graph snapshots already serialize through a typed projection (`MemoryGraphProjection`). Add a side-table `graph_snapshot_numa_hints` recording, per snapshot generation: file path, requested NUMA node, MAP_POPULATE flag.
- On snapshot load (`refresh_graph_snapshot` and `compute_*` consumers), invoke `mmap` with `MAP_POPULATE | MAP_NORESERVE` and `mbind(MPOL_PREFERRED, [requesting_node])` when:
  - Host is Linux AND `numa_available() >= 0` AND `[graph.numa_pin.enabled] = true`.
  - Otherwise, fall back to the existing in-memory `Vec<u8>` deserialization (transparent).
- New config:
  ```
  [graph.numa_pin]
  enabled = true              # default
  preferred_node = "auto"     # "auto" detects from CPU affinity; "0"/"1" forces
  populate_on_load = true     # pre-fault all pages on load
  ```
- Cross-platform: macOS (`mlock`/`madvise(MADV_WILLNEED)` only — no NUMA primitives, fall-through path produces `numa_pin_unsupported_platform` in degraded[]). Windows MSVC: same.

### Surface

- `ee status --json` adds a `graph.numaPin` block: `{ supported, enabled, preferredNode, populatedSnapshots, bytesResident, degraded }`.
- `ee doctor --json` adds a numa-pin readiness check.
- No new CLI flag — the optimization is internal and config-driven.

### File surface

| Path | Change |
|---|---|
| `src/graph/numa_pin.rs` | NEW. Wraps libc/syscalls. `pub fn pin_snapshot_blob(path, node) -> NumaPinResult` and `pub fn detect_preferred_node() -> Option<i32>`. cfg-gated on `target_os = "linux"`. |
| `src/graph/mod.rs` | Wire `pin_snapshot_blob` into `refresh_graph_snapshot` and `load_graph_snapshot`. |
| `src/core/status.rs` | Surface `numaPin` block. |
| `src/config/mod.rs` + `src/config/merge.rs` | New `[graph.numa_pin]` keys. |
| `tests/numa_pin_unit.rs` | NEW. Unit tests; Linux-only tests behind `#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]`. |
| `tests/snapshots/graph_numa_pin_status.snap` | NEW. Golden snapshot for `ee status --numa-pin --json`. |
| `benches/graph_pagerank_numa.rs` | NEW. A/B bench: pinned vs unpinned. Runs only on Linux multi-socket hosts (else marks the criterion group as skipped). |
| `scripts/e2e_overhaul/sx4_numa_pin.sh` | NEW. Drives the surface on the host; if non-Linux or single-socket, asserts the degraded sentinel path. |
| `tests/fixtures/failure_modes/numa_pin_unsupported_platform.json` | NEW. |
| `tests/fixtures/failure_modes/numa_pin_disabled.json` | NEW. |
| `docs/agent-ux/numa-pin.md` | NEW. Operator guide and host-class requirements. |
| `docs/schemas/ee.status.graph.numa_pin.v1.json` | NEW. |

### Forbidden-dep policy

- `libc::mmap`, `libc::mbind`, `libc::numa_*` all live in `libc` (already in deps). NO new C lib bindings needed.
- No `tokio`-based runtime; the load happens on the existing Asupersync scope with explicit `&Cx`.

### Acceptance

- On Linux multi-socket host (CI: `ubuntu-24.04-arm` + Linux x86_64 self-hosted runner if available): PageRank wall-clock 30%+ lower with `[graph.numa_pin] enabled=true` vs `enabled=false`, on the 14k-memory fixture corpus.
- On macOS (no NUMA): degraded sentinel `numa_pin_unsupported_platform` present in `ee status --json`; no functional regression.
- Same workspace + same query → byte-identical pack hash regardless of NUMA pinning (the algorithm output is the same; only the wall-clock changes).
- Unit: 4 cases (pin success, pin failure on unsupported platform, preferred-node detection, MAP_POPULATE pre-fault verification via `mincore`).
- Bench: criterion baseline pinned in `benches/baselines/swarmx-v0.1.json` with `numa_pin_on` and `numa_pin_off` rows.

### Dependencies

- Parent: bd-1prrl.
- Blocks: nothing yet. swarmx.7 (adaptive-pack-budget) and swarmx.11 (RCU read snapshots) can both benefit from NUMA pinning but neither depends on it.
- Cooperative: `bd-oja31` (SRR1: ee daemon --hot-mode RAM-pinned ANN). Same hardware-class dependency; merge the topology detection into `[host.topology]` in a later refactor.
- Soft dependency on `bd-1zb7k.12` (host calibration & topology-aware resource profiles) — that bead delivers the topology probe used by `detect_preferred_node()`.

### Risks / open questions

1. **NUMA on aarch64 darwin (Mac)**: macOS does not expose NUMA APIs at all. The macOS path uses `madvise(MADV_WILLNEED)` + `mlock` as the closest available; document that the perf gain on Mac is bounded by RAM size, not NUMA locality.
2. **Forbidden-dep bleed**: `numa-sys` would be a clean wrapper but pulls extra deps. Stick to raw `libc::syscall(SYS_mbind, ...)` to keep the dep tree clean.
3. **Snapshot lifecycle interaction**: when `ee graph snapshot prune` runs, pinned blobs must be unmapped before the file is deleted; add `munmap` + reservation release to the prune path.

— StormyCove (idea-wizard Phase 5)

title: swarmx.7 — adaptive context-pack token budget via task-complexity classifier
description:
## swarmx.7 — adaptive context-pack token budget

### Why

Today every `ee context` invocation uses the configured `[pack].default_max_tokens` (4000 by default). Simple lookup tasks waste tokens by getting a full pack; complex refactors get truncated. With a task-complexity classifier driving the budget, simple tasks finish in ~1k tokens (faster pack + leaves agent context headroom) while complex tasks expand to 8k-32k without operator intervention.

### What the surface does

- Adds `[pack].adaptive_budget = true` (default false). When enabled, the budget for a given query is computed at pack assembly time as:
  ```
  budget(query) = clamp(
      base = 1000,
      multiplier = 1.0 + 0.5 * normalized_entropy(retrieval_top_k)
                       + 0.3 * graph_fanout_factor(seed_set)
                       + 0.2 * task_keyword_score(query),
      max = config.pack.max_tokens,
  )
  ```
  where `normalized_entropy` is the Shannon entropy of the top-20 retrieval scores divided by log(20), `graph_fanout_factor` is the average out-degree of seed nodes capped at 3.0, and `task_keyword_score` is +0.3 if the query contains task-complexity markers (refactor, migrate, rewrite, audit, security, performance) else 0.
- The computed budget is reported in the explain block: `pack.budget = { adaptive: true, computedTokens: N, classifierContributions: {...} }`.
- Explicit `--max-tokens N` always wins (no override even when adaptive=true).

### Surface

- `[pack].adaptive_budget = bool` config key.
- `ee context "<query>" --explain --json` adds the `budget` block with classifier contributions and the final number.
- `ee status --json` reports counts of pack invocations by budget bucket (1-2k / 2-4k / 4-8k / 8k+) for the last 24h, useful for tuning the multipliers.

### File surface

| Path | Change |
|---|---|
| `src/pack/budget_classifier.rs` | NEW. Pure-function classifier returning `BudgetContribution`. |
| `src/pack/mod.rs` | Wire classifier into pack assembly. |
| `src/core/context.rs` | Honor `[pack].adaptive_budget` flag. |
| `src/output/mod.rs` | Render budget block in explain JSON. |
| `src/cli/mod.rs` | Surface adaptive-budget state in `ee status` budget-bucket counts. |
| `src/config/mod.rs` + `src/config/merge.rs` | Register `[pack].adaptive_budget` config key. |
| `tests/pack_adaptive_budget_unit.rs` | NEW. Unit tests for classifier (entropy calc, fanout factor, keyword score, clamps). |
| `tests/snapshots/adaptive_budget.snap` | NEW. Golden snapshot of budget block. |
| `scripts/e2e_overhaul/sx7_adaptive_budget.sh` | NEW. End-to-end: trivial query → ~1k pack; complex refactor query → ~8k pack; explicit --max-tokens override → exact override budget. |
| `benches/adaptive_budget.rs` | NEW. Criterion bench: classifier overhead ≤2ms p50. |
| `docs/agent-ux/adaptive-pack-budget.md` | NEW. Operator/tuning guide. |
| `docs/schemas/ee.context.budget.v1.json` | NEW. Schema for budget block. |
| `tests/fixtures/failure_modes/adaptive_budget_classifier_unavailable.json` | NEW. |

### Determinism

- Same query + same DB + same indexes + same config → same budget number → same pack hash. The classifier is pure (no randomness, no time, no env).
- Stress-tested via `tests/cross_platform_determinism.rs` extension: budget(query) yields identical numbers across all 5 target triples for the canonical fixture corpus.

### Acceptance

- Default `[pack].adaptive_budget = false` (no behavior change for existing users).
- When enabled, simple-query latency is ≤80ms p50 (vs current 95ms p50 on `mac-m3-pro` baseline) on the canonical fixture set.
- Complex-query packs grow up to `max_tokens` (config-bounded; never exceeds).
- 8 unit tests + 2 integration + 1 e2e + 1 golden + 1 bench, all green.
- Audit row written on each adaptive computation so operators can replay budget decisions.

### Dependencies

- Parent: bd-1prrl.
- Soft-depends on bd-1prrl.1 (stream-pack) — adaptive budget benefits from streaming's `time_to_first_item` signal to back off on slow-classifier scenarios.
- Pure additive: doesn't block anything else.

### Risks / open questions

1. **Misclassification**: a complex query that the classifier rates as simple gets a small pack and misses context. Mitigation: e2e tests cover false-negative cases; operator tunes multipliers.
2. **Determinism across embedding model updates**: when frankensearch changes embedding model, retrieval scores shift, classifier output shifts. Document that a model change invalidates `pack_with_ppr.snap`-style goldens.
3. **Interaction with PPR**: PPR seeds inform `graph_fanout_factor`. If PPR disabled, fall back to text-only fanout (use 0.0 factor).

— StormyCove (idea-wizard Phase 5)

title: SRR6.34: Share-preview dry run and consent audit UX
description:
Add an explicit dry-run/share-preview surface before a peer is allowed to receive mesh data. Users should be able to ask `ee` what would be shared with a peer under the current workspace, peer group, trust policy, redaction policy, cache/body settings, and command mode without actually exporting anything.

This is a user-safety feature, not a convenience command. The preview must summarize counts by memory kind/level/trust/redaction class, show representative redacted examples, estimate bytes/embedding/body exposure, list denied classes, and emit a durable audit row when the user confirms enrollment or export. It must not leak private content in previews.

Acceptance: CLI/JSON preview command or mode; unit tests for preview redaction and count aggregation; e2e script with structured logs for preview_generated, export_not_performed, consent_recorded, and export_after_consent; golden JSON for metadata-only/body-allowed/embedding-denied cases; docs tell users to run preview before enabling a peer.

title: EE-CURATE-SPEC-001: Operationalize specificity validation for curation candidates
description:
Operationalize specificity validation for proposed curation candidates so the rule "evidence over vibes" becomes a deterministic check rather than a vibe.

Background:
EE-181 implements candidate validation but does not pin what "valid" means; the rest of the curation surface (EE-180 table, EE-183/184/185 candidates/validate/apply, EE-301/302 review queue) inherits that ambiguity. D2 ambiguity-detection mode flagged this directly: "rule mentions concrete tools/files/branches?" has no operational definition, so two implementers will disagree on whether a candidate passes. Without a pinned specificity contract, the curation pipeline becomes non-deterministic across releases.

The README also commits to "Evidence Over Vibes" as a product principle: "A procedural rule with no source session, no feedback events, and no validation stays low-confidence." Specificity is half of that promise (the other half is provenance, which existing beads cover). Without specificity, generic platitudes ("write good code") slip through and pollute the procedural layer.

Intended scope:
This bead is a small, ADR-anchored feature plus a fixture corpus. It does not own the validation framework (that is EE-181) or the review surface (EE-183/184/185). It owns the deterministic specificity check that EE-181 calls.

Public surface:
- A pure function specificity_score(rule_text) -> Outcome<SpecificityReport> with fields: score (0.0-1.0), concrete_tokens (list, e.g. file paths, command names, branch names, error codes, technology names), generic_tokens (list, e.g. "code", "function", "system"), structural_signals (e.g. has_command_block, has_file_path, has_error_code, has_metric_threshold), platform (Linux/macOS/Windows where detectable), and rejected_reasons (list of stable codes).
- A configurable threshold [curation].specificity_min (default 0.45). Candidates below the threshold are rejected with stable code candidate_too_generic and a useful next action.
- A fixture corpus tests/fixtures/specificity/ with one positive and one negative example per rejection class.

Why this matters:
Specificity is the load-bearing test that separates a useful procedural rule from a fortune-cookie aphorism. Pinning it deterministically once costs less than re-litigating it in every curation discussion.

## Acceptance Criteria

Detailed closure criteria are stored in this bead's structured acceptance_criteria field. Treat those criteria as part of this bead's implementation contract, including the deterministic specificity score, configurable threshold, redaction-aware report, validate command integration, positive/negative fixture corpus, property tests, adversarial cases, and e2e logging requirements.
design:
Recommended design:
- Implement structural signals as a small composable detector: has_command_block (regex on backticked or fenced shell-like content), has_file_path (regex matching workspace-relative or absolute paths), has_error_code (regex matching project- or language-specific error tokens, e.g. "E\\d+", "panic:", "exit code N"), has_metric_threshold (regex matching numbers paired with units), has_branch_or_tag (regex matching "main", "release/x.y", "v0.1.0"), has_provenance_uri (any token resembling cass:, file:, session:).
- Generic-token detection uses a small embedded list (project-tunable via config) plus a length heuristic: a single-word token under 4 chars is rarely concrete. Avoid pulling in NLP stacks.
- The redaction-aware reporting layer composes with the privacy bead set: any concrete token that matches the redaction policy is replaced with REDACTED:<class> and counted but not stored verbatim in the SpecificityReport.
- The threshold default (0.45) is chosen to admit clear release-failure-style rules while rejecting platitudes; ship with the threshold as configurable so projects can tighten or loosen.
- The function is intentionally not LLM-driven in v1: see §29.1 Open Questions in the OPUS plan, which defers LLM-driven consolidation. A later ADR can add an LLM-assisted override.
- Compose with EE-CURATE-TTL-001 (specificity gates auto-promote), EE-FEEDBACK-RATE-001 (specificity is a precondition for protected-rule status), and EE-TRUST-RECON-001 (specificity affects which trust class transitions are allowed automatically).
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

Acceptance criteria:
- specificity_score is pure (no I/O, no global state, no random) and deterministic for fixed input.
- The score is an explicit weighted sum of structural signals with documented weights; weights are configurable but ship with conservative defaults.
- A candidate is rejected by the threshold path with stable code candidate_too_generic and a concrete reason chain (e.g. "no concrete tokens found", "all tokens are generic English nouns", "no command block, file path, error code, or metric threshold present").
- A reverse-test asserts that a known-good rule corpus (release-failure rules from the README example, project conventions from CASS imports) all score above the threshold; a known-bad corpus (LLM-style platitudes) all score below.
- The check produces a redaction-aware report: any concrete token that matches the redaction policy is reported as a redacted_concrete_token rather than the literal.
- The function is callable from the curation framework (EE-181), the dry-run path of `ee curate validate <id> --json`, and the property test harness. It is not callable from outside the curation module.

Testing and logging requirements:
- Unit tests cover the pure function for: empty input, all-generic input, all-concrete input, mixed input at threshold boundary, multi-line rules with code blocks, multi-language rules (English plus a non-English snippet), input containing redactable tokens, and very long input (>10kB).
- Property tests assert: monotonicity (adding a concrete token never decreases the score), idempotency (specificity_score(rule) == specificity_score(rule)), and stability across whitespace normalisation.
- Adversarial fixtures cover: prompt-injection attempts disguised as concrete tokens (must not pass without secondary checks), tokens that look like file paths but are not, tokens that look like command names but are misspelled, and tokens that look concrete but are language-specific platitudes ("just be careful with mutexes").
- Integration tests via `ee curate validate <id> --json` seed candidates of each archetype, run the validate path, and assert the JSON shape and the rejected reasons.
- E2E logs capture the score, the structural signals, the rejected_reasons, and the audit log entry written when the threshold path fires.
- Closeout evidence cites the specificity fixture corpus, the validate integration test, and the threshold weights as committed.
notes: Operationalizes the README product principle 'Evidence Over Vibes' by pinning specificity to a deterministic, testable score. Without this, EE-181 ships with implementation-defined specificity, which means every release can drift the curation pass/fail boundary. Default threshold 0.45 chosen empirically against the release-failure rule corpus from the README example.
close_reason: Completed specificity scoring contract, config threshold, fixture coverage, validation integration, and ADR; EE-184 owns the CLI dry-run surface.

title: [reality-check] schema export misses schemas emitted by current commands
description:

- Current `public_schemas()` registry in src/output/mod.rs:4612-4685 exposes only a small catalog/envelope subset.

title: [MEDIUM] steward: decay sweep consumes positive feedback as applied

title: [idea-wizard][swarm-brief] Epic: coordination-aware swarm preflight and work advisor
description:
Background:
The current backlog has strong foundations for swarm-scale resource governance (ADR 0017), host profiles (ADR 0023), performance forensics (ADR 0024), handoff capsules, agent inventory, Beads/BV triage, and Agent Mail reservations. What is still missing is a first-class, read-only answer to the question an agent asks before starting work on a crowded machine: "what can I safely and usefully work on right now without colliding with other agents or overloading the host?"

This epic creates a coordination-aware preflight/brief surface for large local agent swarms. It is not an agent scheduler, not an Agent Mail replacement, not a Beads/BV replacement, not a daemon requirement, and not a task-claiming tool. It should be a deterministic local report that gathers existing coordination signals, makes non-overlap and resource-pressure risks visible, and emits stable JSON/Markdown that a human or agent harness can use before choosing work.

Idea-wizard rationale:
The 30-idea pass produced several swarm-oriented candidates: coordination brief, stalled-work detector, file-reservation conflict advisor, RCH/build-storm advisor, degraded-capability dashboard, handoff drift detector, support-bundle coordination summary, command stdout discipline preflight, workspace ambiguity canary, and resource profile advisor. The best accretive slice is the coordination brief because it can include the useful read-only parts of those ideas while preserving product boundaries. It makes massive-agent-swarm work more responsive by reducing duplicate exploration, file conflicts, accidental local builds, and stale blocked-task selection.

Intended UX:
- Preferred public shape is `ee swarm brief --workspace . --json` plus a Markdown renderer, unless implementation finds a better existing namespace that preserves the same semantics.
- Output uses `ee.response.v1` carrying `ee.swarm.brief.v1` data.
- The report summarizes ready/blocked Beads, BV critical path/parallel tracks, active file reservations when available, current dirty file surfaces, recent local commits, optional Agent Mail thread/reservation state, optional RCH/build pressure, host profile/budget posture, degraded sources, and deterministic next-work recommendations.
- Recommendations are advisory and never claim a bead, reserve a file, send mail, release locks, run builds, edit files, or mutate EE state.

Out of scope:
- No scheduler, autonomous worker, task router, or approval manager.
- No replacement for Agent Mail, Beads, BV, RCH, handoff capsules, support bundles, or `ee agent status`.
- No interactive TUI or daemon-only mode.
- No raw secret-bearing mail bodies, transcripts, environment dumps, or arbitrary path listings in stdout.

Success criteria:
- Agents can run one read-only command before work and see non-overlap guidance, resource pressure, and degraded coordination sources in stable JSON.
- The command remains useful when some optional tools are absent by reporting stable degraded codes and repair commands.
- It builds on ADR 0017/0023/0024 and existing handoff/support-bundle surfaces without duplicating their collection logic.
- Contract, golden, unit, and logged no-mock E2E coverage prove deterministic ordering, stdout discipline, redaction safety, and no hidden mutation.
close_reason: Completed coordination-aware swarm brief epic; all blocking children are closed with contracts, E2E, support/handoff summaries, docs, and RCH verification.

title: [LOW] UUIDv7 monotonicity is process-local — cross-process / cross-host bursts can produce out-of-order IDs
description:
## Surface
UUIDv7 generation in ee (audit cycle 6, surface 4)

## Finding
ee depends on `uuid = { version = "1", features = ["v7"] }` (Cargo.toml). With uuid 1.10+ the `Uuid::now_v7()` impl uses a per-process atomic counter to break ties at sub-millisecond granularity, so within ONE process, IDs generated in tight bursts are monotonic.

But the monotonicity is bounded by process lifetime:
- Two ee invocations on the same host that both call now_v7() within the same millisecond start independent counters seeded from random bytes. Their IDs may interleave in arbitrary order when sorted.
- Two ee invocations on different hosts (multi-agent swarm across machines, or a backup restore from another host) have no clock-sync guarantee; clock skew of even a few ms can flip ordering.

The id-module doc comment at src/models/id.rs:21 acknowledges 48-bit timestamp + random bytes but does not state the cross-process limitation. AGENTS.md 'Key Dependencies' table lists 'uuid (v7) | Time-ordered IDs' without qualification.

## Existing test
src/models/id.rs:903-912 (`ids_from_now_v7_are_unique_within_a_burst`) only checks UNIQUENESS, not monotonic ordering across calls.

## Why it matters
1. audit_log V033 hash chain orders by insertion sequence — chain order does NOT depend on UUID ordering, so the chain itself is safe. Confirmed: src/core/audit.rs hashes prev_hash + row_payload by insert order.
2. recorder events: src/core/recorder.rs:128 generates run_id and src/core/recorder.rs:303 generates evt_<uuid>. If a downstream tool sorts events by ID for display, sub-ms bursts within one process appear in order, but events from concurrent recorder processes do not.
3. memory IDs: queries that say 'order by id desc' as a proxy for 'newest first' will be slightly wrong at sub-ms scale across processes.
4. Multi-agent swarm scenarios from project memory (active swarm session 2026-05-02) generate IDs across many panes — cross-process ordering matters.

## Severity
LOW because:
- ee almost never sorts by ID for correctness; persisted timestamps (`created_at`, `recorded_at`) provide explicit ordering.
- The hash chain is decoupled from UUID order.
- Within-process monotonicity (the most common case) IS guaranteed by uuid 1.10+.

## Fix options
A) Document the cross-process limitation in src/models/id.rs and AGENTS.md. State explicitly: 'UUIDv7 ordering is monotonic within one process; for cross-process / cross-host ordering use the explicit timestamp columns.'
B) Add a contract test that asserts intra-process burst monotonicity (>1000 IDs strictly ascending) so a future uuid-crate downgrade is caught.
C) For features that genuinely need cross-process monotonicity (none today, but the audit chain is the candidate), add an explicit sequence column populated via a transaction-scoped MAX+1 query.
close_reason: Documented UUIDv7 process-local ordering limits and added in-process monotonic burst contract test

title: EE-TST-REDACT-FUZZ-001: Add deep redaction fuzz corpus, mutation generator, and coverage report
description:
Add a deep redaction fuzz/property corpus that tests the privacy pipeline against the kind of adversarial input that real codebases and chat logs actually contain.

Background:
The OPUS plan §27.6 explicitly notes redaction fuzz coverage "could be deeper" and §22 commits the system to redacting before storage. The README lists default redaction classes (api_key, jwt, password, private_key, ssh_key, aws_secret, oauth_token) and promises that the original is "never written to disk". EE-TST-011 (adversarial fuzz and property-test harness for agent-facing inputs) is the existing umbrella, but it is generic; it does not own a redaction-specific corpus or the property assertions that prove the pipeline is robust against pattern mutations and multilingual or encoded payloads.

Real coding-agent traffic carries: secrets split across multiple lines, secrets embedded in JSON or YAML, base64-encoded secrets, secrets with custom prefixes that defeat naive detectors, secrets in non-Latin scripts, secrets in code comments, secrets in file paths (e.g. ".aws/credentials"), and secrets that look like ordinary tokens until paired with a context word. F4 failure-mode and H2 adversarial review both flagged that a single false-negative in the redaction pipeline destroys the trust promise of the system.

Intended scope:
This bead adds a redaction-specific fuzz corpus, the property assertions that compose with it, and the multilingual/encoded mutation strategies. It does not replace EE-TST-011; it extends the harness with the redaction-specific test pack.

Public surface (test-only):
- A corpus directory tests/fixtures/redaction/ with categorised payloads: by class (api_key, jwt, etc.), by encoding (raw, base64, percent-encoded, json-escaped, yaml-quoted), by language (English, plus at minimum one Cyrillic and one CJK example), by structural context (code comment, JSON value, YAML block, environment-variable assignment, error message body, file path).
- A property assertion harness that for every fixture: runs the redaction pipeline, asserts no raw payload appears in the redacted output, asserts the audit log records the redaction class and a stable evidence hash but NOT the raw payload, and asserts deterministic redaction (same input -> same output).
- A pattern-mutation generator that takes a known-good detector and asserts the detector still fires after small mutations (whitespace insertion, case changes, line breaks, leading/trailing punctuation, base64 wrapping, YAML quote wrapping).
- A coverage report that lists every redaction class against every encoding and every structural context, with green/red status.

Why this matters:
Redaction is the single most visible privacy promise of EE. A fuzz corpus that codifies the realistic adversarial patterns is the only durable defense against detector regressions. Plan §27.6 explicitly named this as under-covered.

## Acceptance Criteria

Detailed closure criteria are stored in this bead's structured acceptance_criteria field. Treat those criteria as part of this bead's implementation contract, including the redaction fixture corpus, mutation generator, positive/negative corpora, coverage report, property tests, support-bundle/import/remember integration tests, and e2e logging requirements.
design:
Recommended design:
- Treat the corpus as code-adjacent fixtures, not test-only inputs. Every fixture is a small JSON file with raw, encoding, context, expected_class, expected_redacted_form. The test loader iterates the directory and builds the test matrix at runtime.
- The mutation generator is a deterministic function with seeded randomness; same seed -> same mutations. Seeds are committed alongside the corpus.
- For multilingual coverage, lean on existing locale-tagged sample tokens (e.g. UTF-8 password fixtures from public security research). Avoid bundling actual production secrets.
- Compose with EE-TST-011 (adversarial fuzz harness) by reusing its property-testing utilities; do not fork them.
- Compose with EE-DIAG-001 (support bundle) by including a redaction-coverage-aware integration test in the support-bundle path.
- The negative corpus is load-bearing: false positives erode user trust as much as false negatives. Both directions must be asserted.
- Document a quarterly review: the corpus must grow as new agent traffic patterns emerge. The notes field captures this expectation.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

Acceptance criteria:
- The fixture corpus under tests/fixtures/redaction/ covers every redaction class named in the README (api_key, jwt, password, private_key, ssh_key, aws_secret, oauth_token) crossed with at minimum five encodings (raw, base64, percent-encoded, json-escaped, yaml-quoted) and at minimum five structural contexts (code comment, JSON value, YAML block, environment variable assignment, error message body, file path).
- For each fixture, the redaction pipeline produces a deterministic redacted form, audits the redaction with class and a stable evidence hash, and never writes the raw payload to any artifact (DB, audit log, stderr diagnostics, support bundle, JSONL export).
- The mutation generator takes any positive fixture and produces a documented set of mutations: whitespace insertion at every position, case mutation for case-insensitive prefixes, line-break insertion, leading/trailing punctuation, base64 wrapping, yaml quote wrapping, json-escape wrapping. Each mutation is asserted to still fire the detector.
- A negative corpus tests/fixtures/redaction/negative/ contains tokens that look like secrets but are not (e.g. example tokens from public docs, base64 of harmless strings). The pipeline asserts no false positive on these.
- A coverage report tests/contracts/redaction_coverage.json is regenerated as part of the test run and asserted byte-stable; a missing class*encoding*context cell fails CI.
- Multilingual coverage includes at minimum one Cyrillic example and one CJK example for password and api_key classes.
- All assertions go through the audit log and not through stdout, so the test produces a stable JSON contract on stdout that consumers can parse.

Testing and logging requirements:
- Unit tests cover detector correctness on the negative corpus (no false positives) and on the positive corpus (no false negatives), plus deterministic redaction output for all fixtures.
- Property tests assert: redaction is idempotent (redact(redact(x)) == redact(x)), deterministic (redact(x) == redact(x) across process restarts), and never lengthens the output beyond a documented bound.
- Adversarial: a fixture that hides a secret inside a UTF-8 BOM, a fixture that uses zero-width joiners, a fixture that splits a secret across log lines, a fixture that encodes a secret in URL-encoded form within a query string. Each must redact correctly.
- Integration tests via the real ee binary run `ee remember`, `ee import cass --dry-run`, and `ee support bundle --dry-run` against a workspace seeded with redaction fixtures and assert no raw payload appears anywhere.
- E2E logs capture the corpus run, the per-fixture verdict, the audit log diff, and a coverage summary. Logs go to stderr and a per-fixture log artifact.
- Closeout evidence cites the corpus directory, the coverage report, the negative corpus, and the integration test outcomes.
notes: Closes the §27.6 explicitly-named coverage gap. Composes with EE-TST-011 rather than duplicating it: this bead owns the redaction-specific corpus and assertions, EE-TST-011 owns the harness primitives. Multilingual coverage is required because real coding-agent traffic includes non-ASCII passwords and identifiers.
close_reason: Initial fuzz corpus and harness landed (commits 77b72a4, 993a45d). Corpus: 10 positive, 3 negative, 3 gap fixtures. Test harness validates detection, determinism, coverage. Remaining: mutation generator, full encoding matrix, multilingual fixtures, coverage report JSON artifact, adversarial corpus.

title: [reliability] Index publish lock retry exhausts without logging attempts
description:
**File:** src/core/index.rs:46-76

**Defect:** The `acquire_index_publish_lock` function retries 200 times with backoff, but doesn't log intermediate attempts. If all attempts fail, the error message only shows the last holder:
```rust
Err(IndexRebuildError::Index(format!(
    "Index publish lock held by {other} since {acquired_at}. Another index operation may be in progress."
)))
```

**Observable:** User sees cryptic error after ~10s of silent waiting with no indication of retry progress. Difficult to diagnose whether the lock is legitimately held vs. stale.

**Repro:**
1. Start a long-running index rebuild
2. In another terminal, start another index rebuild
3. Second one waits silently, then fails with no progress indication

**Fix:** Add tracing at INFO level every ~10 attempts:
```rust
if attempt > 0 && attempt % 10 == 0 {
    tracing::info!(attempt, holder = %other, "waiting for index publish lock...");
}
```

Low severity - rare condition, but poor UX when it occurs.
close_reason: Index publish lock contention reports retry progress and stable JSON error code

title: EE-270: Implement legacy Eidetic dry-run scanner
description:
Source plan item: EE-270 from the `Trust, Schema Evolution, And Legacy Import` backlog.

Task: Implement legacy Eidetic dry-run scanner

Background and intent:
Defend against poisoning, stale schemas, legacy architecture leakage, and untrusted imported content while preserving useful historical value.

Why this matters:
This bead contributes to the overarching goal of making `ee` a dependable local memory substrate for coding agents: useful before work, auditable after work, and safe under degraded conditions. The work should be implemented in the smallest coherent slice that fully satisfies the public contract implied by the title.

Dependency context:
Original plan dependencies: EE-107, EE-264. These are also represented as br dependency edges where the referenced bead exists.

Non-negotiable constraints:
Global implementation invariants for this task:
- Keep the CLI local-first, deterministic, and agent-native; stdout is data, stderr is diagnostics.
- Preserve the no-Tokio and no-rusqlite constraint unless a later ADR explicitly changes the architecture.
- Use SQLModel Rust plus FrankenSQLite for durable data; do not introduce a second storage stack.
- Use Asupersync for async edges and cancellation/budget behavior; do not smuggle in a Tokio executor.
- Keep JSON as the canonical public contract. TOON, Markdown, diagrams, and MCP are renderers or adapters over the same domain data.
- Mutating commands need dry-run/idempotency/audit behavior unless the task explicitly says otherwise.
- Add focused tests proportional to risk: unit tests for domain logic, contract/golden tests for public output, and integration/evaluation tests for cross-subsystem behavior.

## Acceptance Criteria

Detailed closure criteria are stored in this bead's structured acceptance_criteria field. Treat those criteria as part of this bead's implementation contract, including the comprehensive testing and logging requirements.
design:
Suggested design approach:
- Command output must use the stable `ee.response.v1` envelope, preserve stdout/stderr isolation, and provide useful degraded-state metadata.
- Privacy and trust rules dominate optimization. Never surface quarantined, secret-bearing, or instruction-like memory as authoritative advice.

Implementation guidance:
- Read the surrounding modules and existing project conventions before editing.
- Prefer the planned crate boundaries from the comprehensive plan: CLI wiring in `ee-cli`, reusable domain/services in `ee-core`, models in `ee-models`, persistence in `ee-db`, output rendering in `ee-output`, and adapters in their own optional crates.
- Keep public contracts stable and versioned. Any data structure that leaves the process through CLI/MCP/hook/export should have a schema and at least one golden fixture.
- If a dependency or upstream Franken project is not ready, implement the smallest honest diagnostic/degraded path rather than faking behavior.
- Document any architectural exception with an ADR-oriented note and a verification hook.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

Acceptance criteria:
- The behavior described by `Implement legacy Eidetic dry-run scanner` is implemented or, for spikes, conclusively reported with a clear go/no-go recommendation.
- The implementation preserves local-first, no-Tokio, no-rusqlite, agent-native CLI behavior.
- Public command output, if any, validates against the stable response envelope and does not pollute stdout with diagnostics.
- Relevant unit, integration, golden, contract, or evaluation tests are added and named so future agents can find them.
- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, and the relevant test subset pass after implementation.
- Any degraded or unavailable dependency state returns a stable error/degradation code with a useful next action.

title: [context] Serialize context pack persistence under writer pressure
description:
Finding from deadlock-finder-and-fixer audit.

Evidence:
- src/core/context.rs:525-541 treats pack-record persistence failure as recoverable, but every non-dry context pack still attempts a DB write.
- src/core/context.rs:913-995 resolves the workspace and inserts a pack record/items/omissions through DbConnection.
- The write-owner/spool machinery exists in src/core/write_owner.rs:197-328 and src/core/write_owner.rs:951-1055, but ordinary ee context execution writes directly instead of queueing through it.

Reproduction conditions:
- File-backed .ee/ee.db.
- Launch many agent panes that call ee context "task" --workspace . --json while other panes run ee remember, cass import, graph refresh, or index jobs.
- Context looks like a read operation to callers, but it becomes a writer at pack persistence and can join the writer storm.

Fix target:
- Route context pack persistence through the same serialized write path as other durable writes, or add an explicit bounded persistence mode that queues the pack record when the writer is busy.
- Preserve the requirement that pack records are normally persisted, but make lock pressure visible and testable.
- Add a multi-process test with concurrent context + remember calls and assert pack records either persist or queue without raw SQLite lock errors.
close_reason: Completed by adding real multi-process context+remember contention coverage in tests/e2e_multi_process_write.rs. Code path audit: ee context persists via persist_pack_record -> DbConnection::insert_pack_record -> with_transaction, which holds the file write-owner gate through BEGIN IMMEDIATE/commit on file-backed DBs in current main. Commit 0716a78 adds concurrent_context_and_remember_processes_persist_pack_records, launching 2 ee context processes against 2 ee remember writers, asserting JSON success, no raw SQLite lock stderr, no context_pack_persist_failed degradation, selected memories, persisted pack_records created_by=ee context, and DB integrity. Verification: RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec -- env CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/data/tmp/rch_target_eidetic_g2gn cargo test --test e2e_multi_process_write concurrent_context_and_remember_processes_persist_pack_records -- --nocapture passed: 1 passed, 0 failed, test body 16.47s after remote compile. rustfmt --edition 2024 --check tests/e2e_multi_process_write.rs passed locally. Whole-repo RCH cargo fmt --check was attempted and currently fails only on unrelated active dirty reserved surfaces: src/core/why.rs (eidetic_engine_cli-lqnh/LavenderGate) and src/policy/mod.rs (eidetic_engine_cli-rjrd), so full fmt/check/clippy closeout is deferred to those owners rather than attributed to g2gn.

title: [CONCURRENCY] cass import: session check-then-insert races concurrent imports
description:
Files: src/cass/import.rs:346, src/cass/import.rs:373, src/db/mod.rs:4231, src/db/mod.rs:4242.
Code path: import_cass_sessions checks connection.get_session_by_cass_id(&workspace_id, &session.source_path) before the write transaction. Only after optional span loading does it enter connection.with_transaction to insert_session, insert_evidence_span, and insert_search_index_job.
Hazard: two imports of the same workspace/source can both observe no existing session, then both compute the same stable session_id/index_job_id. Repro plan: use a fake CASS client or saved cass JSON fixture returning one session, start two import_cass_sessions callers against the same file DB with a barrier after the existence check, and assert both commands succeed with exactly one imported session and one skipped session.

title: [MEDIUM] ee never sets PRAGMA journal_mode/synchronous — crash safety relies on undocumented FrankenConnection defaults
description:
## Surface
ee SQLite WAL handling under crash (audit cycle 5)

## Finding
`src/db/mod.rs` opens databases via `FrankenConnection::open_file(path)` and only sets `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` (`src/db/mod.rs:744-748`). It never explicitly configures:
- `journal_mode` (rollback vs WAL)
- `synchronous` (FULL/NORMAL/OFF)
- `busy_timeout` (sqlmodel may set this internally; not verified)
- `wal_autocheckpoint`

Verified via `grep journal_mode|WAL|synchronous|busy_timeout src/db/mod.rs src/core/recorder.rs src/core/index.rs src/pack/mod.rs src/core/memory.rs` → only `PRAGMA foreign_keys` appears.

Searched `/data/projects/sqlmodel_rust/crates/sqlmodel-frankensqlite` and `/data/projects/frankensqlite/src` for `journal_mode|WAL|PRAGMA`. The fsqlite-wal crate exists (so WAL is the default storage layout), but ee does not explicitly opt in or pin durability semantics.

## Why it matters
Crash safety of the audit chain (`audit_log`), pack records, and recorder events depends on:
- WAL + `synchronous=NORMAL` is durable across OS crashes if the WAL is fsync'd before commit.
- `synchronous=OFF` is fast but loses tail-of-WAL on crash.
- Rollback journal + `synchronous=FULL` is the SQLite default but ee uses `fsqlite` which may differ.

ee makes strong durability claims (V033 hash chain, V036 append-only triggers) that are only as strong as the underlying durability config. If fsqlite's default is `synchronous=OFF` on a write batch, a crash mid-commit could:
- Truncate the audit chain so `verify_audit` reports a hash mismatch on the partial last block.
- Drop pack-record children but keep the parent (FK violations on next open if foreign_keys was OFF — but ee sets it ON so this would error rather than silently corrupt).

## What I checked
- `with_transaction` uses `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` (`src/db/mod.rs:307`) — correct for write contention.
- Per-write file lock via `lock_file_write_owner_gate` — coordinates multiple ee processes.
- No explicit checkpoint / `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint` calls.

## Fix
Either:
A) Add explicit `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL; PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL; PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint=1000;` in `enable_foreign_key_enforcement` (rename it to `enable_durability_pragmas`), and document the choice in an ADR.
B) Add an `open_durability_check` test that asserts the effective `PRAGMA journal_mode` and `PRAGMA synchronous` values match expectations after `open_file`. This way fsqlite default drift would be caught.

## Note
Not claiming corruption is observable today — the fsqlite default may be safe. The bug is that ee does not state or test what it depends on, so a silent fsqlite default change could regress durability without anyone noticing.
close_reason: Implemented explicit WAL and synchronous=NORMAL pragmas at DB open; rch verification attempted but repo-wide gates are blocked by unrelated dirty work in src/output/mod.rs, src/core/claims.rs, src/core/preflight.rs, and formatting drift outside src/db/mod.rs.

title: MCP tool registry refactor: data-driven dispatch instead of 3-site enum match (idea-wizard MagentaPanther 2026-05-18)

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel
comments.text:
FULL SPEC (MagentaPanther idea-wizard + reality-check 2026-05-18)

DESIGN:
1. Replace McpTool enum + 3 match arms with a static registry: const TOOL_REGISTRY: &[ToolEntry] = &[ ... ];
2. ToolEntry struct: { name: &str, cli_subcommand: &[&str], schema_id: &str, args_builder: fn(&Value) -> Vec<String>, description: &str }.

title: [e2e] Prove silent-fallback failures surface as stable machine errors
