title: shard-fanout.4: deterministic migration and preserved rollback path
description:
## Goal
Implement `ee migrate shard-fanout` as a deterministic, auditable migration from the legacy single database to catalog plus per-workspace shards, with dry-run first and a preserved rollback path. This bead owns the mutating migration command, not the router hot path.

## Scope
- CLI surface: `ee migrate shard-fanout --dry-run --json` and explicit apply mode after the command naming is finalized.
- Dry-run reports every planned shard, row counts by table, source hash, target paths, expected audit rows, and blockers without writing.
- Apply mode creates catalog and shard DBs, copies rows by workspace ownership, writes `ee.migration.shard_fanout.v1` audit evidence, and preserves the original `ee.db` by rename or copy to `.pre-shard-fanout.db` according to the ADR.
- No deletion under any path. Any cleanup is outside scope and requires explicit human approval.
- Idempotence: second dry-run/apply reports already-migrated state without duplicating rows or audit records.

## Acceptance
- Migration preserves memory, workspace, audit, pack, graph/cache metadata needed by downstream surfaces, with explicit documented handling for global rows that cannot be assigned to a workspace.
- Unit/contract tests cover empty DB, one workspace, multiple workspaces, existing shard, interrupted marker, corrupt target hash, and idempotent rerun.
- E2E fixture compares legacy single-DB behavior and shard layout behavior for remember/search/context/why/status over the same logical rows.
- The rollback/off path is documented and covered by a sibling bead; this bead must at least preserve enough source evidence for rollback to be possible.
- All Cargo verification through RCH only.

title: shard-fanout.5: cross-shard read attach and search parity
description:
## Goal
Teach read-only retrieval surfaces how to query the local workspace shard plus allowed peer workspace shards without reintroducing cross-shard writes or nondeterministic ordering.

## Scope
- Define the read-only `ATTACH` or equivalent path for peer shards, including path safety and attach failure degradation.
- Wire search/context/pack candidate loading through the shard router for shard-enabled workspaces.
- Preserve memory-scope and mesh policy semantics: workspace/self/team/swarm scope still decides what is eligible; shard fan-out only changes where eligible rows live.
- Update integrity checks that currently treat cross-workspace pack items as invalid so intentional cross-shard peer reads are represented explicitly and still audited.
- Emit degraded codes for shard_attach_failed and cross_shard_skew_detected with fixtures and taxonomy docs.

## Acceptance
- Golden parity test: the same logical memories in legacy single DB and shard layout produce byte-identical search/context results after volatile fields are scrubbed.
- Peer shard attach failure degrades one peer and still returns local eligible results unless strict/required mode demands fail-closed behavior.
- Cross-shard result ordering is deterministic by score, workspace_id, memory_id, and existing tie-breakers.
- No cross-shard write transactions are introduced.
- RCH-only focused tests cover search parity and context pack parity; local Cargo is not used.

title: shard-fanout.6: per-shard audit chains and global timeline view
description:
## Goal
Move audit-chain semantics from one global database file to per-shard chains plus a deterministic global read view, preserving audit explainability and chain verification under shard fan-out.

## Scope
- Define audit chain ownership: each shard owns its local prev_hash sequence for workspace-scoped mutations.
- Define how catalog/global audit events are recorded without creating a cross-shard transaction requirement.
- Implement or specify global timeline read behavior as a UNION over per-shard audit chains sorted by audit_ts, workspace_id, audit_id, with stable tie-breakers.
- Add `shard_chain_mismatch` degradation and failure-mode fixture when one shard chain is broken.
- Coordinate with bd-wp5ac audit-lane work: this bead should compose with per-workspace audit channels rather than conflict with them.

## Acceptance
- Unit tests prove per-shard chain continuity and detect a deliberate break in one shard without poisoning other shards.
- Global audit timeline ordering is deterministic across shards and does not imply a global prev_hash chain unless the ADR explicitly adds one.
- `ee why`, `ee audit timeline`, support bundles, and migration evidence can explain which shard produced each audit row.
- No audit row is silently dropped during migration or cross-shard reads.
- RCH-only tests or an explicitly blocked RCH proof are recorded.

title: shard-fanout.7: backup, restore, and side-path parity for shards
description:
## Goal
Extend backup/export/restore support so shard fan-out is not a performance-only feature that loses disaster-recovery parity.

## Scope
- `ee backup create` includes catalog.db plus every per-workspace shard DB needed to reconstruct the logical workspace set.
- Backup manifest records each shard path, workspace_id, shard_id, byte size, BLAKE3 hash, schema version, and derived-asset relationship.
- `ee backup restore --side-path` reconstructs the shard layout without overwriting existing files and without deleting any preserved legacy database.
- Export/import JSONL behavior is documented for shard-enabled stores: source-of-truth rows remain portable records, while physical shard layout is a backup concern.
- Integrate per-shard audit chain metadata from shard-fanout.6.

## Acceptance
- Contract/e2e tests cover backup create, inspect, verify, restore to side path, and logical row parity across legacy and shard-enabled stores.
- Restore refuses unsafe existing targets, symlinked shard paths, missing catalog entries, and hash mismatches with structured degraded/error output.
- Manifest and support-bundle summaries are redaction-safe and do not leak raw memory content.
- No command deletes old backup artifacts or original DB files.
- All Cargo verification uses RCH only.

title: shard-fanout.8: concurrency e2e and throughput benchmark harness
description:
Scope: build the proof harness that makes the shard-fanout performance claim falsifiable before implementation is considered done. This bead owns the concurrency e2e/benchmark surface for bd-f6jfs and must not broaden into production router or migration code except for tiny test hooks that are explicitly justified.

Background: parent bd-f6jfs promises that writes against workspace A do not block writes against workspace B once EE_SHARD_FANOUT_ENABLED=1. The acceptance gate is intentionally concrete: 8 OS threads x 4 workspaces x 100 remember calls, with total throughput at least 3.5x the single-writer baseline and structured ee.test_event.v1 JSONL evidence for phase=enqueue|grant|commit.

Required artifacts:
- e2e or integration harness for multi-workspace write contention under shard fanout.
- Baseline mode that exercises the current single-writer/global-gate path for comparison.
- Shard-fanout mode that exercises independent workspace shards.
- JSONL event log using schema ee.test_event.v1 with fields: workspace_id, shard_id, request_id or operation_id, phase, elapsed_ms, thread_id or worker_id, degraded_codes, and timestamp if already standard for test events.
- Summary output with p50/p95/p99 latency, total throughput, per-workspace throughput, and speedup ratio.

Acceptance:
1. The harness fails loudly if shard-fanout throughput is less than 3.5x the baseline on the calibrated local/remote test profile, or records a structured blocked/degraded reason when RCH topology prevents execution.
2. The harness proves same-shard writes remain serialized while different-shard writes can proceed concurrently.
3. Output is deterministic enough for CI comparison after scrubbing volatile timings; ordering rules and tie-breakers are documented.
4. The test log is useful for future tail-latency analysis, including enqueue-to-grant and grant-to-commit durations.
5. All heavy Rust build/test execution is routed through RCH only. If RCH is unavailable, leave dry-run/static evidence and an explicit blocker note rather than running local Cargo.

Coordination notes: this bead depends on the router and cross-shard read/audit surfaces being present enough to test. Do not edit peer-owned RCH topology files or restart workers while collecting evidence.

title: shard-fanout.9: rollback, off-switch, and fail-closed behavior
description:
Scope: make shard fanout safely reversible and operationally boring. This bead owns the off-switch, rollback semantics, and fail-closed/degraded behavior around the new catalog/shard layout.

Background: bd-f6jfs is intentionally invasive: it changes the write topology from one global ee.db writer to per-workspace fsqlite shards plus a catalog. Because this will run on crowded agent-swarm hosts, operators need a deterministic way to disable the feature, understand posture, and recover from partial or bad migrations without deleting the preserved source DB.

Required behavior:
- EE_SHARD_FANOUT_ENABLED=0 keeps current single-DB behavior byte-compatible for the same DB content.
- Enabled mode refuses ambiguous dual-write states; it must not silently write some records to old ee.db and others to shards.
- Rollback path uses the preserved .pre-shard-fanout.db from the migration bead and never deletes user data.
- status/doctor/support-bundle output clearly reports feature state, catalog path, shard count, migration phase, rollback availability, and degraded/fail-closed reasons.
- Structured degraded/error codes cover missing catalog, missing shard, catalog-shard mismatch, unsafe rollback target, unsupported cross-shard transaction request, and disabled feature with migrated layout.

Acceptance:
1. Unit/contract tests cover enabled, disabled, partially migrated, corrupt catalog, missing shard, and rollback-available states.
2. Rollback dry-run reports exact affected paths, hashes, row counts, and safety checks before any mutation.
3. Apply rollback restores byte-identical behavior to v0.x for the same DB content, modulo explicitly documented volatile audit timestamps or IDs.
4. No file is deleted during rollback; obsolete shard files may only be left inert or moved/renamed through a separately approved no-delete-safe path.
5. User-facing recovery actions use error.details.recovery[] rather than prose-only repair strings.
6. All heavy Rust verification is RCH-only; when RCH is blocked, leave command hashes/dry-run/static checks and a tracker comment.

Coordination notes: depends on catalog/resolver, migration, cross-shard read parity, audit chain, and backup/restore work. Do not implement a compatibility shim that keeps two live write paths active; the safe state is exactly one authoritative layout at a time.

title: [MEDIUM] tail_recording_from_events from_sequence is INCLUSIVE (>=) — ambiguous for follow-mode pagination
description:
Cycle-4 reviewer audit (REVIEWER pane). Surface: recorder tail pagination off-by-one.

src/core/recorder.rs:1308 tail_recording_from_events filters with: event.sequence >= from_sequence (line 1323).

The conventional semantic for an opaque pagination cursor in follow/streaming mode is EXCLUSIVE ('give me events newer than the last one I saw'). The current INCLUSIVE behavior means a follower that calls tail(from_sequence=last_seen) re-receives the last event every poll cycle.

EVIDENCE: poll_follow_events (recorder.rs:1446) is a stub: pub fn poll_follow_events(run_id: &str, _from_sequence: u64, _limit: u32) -> TailFollowResult — _from_sequence and _limit are explicitly ignored. So no real follow path is wired yet; choose the contract NOW before callers depend on the wrong semantics.

FIX OPTIONS:
  (1) Change to event.sequence > from_sequence (exclusive). Update the docstring on RecorderTailOptions::from_sequence to read 'Return events with sequence STRICTLY greater than this value (exclusive cursor for follow-mode).'
  (2) Keep inclusive and add a separate after_sequence (exclusive) field. More API surface; not preferred.
  (3) Document the inclusive contract loudly and require callers to pass last_seen+1.

REPRO TEST TO ADD:
  events = [seq=1, seq=2, seq=3]
  tail(from_sequence=2, limit=10).events.len() — currently 2 (seq=2, seq=3). Pick contract and pin.

Priority MEDIUM because no production follower exists yet — easy to fix cleanly before someone wires a follow loop and discovers duplicate-event bug.
close_reason: Fixed inclusivity semantics with regression test

title: HIGH: Retrieval JSON uses unstable mixed field naming across context/search/why
description:
Reviewer finding focused on context/search/why machine output.

Locations:
- src/output/mod.rs:1329-1407 (`render_context_response_json`) emits camelCase fields such as `maxTokens`, `candidatePool`, `memoryId`, `estimatedTokens`, `provenanceFooter`.
- src/core/search.rs:230-287 and 336-363 (`SearchReport::data_json`, `RetrievalMetrics::data_json`) emit snake_case fields such as `doc_id`, `result_count`, `elapsed_ms`, `requested_limit`, `source_counts`, `fast_score_count`. The CLI wraps this at src/cli/mod.rs:11018-11023.
- src/cli/mod.rs:11447-11559 (`format_why_json`) mixes both styles in the same response/object: `trust_class`, `provenance_uri`, `created_at`, `memory_id` next to `validFrom`, `selectionScore`, `latestPackSelection`, `eventId`, `linkedMemoryId`.

Why this is a bug:
The core retrieval surfaces are the documented machine-facing workflow (`ee context`, `ee search`, `ee why`). Stable field names are part of the public contract. Mixing casing across those commands, and within `why` itself, makes consumers brittle and undermines deterministic explainable retrieval output.

Acceptance criteria:
- Pick one documented field naming convention for retrieval JSON and apply it consistently across context/search/why.
- Add golden/schema tests that fail on casing drift for all three commands.
- Preserve stdout-only JSON behavior for --json/--robot/--format=json.

title: Epic: Swarm-scale responsiveness and resource-governance roadmap
description:
## Background
The project vision is a local-first memory substrate for coding agents, and the user explicitly wants it to be compelling for massive agent swarms on machines with 256GB+ RAM and 64+ CPU cores. The current backlog already covers the walking skeleton, implements-surface gaps, daemon, release, and baseline performance budgets. This epic captures the next layer: proving and improving behavior when many agent harnesses read context, write outcomes, import evidence, and rebuild derived indexes concurrently.

## Idea-wizard rationale
Phase 2 generated 30 possible improvements and winnowed to the strongest theme: swarm-scale responsiveness with resource governance. Phase 3 kept complementary ideas around benchmark fixtures, hotset prewarming, write coalescing, explainable profiling, and failure evidence. Phase 4 overlap check found related but narrower beads (`eidetic_engine_cli-htjd`, `eidetic_engine_cli-59dp`, `eidetic_engine_cli-9s0q`, recorder/support-bundle surfaces), so this epic is deliberately framed as an integration track that depends on those foundations instead of duplicating them.

## Goals
- Provide reproducible swarm-scale workloads that exercise many readers, serialized writers, index rebuilds, graph refreshes, and pack generation.
- Make latency and memory behavior explainable enough for agents to diagnose regressions without a profiler first.
- Keep the product boundary intact: `ee` remains a CLI-first memory substrate, not an agent harness or scheduler.
- Use Frankensearch, FrankenSQLite/SQLModel, FrankenNetworkX, and Asupersync correctly rather than adding custom search, DB, graph, or runtime stacks.

## Non-goals
- No daemon requirement for ordinary commands.
- No custom BM25/vector/RRF implementation.
- No web UI or central orchestration service.
- No replacement for Agent Mail, Beads, Codex, Claude Code, or other harnesses.

## Closure evidence
This epic closes only when its child beads provide scale fixtures, benchmark gates, cache/write-governance implementation beads, and logged E2E coverage with clear resource metrics. Closure requires `bv --robot-insights` showing no dependency cycles and the relevant Cargo/script gates passing through `rch`.
close_reason: All child beads closed: ADR (fcq1.8), workload model (fcq1.1), benchmark harness (fcq1.2), cache/prewarm (fcq1.3), write spool (fcq1.4), explain-plan (fcq1.5), E2E contention suite (fcq1.6), support bundle (fcq1.7), plus oxt2 Appendix C parity scenario. Swarm-scale responsiveness and resource-governance roadmap complete.

title: [swarm-scale] Define workload model and deterministic scale fixtures
description:
## Background
Before optimizing for massive agent swarms, the project needs a shared workload model. Existing performance beads cover README p50/p99 numbers and a specific submodular packing hotspot; this bead defines the scale corpus and traffic shapes those future measurements run against.

## What ships
1. A documented scale workload taxonomy: read-heavy context bursts, remember/outcome write bursts, CASS import spikes, index rebuilds, graph refreshes, daemon maintenance, and mixed-mode swarm traffic.
2. Deterministic fixture generators for small, medium, large, and stress corpora. The stress target should model 100k+ memories and many agent/session/provenance records without requiring paid APIs or nondeterministic embedding models.
3. A resource profile manifest recording expected CPU, RAM, disk, DB rows, index size, and command mix for each fixture.
4. Clear labels for which fixtures are suitable for normal CI, nightly CI, and local 256GB+/64-core validation.

## Implementation notes
Use existing deterministic hash embedders and local fixture conventions. Do not introduce custom search or DB code. Fixture generation must be reproducible from a seed and must not require the daemon for read-only cases.

- A lightweight integration test generates the smallest fixture and verifies it can feed `ee context`/`ee search` once the shared tree compiles.
- Logs must include seed, corpus size, row counts, and artifact paths.

title: [bench] RCH-friendly swarm benchmark harness and budgets
description:

title: [cache] Hotset prewarm and cache-governor for context/search
description:
## Background
Large agent swarms repeatedly ask similar before-work questions. The system should make repeated `ee context` and `ee search` calls fast without making indexes authoritative, bypassing policy, or requiring a daemon for correctness.

## What ships
1. A hotset model for frequently used memories, query shapes, search documents, graph neighborhoods, and pack sections.
2. A prewarm command/job that can materialize safe derived caches from FrankenSQLite + Frankensearch state and discard them when generations change.
3. Cache-governor policy that uses explicit memory budgets, generation checks, and graceful degradation when memory pressure is high.
4. Status/reporting fields that explain cache hit rate, stale generation, memory footprint, and fallback reason.

## Implementation notes
Derived caches must be safe to delete and rebuild. They must not store secrets outside the existing redaction policy. Use existing `cache/`, `search/`, `pack/`, and status/capability reporting patterns. Do not add a custom vector store or custom BM25/RRF logic.

## Tests and logging
- Unit tests cover generation invalidation, budget enforcement, stale-cache fallback, and redaction-safe cache entries.
- Integration tests run repeated `context`/`search` calls against a deterministic fixture and assert stable output with and without cache.
- Logged benchmark evidence must show latency improvement or document why the cache was intentionally bypassed.

## Closure evidence
Close only after behavior is deterministic, cache status is visible in JSON, and rch-offloaded tests/benchmarks cover cache-on, cache-off, and pressure-fallback paths.
close_reason: Implemented hotset prewarm with cache-governor; cache-on/cache-off equivalence verified

title: [writer] Batched write spool and backpressure contracts for agent swarms
description:
## Background
The plan correctly avoids pretending that many SQLite writers are safe. For heavy swarms, the optional daemon owns writes, but the product still needs an explicit contract for queuing, batching, cancellation, and failure reporting so agents can write evidence without corrupting or silently dropping state.

## What ships
1. A write-spool design for remember/outcome/import/recorder writes that preserves idempotency keys and auditability.
2. Batch coalescing rules: which writes can be grouped, which require immediate durability, and how batch boundaries appear in audit/job rows.
3. Backpressure JSON errors and human diagnostics when queues exceed budget, including repair/next commands.
4. Crash recovery semantics: pending, committed, cancelled, and failed writes are distinguishable after restart.
5. Metrics exposed via status/support bundle: queue depth, oldest queued age, batch sizes, rows/sec, and last failure.

## Implementation notes
This depends on the real daemon/write-owner surface. Keep one-shot CLI semantics intact: when daemon is absent, direct commands still use existing advisory locking and clear degraded behavior. Preserve `&Cx` cancellation and `Outcome` until boundaries.

## Tests and logging
- Unit tests for batch eligibility and idempotency.
- LabRuntime tests for cancellation, backpressure, and queue timeout.
- E2E tests for many concurrent agent writes using temporary workspaces and detailed per-process logs.

## Closure evidence
Close only after no Tokio/rusqlite/petgraph dependencies appear, crash recovery is tested, and `rch`-offloaded Cargo gates pass.
close_reason: Implemented batched spool with backpressure tested under simulated swarm load

title: [explain] Query and pack performance explain-plan report
description:

Agents need to understand why `ee context` is slow or memory-heavy before they can fix it. Today explainability focuses on why a memory was selected; swarm-scale operation also needs explainability for query plans, pack assembly, cache behavior, and derived-index state.

## What ships
1. `--explain-performance` or equivalent JSON report for context/search/pack commands, gated so normal stable JSON remains unchanged unless requested.
2. Breakdown of DB reads, search hits, candidate count, pack pruning stages, graph/cache usage, token budgeting, elapsed time, and degradation/fallback reasons.
3. Stable schema suitable for golden tests and support bundles.
4. Redaction-safe output: no secret-bearing memory content in the performance report.

## Implementation notes
This should instrument existing code paths and score components, not fork retrieval logic. It should complement `ee why` and support bundle diagnostics. Keep output deterministic where timings are not asserted; timing fields may be bucketed or separately marked non-deterministic if needed.

## Tests and logging
- Unit tests pin the report schema and redaction behavior.
- Golden tests cover context/search/pack examples.
- Bench tests compare report overhead and ensure explain mode does not materially change selection results.

## Closure evidence
Close only after explain reports catch at least one known hotspot or cache fallback in a deterministic fixture and after rch-offloaded verification passes.

title: [adr] Swarm-scale resource governance and cache/write contracts
description:
## Background
AGENTS.md requires an ADR before every major new subsystem. The swarm-scale roadmap cuts across cache policy, write-owner/backpressure, benchmark fixtures, support bundles, and performance explainability, so future implementers need one architectural decision record before code work starts.

## What ships

2. Explicit boundaries: `ee` remains CLI-first and harness-agnostic; daemon improves heavy-swarm writes but is not required for ordinary reads or one-shot commands.
3. Cache contract: derived, generation-checked, redaction-safe, rebuildable, and bounded by explicit memory budgets.
4. Write contract: single-writer semantics, queued/batched writes only where auditability and idempotency are preserved, clear backpressure errors otherwise.
5. Verification hook list: scale fixtures, benchmark reports, e2e contention logs, no forbidden dependencies, and support-bundle artifacts.
6. Rejected alternatives: custom vector store, custom graph algorithms, central web service, harness scheduler, always-on daemon requirement.

This is a docs/design bead, but it must include acceptance hooks that map to concrete test beads in this epic. Future code beads should reference this ADR in their closure evidence.

title: G2: Pack DNA composite for ee context --explain — Voronoi + Louvain + ego + PPR
description:
# G2 — "Pack DNA" composite for `ee context --explain`

## Idea (one-liner)

For an explained pack, emit ONE JSON block that triangulates multiple orthogonal graph signals — Voronoi-cell dominator, Louvain community-of-mass, ego subgraph, PPR-ranked neighbors. This is the beads_viewer `--robot-insights` analogue for context packs.

## Why this matters

Pack composition is a black box today. `ee context --explain` returns per-result scores but no *structural* explanation of where the pack came from. Pack DNA makes the pack's *origin in the knowledge graph* legible:

- **Voronoi cell dominator**: For the query (embedded into the same space as memories via the seed set), which trust-anchor memory is "closest" by graph distance? Answers: "the spiritual center of this pack."
- **Louvain community-of-mass**: Across the pack's memories, which Louvain community has the largest fraction? Answers: "you're pulling from this topic cluster."
- **Ego subgraph at radius 2 of the dominator**: The 2-hop neighborhood of the dominator memory, rendered as nodes + edges. Answers: "here's the structural context of the pack's center."
- **PPR-ranked neighbors**: Top-10 memories ranked by PPR (from G1). Answers: "structurally relevant memories the pack drew from, ranked."

None of these individually beats user intuition; together they make pack composition legible in a way no single metric does. Compelling demo; sophisticated under the hood (Voronoi cells, Louvain, ego graph, PPR); single-screen output.

## Algorithm composite

For each `ee context --explain --json` call:

1. **Run G1's PPR** on the pack candidate pool (already computed if pack was assembled with G1; cached otherwise).
2. **Identify trust anchors** = memories with trust_class ∈ {human_explicit, agent_validated}, filtered to those with PageRank ≥ 75th-percentile (the "trust backbone").
3. **Voronoi cells** = `fnx_algorithms::voronoi_cells_rust(graph, trust_anchors)`. For each memory in the pack, look up its Voronoi cell (= nearest trust anchor). The **dominator** = the trust anchor whose cell contains the most pack memories.
4. **Louvain communities** = `fnx_algorithms::louvain_communities(graph, weight_attr='weight')`. Group pack memories by community; the **community-of-mass** = the community with the largest count.
5. **Ego subgraph** = `fnx_algorithms::ego_graph_rust(graph, dominator, radius=2)`. Render as JSON node-edge list.
6. **PPR neighbors** = top-10 from PPR by score, excluding pack members.

Combine into one JSON block:

```jsonc
"packDna": {
  "schema": "ee.context.pack_dna.v1",
  "voronoiDominator": {
    "memoryId": "mem_...",
    "trustClass": "human_explicit",
    "containedPackMembers": 7,
    "totalPackSize": 10
  },
  "communityOfMass": {
    "louvainId": 3,
    "label": "release-engineering",
    "size": 12,
    "fractionOfPack": 0.7
  },
  "egoSubgraph": {
    "rootMemoryId": "mem_...",
    "radius": 2,
    "nodes": [{ "id": "mem_...", "trustClass": "...", "inPack": true }, ...],
    "edges": [{ "src": "mem_...", "dst": "mem_...", "relation": "supports", "weight": 0.8 }, ...]
  },
  "pprNeighbors": [
    { "memoryId": "mem_...", "pprScore": 0.034, "inPack": false, "preview": "first 80 chars..." },
    ...
  ],
  "degraded": []
}
```

## Performance

- Voronoi cells + Louvain run on the cached snapshot, not synchronously. Both algorithms cap at ~150ms on a 1k-memory workspace.
- Ego graph at radius 2 is O(degree²) — typically <5ms.
- Full Pack DNA assembly target: ≤ 250ms (foreground; budget enforced via F2).

## Surface

`ee context <query> --explain --json` — output gains a `"packDna"` block alongside the existing `"selection"`, `"results"`, etc. blocks. Optional flag `--no-pack-dna` to suppress (for size-sensitive consumers).

## Acceptance

- New module `src/graph/pack_dna.rs` with `compute_pack_dna(graph, pack, query_seeds) -> PackDna`.
- Integration in `src/cli/context.rs` (or wherever `ee context --explain` renders).
- JSON schema documented at `docs/schemas/ee.context.pack_dna.v1.json`.
- 5 unit tests + 1 e2e test + 1 golden snapshot (insta).
- Determinism: 3 runs against the same database produce byte-identical packDna block.
- Pack DNA can be omitted via `--no-pack-dna`.

## Dependencies

Blocked by: G1 (PPR scores), G4 (Louvain communities — uses the modularity-detection wrapper there), F1, F2, F3 (insights surface conventions), F4.
Blocks: nothing downstream.
Parent: bd-bife.

## Related code

- `src/cli/context.rs` (or `src/core/context.rs`) — explain rendering point.
- ADR 0008 (derived state — Pack DNA is fully recomputable from snapshot + pack).

comments.text:
## Phase 6 refinement notes — empty trust-anchor fallback

Voronoi cells on a graph with no anchors is undefined. Fresh workspaces (no human_explicit OR agent_validated memories yet) have zero anchors.

1. **Fallback chain** (in order):
   a. trust_class ∈ {human_explicit, agent_validated} with PageRank ≥ 75th percentile (the canonical 'trust backbone' described in G2 body).
   b. If empty: trust_class ∈ {agent_validated, agent_assertion} with PageRank ≥ 90th percentile.
   c. If still empty: top-3 by PageRank, any trust_class (emit degraded.no_trust_anchors).
   d. If graph has <3 memories: skip Pack DNA entirely; emit degraded.workspace_too_small in the packDna block.
2. **Renderer responsibility**: ee context --explain MUST always emit a packDna block — null or populated — never omit the field entirely. Agents detect 'no Pack DNA' by inspecting packDna == null OR packDna.degraded[*].

Update G2.a + G2.c (schema docs) accordingly.

title: EE-025: Implement `ee doctor --json` skeleton
description:
Source plan item: EE-025 from the `Config And Workspace` backlog.

Task: Implement `ee doctor --json` skeleton

Background and intent:
Resolve config, paths, workspace identity, status, health, and doctor output in a deterministic way that makes local-first operation reliable.

Why this matters:
This bead contributes to the overarching goal of making `ee` a dependable local memory substrate for coding agents: useful before work, auditable after work, and safe under degraded conditions. The work should be implemented in the smallest coherent slice that fully satisfies the public contract implied by the title.

Dependency context:
Original plan dependencies: EE-024, EE-035. These are also represented as br dependency edges where the referenced bead exists.

Non-negotiable constraints:
Global implementation invariants for this task:
- Keep the CLI local-first, deterministic, and agent-native; stdout is data, stderr is diagnostics.
- Preserve the no-Tokio and no-rusqlite constraint unless a later ADR explicitly changes the architecture.
- Use SQLModel Rust plus FrankenSQLite for durable data; do not introduce a second storage stack.
- Use Asupersync for async edges and cancellation/budget behavior; do not smuggle in a Tokio executor.
- Keep JSON as the canonical public contract. TOON, Markdown, diagrams, and MCP are renderers or adapters over the same domain data.
- Mutating commands need dry-run/idempotency/audit behavior unless the task explicitly says otherwise.
- Add focused tests proportional to risk: unit tests for domain logic, contract/golden tests for public output, and integration/evaluation tests for cross-subsystem behavior.

## Acceptance Criteria

Detailed closure criteria are stored in this bead's structured acceptance_criteria field. Treat those criteria as part of this bead's implementation contract, including the comprehensive testing and logging requirements.

- Command output must use the stable `ee.response.v1` envelope, preserve stdout/stderr isolation, and provide useful degraded-state metadata.

- If a dependency or upstream Franken project is not ready, implement the smallest honest diagnostic/degraded path rather than faking behavior.

title: SECURITY: generated hooks execute ee through PATH and allow hook-time binary hijack
description: HIGH. The generated hook script is #!/bin/sh and executes ee hooks run {hook_type} "$@" (src/hooks/installer.rs:223, src/hooks/installer.rs:233). It does not pin the installed binary path or verify argv[0]. Hooks commonly run inside project and agent environments where PATH may be attacker-controlled. A malicious ee earlier on PATH gains arbitrary code execution whenever the installed hook fires. Expected fix: generate hooks with an absolute canonical ee binary path captured at install time or a secure launcher, quote it, and test that PATH-prepended fake binaries are not invoked.

title: Meta-doc: docs/determinism_seed_labels.md — child-seed label registry for N4 stack
description:
# Meta-doc: determinism seed labels

## Why

N4.2 introduces \`Deterministic<Id>::child(label)\` which forks a child seed by deriving a new key from the parent seed + the label string. Changing a label changes the seed (by design — labels are part of the determinism contract).

The label registry documents EVERY label used in production so:
1. A reviewer can trace every call site forking randomness.
2. A maintainer doesn't accidentally re-use a label in a different context.
3. The lint can validate every label appears in the registry.

## Acceptance

### File: docs/determinism_seed_labels.md

Table (canonical):

| Label                          | Producer call site                                 | Consumer (what uses the child seed)                 |
|--------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| \"pack.mmr_tiebreak\"          | src/core/pack.rs:assemble_pack                     | MMR diversity tie-break                              |
| \"search.score_jitter\"        | src/core/search.rs:run_search                      | Score perturbation for stability tests              |
| \"ulid.memory\"                | src/db/id_gen.rs:next_memory_id                    | Memory ULID generation                              |
| \"ulid.audit\"                 | src/db/id_gen.rs:next_audit_id                     | Audit ULID generation                               |
| \"ulid.workspace\"             | src/db/id_gen.rs:next_workspace_id                 | Workspace ULID                                      |
| \"clustering.kmeans_init\"     | src/curate/clustering.rs                           | Cluster centroid initialization                     |
| \"counterfactual.replay_<id>\" | src/lab/counterfactual.rs                          | Replay-specific child seed                          |
| ... (add per call site)                                                                                                    |

### File: src/core/determinism.rs

```rust
/// Canonical labels used to derive child seeds via Deterministic<Id>::child().
/// Adding a new label requires (a) adding it here, (b) updating
/// docs/determinism_seed_labels.md, (c) updating the call site.
pub const SEED_LABELS: &[&str] = &[
    \"pack.mmr_tiebreak\",
    \"search.score_jitter\",
    \"ulid.memory\",
    \"ulid.audit\",
    \"ulid.workspace\",
    \"clustering.kmeans_init\",
    \"counterfactual.replay\",
    ...
];

pub fn assert_label_registered(label: &str) { ... }
```

The N4.4 lint checks that every `.child(label)` call uses a label from the registry. Unknown labels fail compile.

### Test: tests/seed_labels_consistency_test.rs

1. Every label in `SEED_LABELS` appears in `docs/determinism_seed_labels.md`.
2. Every label in the doc appears in `SEED_LABELS`.
3. Grep src/ for `.child(` calls; assert every argument is a literal that exists in `SEED_LABELS`.

## Depends on

- N4.2 (Deterministic<Seed> type; bd-17c65.14.4.2)
- N4.4 (lint; bd-17c65.14.4.4)

## Blocks

- N4.3 (threading) — soft dep; the labels can be defined as call sites land.

title: Meta-doc: docs/degraded_code_taxonomy.md — build-time vs response-time classification
description:
# Meta-doc: degraded code taxonomy

## Why

E5 (bd-17c65.5.5) requires moving \"build-time\" degraded codes (e.g., \`search_lexical_unimplemented\` — a feature flag, not a per-call condition) from response \`degraded[]\` arrays to top-level \`capabilities.unimplemented[]\`. Before E5 can implement that move, every emitted code needs categorization.

This bead produces and maintains the taxonomy.

## Acceptance

### File: docs/degraded_code_taxonomy.md

For every degraded code emitted by ee, a row:

| code                                | current_location                  | category       | rationale                                       |
|-------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|----------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| index_stale                         | search.degraded[]                 | response_time  | depends on DB gen vs index gen at call time     |
| search_lexical_unimplemented        | search.degraded[]                 | build_time     | feature flag; doesn't vary per call             |
| no_relevant_results                 | search.degraded[]                 | response_time  | depends on query + corpus                        |
| graph_feature_disabled              | graph.degraded[]                  | build_time     | feature flag                                     |
| daemon_background_mode_unimplemented| status.degraded[]                 | build_time     | feature flag                                     |
| handoff_capsule_tampered            | handoff.degraded[]                | response_time  | depends on HMAC verification                     |
| lab_replay_unavailable              | lab.degraded[] (x3 emission sites)| build_time     | feature flag                                     |
| revision_write_unavailable          | memory.degraded[]                 | build_time     | feature flag                                     |
| ...                                                                                                                          |

### Bootstrapping the taxonomy

Run `grep -rhE '\"code\":\\s*\"' src/ | sed -E 's/.*\"code\":\\s*\"([^\"]+)\".*/\\1/' | sort -u`. For each unique code:
1. Find the emission site(s).
2. Classify as build_time | response_time | ambiguous.
3. If build_time: schedule for E5 migration.
4. If ambiguous: file a needs_review note.

### Categorization rules (canonical)

- **build_time**: emission decision is determined at binary-build time (feature flags, feature presence). Does not vary per call against the same binary.
- **response_time**: emission decision depends on workspace state, query, or runtime conditions.
- **mixed**: emission depends on BOTH (e.g., \`search_index_stale\` is response_time but only emitted in builds that support search at all).

For \`mixed\` codes: the response_time aspect lives in \`degraded[]\`; a presence marker lives in \`capabilities.available[]\`.

### Test: tests/degraded_code_taxonomy_consistency_test.rs

1. Every code emitted in src/ appears in the taxonomy.
2. Every code in the taxonomy is emitted in src/ (no orphans).
3. After E5 lands, no build_time code appears in any \`degraded[]\` output (composes with J6 + E5 acceptance).

## Depends on

- J6 (catalog; bd-17c65.10.6) — codes are cross-referenced with J6 fixtures.

## Blocks

- E5 (bd-17c65.5.5) — E5 needs this taxonomy to know which codes to migrate.
- K3 (degraded codes doc; bd-17c65.11.3) — K3's auto-generated doc uses this taxonomy to categorize entries.

3. Author docs/degraded_code_taxonomy.md with the full table.
4. (Optional) Stand up tests/degraded_code_taxonomy_consistency_test.rs to assert taxonomy ⇔ src/ correspondence.

title: Add command-surface coverage matrix for every ee subcommand
description:
## Background

The safest way to ensure we really covered every piece of `ee` functionality is to make command coverage itself a tracked artifact. A one-time inventory can go stale as commands are added or renamed. This bead creates a regression gate that maps the public CLI surface to the mechanical-boundary classification and implementation/skill/degraded beads.

This is plan-space insurance: future contributors should not be able to add a smart-sounding command without choosing where it belongs and what tests prove the boundary.

## Acceptance Criteria

See this bead's structured acceptance_criteria field for the detailed completion contract, including unit/static checks, e2e or docs/e2e coverage, detailed logging, and no-feature-loss requirements.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

- A command-boundary matrix exists and includes every public `ee` command/subcommand visible through Clap/help, including optional feature-gated surfaces where practical.
- Each row records classification, owning bead/ADR, README workflow(s), mechanical data sources, skill handoff if any, degraded code if unavailable, side-effect/idempotency class, runtime/cancellation posture, fixture/golden coverage, JSON schema expectation, and required unit/e2e coverage.
- The matrix explicitly includes boring infrastructure commands as well as smart-sounding command families.
- Tests fail when a public command is added, renamed, or removed without updating the matrix.
- Tests fail when a command marked skill-only appears as Rust CLI reasoning behavior.
- Tests fail when a command lacks a side-effect classification, degraded behavior, or coverage owner.
- E2E logs include generated command list, matrix path/hash, missing/extra command rows, classification summary, side-effect coverage summary, schema coverage summary, workflow parity coverage, and first-failure diagnosis.
- The matrix explicitly preserves README functionality by showing where each advertised workflow lives after the split.

title: [hardening] FuzzRng::next_usize truncates u64 to usize on 32-bit
description:
**File:** src/fuzz.rs:66

**Defect:** The `next_usize` method casts `u64` to `usize` directly:
```rust
(self.next_u64() as usize) % max
```

On 32-bit systems, `usize` is 32 bits, so values from `next_u64()` are silently truncated before the modulo. This reduces randomness from 64-bit to 32-bit entropy on those platforms.

**Observable:** On 32-bit: reduced randomness, potentially biased distribution. On 64-bit: no issue.

**Repro:** Build and run on a 32-bit target (wasm32, i686).

**Fix:** Use explicit truncation with full 64-bit modulo:
```rust
(self.next_u64() % (max as u64)) as usize
```

Low severity since ee doesn't target 32-bit, but correct for portability.
close_reason: Fixed truncation: modulo now computed on full u64 before cast to usize. Added distribution uniformity property test (10k samples, bucket variance check).

title: Epic: Diagnostics, ee why Targets, doctor --apply, Audit-Event Completeness (§21)
description:
Source: COMPREHENSIVE_PLAN_TO_MAKE_EE__OPUS.md §21 (Diagnostics, repair, and `ee why`), §21.3 (health checks), §21.4 (degradation codes), §21.5 (`ee why`), §21.7 (audit events).

# Epic: Diagnostics, ee why Targets, doctor --apply, Audit-Event Completeness

## Why this epic exists

§21 specifies an 11-row health-check table, 14 stable degradation codes, four `ee why` targets (memory, rule, `result:<doc-id>`, `pack:<id>`), a `doctor --apply` repair UX with per-step approval, and a 12-event audit vocabulary (command lifecycle × 4, job lifecycle × 4, plus migration applied, import advanced cursor, index manifest changed, graph snapshot created, context pack emitted, memory written, memory redacted, rule promoted, rule demoted).

Today the doctor / status / health skeletons exist and `ee why` works for memories, but:

- `ee why <rule-id>` and `ee why result:<doc-id>` and `ee why pack:<id>` are not first-class — they fall through the memory-id branch.
- `ee doctor --fix-plan` is in place; `ee doctor --apply` (with per-step approval, audit row per applied repair, and a refusal path) is not.
- The 14 degradation codes are defined but not asserted to be reachable from real production code paths.
- The 12 audit-event types are not asserted to be emitted; some categories (rule_promoted, rule_demoted) have no test asserting they fire on the corresponding lifecycle transition.
- Three plan-listed health checks are missing: stuck-writer / daemon-lock detection, config-conflict surprise reporter, forbidden-deps inspector inside `ee doctor`.

This epic exists so that when an agent or a human runs `ee doctor`, the output is reliably actionable, and so that `ee why <anything>` always has a useful first-class answer.

## Cross-cutting constraints (apply to every child bead under this epic)

- Every health check has: a unique stable code, a severity (info/warning/error), a remediation command string, a JSON shape, and a logged-e2e test that triggers the failure mode.
- Every degradation code is reachable from at least one real (not-test-only) production code path, asserted by a "code-reachability" test that grep-finds each code's emit site.
- Every audit-event type is emitted on the corresponding domain action AND asserted by a focused integration test that drives that action and tail-reads audit.jsonl.
- `ee why` accepts: `<memory-id>` (default), `<rule-id>` (when prefix is rule_), `result:<doc-id>` (search-result explanation), `pack:<id>` (pack-element explanation). The dispatch is unambiguous and a fuzz target ensures arbitrary input produces a typed error rather than a panic.
- `ee doctor --apply` requires either `--yes` for full-auto or an interactive per-step prompt. Each applied repair generates an audit row of type `doctor_repair_applied` with before/after fingerprints. A failed repair short-circuits and surfaces the partial state.
- Tests log: the failure mode triggered, the exact JSON envelope returned, the repair command suggested, the audit rows that fired, total elapsed_ms.

## Closure criteria

- 4 `ee why` targets each have a dedicated bead, implementation, and golden.
- 14 degradation codes each have at least one reachability test.
- 12 audit events each have at least one emission test.
- 11 health checks each have at least one trigger test (positive: failure detected; negative: pass cleanly).
- `ee doctor --apply` implemented with audit + per-step approval; integration test covers happy + refusal + partial-failure paths.

## Verification path

- Unit tests under `src/diag/`.
- Goldens in `tests/snapshots/diag_*` and `tests/snapshots/why_*`.
- E2E in `tests/doctor_apply.rs`, `tests/why_four_targets.rs`, `tests/audit_event_emission.rs`.

title: [context] Serialize context pack persistence under writer pressure
description:
Finding from deadlock-finder-and-fixer audit.

Evidence:
- src/core/context.rs:525-541 treats pack-record persistence failure as recoverable, but every non-dry context pack still attempts a DB write.
- src/core/context.rs:913-995 resolves the workspace and inserts a pack record/items/omissions through DbConnection.
- The write-owner/spool machinery exists in src/core/write_owner.rs:197-328 and src/core/write_owner.rs:951-1055, but ordinary ee context execution writes directly instead of queueing through it.

Reproduction conditions:
- File-backed .ee/ee.db.
- Launch many agent panes that call ee context "task" --workspace . --json while other panes run ee remember, cass import, graph refresh, or index jobs.
- Context looks like a read operation to callers, but it becomes a writer at pack persistence and can join the writer storm.

Fix target:
- Route context pack persistence through the same serialized write path as other durable writes, or add an explicit bounded persistence mode that queues the pack record when the writer is busy.
- Preserve the requirement that pack records are normally persisted, but make lock pressure visible and testable.
- Add a multi-process test with concurrent context + remember calls and assert pack records either persist or queue without raw SQLite lock errors.

title: Epic: Memory Lifecycle, Workflows, Maintenance, and Forgetting (§12 / §22.4)
description:
Source: COMPREHENSIVE_PLAN_TO_MAKE_EE__OPUS.md §12 (Memory lifecycle), §17 (Procedural memory & playbooks), §22.4 (Data deletion), and §20.1 (CLI surface).

# Epic: Memory Lifecycle, Workflows, Maintenance, and Forgetting

## Why this epic exists

The plan defines a 4-stage lifecycle: Working → Episodic → Semantic → Procedural. The transitions between stages are gated on workflow boundaries, evidence accumulation, and stewarded review. Today the substrate has the columns and the maturity enums, but the *transitions* (the verbs and the queries that perform them) are unevenly bead-covered:

- Working → Episodic on workflow close is not bead-tracked because the `workflows` table itself has no table-creation bead.
- Episodic → Semantic via the cluster-summary proposer (EE-187 in §16.2) has no implementation bead.
- Semantic → Procedural via rule extraction (EE-188 in §16.3) has no implementation bead.
- The decay-and-forget verbs in §22.4 (retire, tombstone, expire, redact, hide-from-packs, forget) are partially implemented but no bead asserts the precedence and interaction matrix among the six.

This epic exists so the durable lifecycle can be exercised from a real CLI, with deterministic golden traces of each transition, and so the "no silent memory mutation" guarantee from §3 stays load-bearing rather than aspirational.

## Cross-cutting constraints (apply to every child bead under this epic)

- Every transition emits an audit-log row of one of the canonical types in §21.7 (memory written, memory redacted, rule promoted, rule demoted, etc.). Tests assert that the audit row exists and carries the actor, target_id, before/after fingerprint, and reason.
- legal_hold blocks all five disposal verbs unconditionally and is never overridden. Every disposal command checks the column and returns a typed error when set.
- Every transition has a --dry-run path that emits the would-be audit rows + would-be DDL effect without writing, with the same JSON envelope shape used by the real path.
- Idempotency: repeated invocations on the same target with the same idempotency_key are no-ops with an explicit `idempotent: true` field in the response. The idempotency_keys table (introduced under the storage epic) is the storage location.
- Determinism: transitions that depend on time use a runtime-injected clock; tests pin the clock and assert byte-identical output across runs.
- Logged tests record: target memory id, before-state fingerprint, after-state fingerprint, transition kind, audit row id, lock contention path, total elapsed_ms, and a first_failure_diagnosis when the assertion fails.

## Closure criteria

- ee workflow create / list / show / close commands implemented; close triggers the Working → Episodic promotion query with explicit gating (`access_count >= 2 OR importance >= 0.5`).
- ee maintenance command implemented; runs TTL expiry on Working memories, recomputes decayed_*/effective_score, marks rules with `effective_score < threshold` as needs_review, and emits an audit summary.
- ee promote `<id>` command implemented for explicit Working → Episodic promotion with reason capture.
- ee forget `<id>` command implemented with explicit `--confirm` flag, legal_hold guard, and audit row.
- ee curate retire / ee curate tombstone implemented with replaced_by_rule_id capture.
- The disposal-verb interaction matrix (`retire then forget`, `tombstone then redact`, `expire then forget`, `redact then forget`, etc.) has a 6×6 matrix golden test asserting the documented precedence.
- Each command has unit tests + a real-binary e2e test that opens a temp workspace, drives the lifecycle through `ee remember` → `ee outcome` → `ee promote` → `ee maintenance` → `ee forget`, and asserts every audit row appears with the expected before/after fingerprint.

## Verification path

- `cargo test --workspace` exercises unit + golden tests for each transition query.
- `tests/lifecycle_walking_skeleton.rs` (new integration test under cat-testing-e2e) seeds a workspace, drives the full lifecycle, asserts each transition's audit row, and tears down with `ee forget`.
- `ee status --diagnostic --json` reports per-stage memory counts and a "lifecycle distribution" histogram so a human or another agent can verify the epic's effect at a glance.

description:
Source plan item: EE-162 from the `Graph` backlog.

Task: Add memory_links table

Background and intent:
Use FrankenNetworkX only as explainable derived features over memory/session/procedure links; graph metrics must be optional and never dominate retrieval opaquely.

Why this matters:
This bead contributes to the overarching goal of making `ee` a dependable local memory substrate for coding agents: useful before work, auditable after work, and safe under degraded conditions. Dependency context:
Original plan dependencies: EE-042. These are also represented as br dependency edges where the referenced bead exists.

Non-negotiable constraints:
Global implementation invariants for this task:
- Keep the CLI local-first, deterministic, and agent-native; stdout is data, stderr is diagnostics.
- Preserve the no-Tokio and no-rusqlite constraint unless a later ADR explicitly changes the architecture.
- Use SQLModel Rust plus FrankenSQLite for durable data; do not introduce a second storage stack.
- Use Asupersync for async edges and cancellation/budget behavior; do not smuggle in a Tokio executor.
- Keep JSON as the canonical public contract. TOON, Markdown, diagrams, and MCP are renderers or adapters over the same domain data.
- Mutating commands need dry-run/idempotency/audit behavior unless the task explicitly says otherwise.

title: Swarm single-flight: coalesce duplicate read-heavy ee computations
description:
## Background

Idea-wizard pass by IcyCave on 2026-05-15 after rereading AGENTS.md and README.md, refreshing Agent Mail, inspecting br ready/list/closed state, checking bv robot insights, and de-duplicating against existing swarm-scale epics. Existing beads cover hot-path latency explanations, hotsets/prewarm, burst admission/backoff, host calibration, disk pressure, incident drills, ownership attribution, and verification reuse. The remaining non-overlapping gap is request coalescing: when many agents ask for the same read-heavy context/search/graph computation at the same workspace generation, ee should compute it once and let duplicate followers reuse the in-flight result.

## Phase 2 30-to-5 winnow

The 30 candidates considered included daemon scheduling, distributed cache federation, RCH replacement, per-agent quotas, query-plan fingerprints, follower wait tokens, stale leader recovery, redaction-safe coalescing keys, graph snapshot coalescing, context pack coalescing, search result coalescing, support-bundle posture, cancellation propagation, fairness, no-starvation, single-process-only operation, multi-process advisory locks, hotset integration, pack hash reuse, branch/workspace-generation invalidation, and e2e burst drills.

Top 5 retained: (1) canonical redaction-safe single-flight keys over workspace/index/graph generation, query shape, profile, flags, and output schema; (2) a core in-process coalescer for duplicate read-heavy context/search/graph operations; (3) follower wait/error posture that is deterministic and never hides degraded results; (4) status/doctor/support-bundle observability for leader/follower counts and avoided duplicate work; (5) no-mock burst tests proving repeated identical agent requests collapse to one leader while distinct requests still run independently.

## Phase 3 next 10 considered

The next ten were stale leader recovery, cancellation propagation from last follower, fairness across non-identical requests, cross-process advisory-lock extension, pack-hash reuse in support bundles, graph snapshot refresh coalescing, query-plan fingerprints for future cache prewarm, redaction proof tests for keys, follower timeout degraded fixtures, and J1 event logging for saved work. These are folded into child beads where they strengthen the single-flight contract.

## Overlap decisions

This epic does not duplicate bd-1zb7k.10 (latency/prewarm/admission), bd-1zb7k.12 (host calibration), bd-1zb7k.14 (incident drills), bd-1zb7k.15 (verification reuse), or bd-1zb7k.16 (ownership attribution). Admission decides whether a request should wait or back off; single-flight decides whether duplicate admitted requests can share the same in-flight read result. Cache prewarm handles prior hotsets; single-flight handles live duplicate bursts. Verification reuse handles RCH/test commands; this handles ee read-heavy memory commands.

## Acceptance

This epic closes when ee can generate canonical single-flight keys, coalesce duplicate in-process context/search/graph computations without mutating source-of-truth state, expose deterministic follower posture and telemetry, include redacted summaries in support/handoff artifacts, and prove the behavior with unit, golden, and no-mock swarm burst tests.

## Non-goals

No central scheduler, no daemon requirement, no cross-machine cache federation, no RCH replacement, no automatic file cleanup, no Beads/Agent Mail mutation, and no hidden mutation of durable memories. The feature is an optimization and observability layer around already-admitted read-heavy commands.
notes:
Phase 6 final refinement by SapphireAnchor, 2026-05-15.

Decision: v1 single-flight remains in-process only. Cross-process advisory locks are deferred to a later child only if no-mock burst evidence or support-bundle evidence shows material duplicate work across processes. This keeps the rollout CLI-first, avoids daemon or central-scheduler drift, and avoids adding durable lock mutation to a read-heavy optimization.

Overlap guard: checked bd-1zb7k.10 hot-path latency, cache prewarm, and burst admission; bd-1zb7k.12 host calibration; bd-1zb7k.14 incident drills; bd-1zb7k.15 verification reuse; bd-1zb7k.16 ownership posture; and F2/F4 graph wrapper and determinism surfaces. Existing code/docs hits cover index coalescing, write-owner batching, search or memory dedupe, and RCH verification reuse. None covers live duplicate admitted ee context/search/graph read computation sharing.

Boundary: admission/backoff decides whether a request may run or wait; cache prewarm prepares derived hot data before requests arrive; verification reuse dedupes Cargo/RCH evidence; ownership posture attributes blockers. Single-flight only shares an already-admitted in-flight read result among equivalent callers at the same workspace/index/graph generation.

Test obligations for children: key/coalescer unit tests, redaction proof tests, byte-stable golden key/posture fixtures, degraded-code fixtures for follower timeout or leader failure, and no-mock swarm burst e2e with J1 logging. No local Cargo fallback, file deletion, worktree, or Agent Mail/Beads mutation from ee is part of the feature.

title: SF2: In-process single-flight coalescer for admitted read-heavy commands
description:
## Goal

Implement a bounded in-process single-flight helper that lets duplicate admitted read-heavy operations share one leader computation and return the same result to followers. This should reduce CPU, memory pressure, and graph/cache churn during agent swarms without introducing a daemon requirement.

## Scope

- Add a small core helper around `OnceLock`/`Mutex` or an existing Asupersync-compatible primitive, with bounded wait time and deterministic follower outcomes.
- Apply first to one low-risk read-heavy surface after SF1 keys exist, preferably context pack assembly or graph feature enrichment; later surfaces can opt in explicitly.
- Preserve cancellation semantics: leader cancellation must be visible, and follower cancellation must not silently cancel the leader while other followers remain.
- Do not share results across requests with different output-affecting flags, schema versions, generations, or redaction posture.

## Acceptance

- Unit tests prove one leader executes for N identical concurrent requests and N distinct keys execute independently.
- Follower results are byte-identical to leader results after volatile-field stripping.
- Timeout/cancellation paths emit structured degraded entries rather than hanging.
- No source-of-truth data, Beads state, Agent Mail state, git state, or cache deletion is introduced by this feature.

title: SF4: No-mock swarm burst e2e proving duplicate requests coalesce
description:
## Goal

Add a no-mock e2e harness that drives a realistic read-heavy burst and proves single-flight behavior under concurrent agent-style requests.

## Scenario

1. Seed a deterministic temp workspace with enough memories and links to exercise search, context packing, provenance, graph feature enrichment, and redaction checks.
2. Launch a bounded fanout of identical `ee context` or graph feature requests plus a smaller set of deliberately distinct requests.
3. Assert identical requests produce one leader and multiple followers, while distinct requests do not collapse into the wrong result.
4. Compare scrubbed response hashes across three runs.
5. Emit J1 JSONL with leader count, follower count, waited_ms distribution, timeout count, p50/p95/p99 latency, result hashes, and degraded-code counts.

## Acceptance

- Script runs against the real binary and temp workspace; no mocks and no local Cargo.
- Small tier is CI-safe; larger 10k-memory tier is opt-in.
- Failures identify whether the key, coalescer, follower posture, or output determinism failed.
- The script performs no cleanup outside its own temporary workspace and never deletes shared repo files or agent artifacts.

title: Epic: Performance Budget Enforcement, Regression Gates, Memory Ceiling (§28)
description:
Source: COMPREHENSIVE_PLAN_TO_MAKE_EE__OPUS.md §28 (Performance budget) and §27.7 (CI gates).

# Epic: Performance Budget Enforcement and Regression Gates

## Why this epic exists

§28 specifies a 16-row latency table with explicit p50 / hard-ceiling targets per command (e.g., `ee remember` p50 8ms / hard ceiling 22ms; `ee context` p50 95ms / hard ceiling 240ms; `ee index rebuild` full p50 18s / hard ceiling 41s), a 100 MB resident-memory budget for typical CLI invocations, a 30 MB DB target on a typical project, and a CI gate that fails the build when any benchmark regresses 30% beyond the rolling baseline.

Today criterion benches per-command exist and the bench harness compiles, but:

- The §28 hard-ceiling thresholds are NOT encoded as criterion-asserted thresholds.
- The 30%-vs-rolling-baseline regression gate is NOT in CI.
- The 100 MB resident-memory budget is NOT measured.
- The eval-harness ↔ ranking-change CI tie-in (rerun eval whenever `ee-search` or `ee-pack` changes) is NOT in CI.
- A GAP bead acknowledges that benches break `cargo check --all-targets`.

This epic exists so the plan's performance promises become CI-blocked invariants, not aspirational targets a human might forget to check.

## Cross-cutting constraints (apply to every child bead under this epic)

- Each criterion bench encodes the §28 p50 + hard-ceiling target as a custom assertion.
- A rolling-baseline JSON file in `benches/baseline.json` is updated by a manual command (`scripts/update_perf_baseline.sh`) but read-only in CI; CI fails if any bench's last result is more than 30% worse than the baseline.
- Memory budget is measured via `psutil`-style sampling (or libc rusage) in a wrapper test; assertions are inclusive of warm cache (after one no-op invocation).
- Eval-harness changes a `ee.eval.v1` JSON envelope; CI uses git diff to detect when files matching `src/search/**` or `src/pack/**` changed and gates the merge on a green eval.
- Tests log: bench name, last p50, last p99, baseline value, regression %, pass/fail status, total elapsed_ms.

## Closure criteria

- All 16 §28 latency rows are encoded as criterion benches with targets.
- The rolling-baseline regression gate is enforced in CI on every PR.
- The 100 MB resident-memory check is implemented and run in CI.
- The eval-harness CI tie-in is wired up.
- The "benches break `cargo check --all-targets`" GAP is closed.

## Verification path

- Bench files under `benches/`.
- CI workflow updates under `.github/workflows/`.
- E2E in `tests/perf_budget.rs` (only checks the harness, not the actual numbers — the bench is the assertion).

title: [HIGH] Pack item redaction happens post-budget — usedTokens / estimatedTokens over-report rendered content
description:
## Surface
`src/pack/mod.rs` MMR / facility-location selection + emit (audit cycle 5)

## Finding
The new `PackDraftItem::from_selected_candidate` (`src/pack/mod.rs:1252-1284`, added in HEAD's working diff) calls `redact_pack_item_content` AFTER the candidate has already been weighed against the token budget:

```rust
fn from_selected_candidate(rank: u32, candidate: PackCandidate) -> Self {
    let PackCandidate { content, estimated_tokens, ... } = candidate;
    let (content, redactions) = redact_pack_item_content(content);
    Self { content, estimated_tokens, redactions, ... }
}
```

`estimated_tokens` is preserved unchanged. But `content` may now be substantially shorter (every redacted secret becomes `[REDACTED:scanner_name]`).

Effects:
1. `response.data.pack.budget.usedTokens` (sum of items' `estimated_tokens`) over-reports the actual size of rendered content.
2. `item.estimatedTokens` in JSON no longer matches `item.content` for redacted items.
3. `compute_pack_hash` (`src/core/context.rs:524-548`) hashes the redacted content AND the un-redacted estimated_tokens — internally consistent, so determinism is fine, but the hash certifies a number that is wrong.
4. Pack underutilizes its budget: secret-heavy content gets penalized 'as if' it was full size, leaving room unused.

## Determinism: not broken
Redaction is deterministic (`SECRET_REDACTION_PLACEHOLDER` is a literal const, reasons sorted+deduped). Same input → byte-identical JSON. `tests/e2e_pack_determinism.rs` still passes.

## Honesty: broken
The JSON contract advertises `usedTokens` / `estimatedTokens` as 'cost of the rendered content'. Post-emit redaction breaks that claim.

## Fix options
A) Recompute `estimated_tokens` after redaction inside `from_selected_candidate` (and revisit `used_tokens` accumulation if the algorithm wants to backfill the saved budget into the next omitted candidate).
B) Redact at candidate-construction time so the budget sees the post-redaction size from the start. Cleaner, but coupling between candidates_from_search and policy::redact_secret_like_content.
C) Keep current behavior but add an explicit field `item.preRedactionEstimatedTokens` and document the over-counting in the contract.

## Repro
```bash
# look at git diff HEAD -- src/pack/mod.rs lines 1252-1284 and 1298-1310
```
close_reason: Fixed in 053917e: pack candidates are redacted before selection token accounting, so rendered item estimates, usedTokens, and selection-certificate costs align.

title: HIGH: migrations can partially apply without ee_schema_migrations records
description:
Reviewer finding in src/db/.

Evidence:
- src/db/mod.rs:189-218 already exposes transaction helpers.
- src/db/mod.rs:2263-2282 migrate applies migration.sql with execute_raw_for and only then inserts the ee_schema_migrations record.
- There is no transaction covering the DDL plus record_migration step.

Impact:
A crash, interruption, or storage error after DDL succeeds but before record_migration succeeds leaves the schema mutated but unrecorded. The next migrate run will try to replay the same CREATE/ALTER statements; any non-idempotent DDL can fail and leave the DB stuck even though the desired tables/columns may already exist.

Suggested fix:
Run each migration SQL and its ee_schema_migrations insert in one transaction, preferably BEGIN IMMEDIATE for file-backed databases. Add a failure-injection test that forces record_migration to fail and verifies migrate can be retried without schema drift.
close_reason: Wrapped each migration SQL and ee_schema_migrations insert in one transaction, with rollback/retry test coverage.

title: SRR4: Roaring-bitmap tag indexes + Bloom prefilters + cross-platform SIMD BM25
description:
# SRR4 — Search Hot Path: Bitmap Tags + Prefilters + SIMD BM25

## Context

`ee search` today routes through Frankensearch's `TwoTierSearcher`. For the 'select memories whose tags include X and Y but not Z' style of filter, the current path materializes intermediate `HashSet<MemoryId>`s and intersects them. For high-cardinality tags this is the bottleneck. Meanwhile, the BM25 scoring stage is scalar, leaving 50-90% of available FLOPS on the floor on AVX-512 / NEON hardware.

SRR4 layers three accelerators behind a single feature flag:

1. **Roaring-bitmap per-tag indexes.** A Roaring bitmap holds the sorted `MemoryId` set for each tag. Tag-intersection becomes a constant-factor bitmap AND. Negation (`NOT containing tag Z`) becomes a difference. Cardinality estimates are O(1).
2. **Bloom prefilters for negation-rich queries.** When a query has `NOT IN (tag_X, tag_Y, ...)`, the prefilter rejects candidates without a Roaring lookup. Tunes false-positive rate from config; default 1%.
3. **Cross-platform SIMD BM25.** Vectorize the inner loop of BM25 token scoring using `std::simd` portable SIMD (or runtime-detected AVX-512 / NEON intrinsics on stable Rust via `is_x86_feature_detected!` / `cfg!(target_arch)`). Falls back to scalar when unavailable.

All three are independently toggleable via `[search.hot_path]` config keys; defaults enable when capabilities are present.

## Why this is the right shape

- **Frankensearch contract honored** — these are *complements* to Frankensearch's hybrid retriever, not replacements. The Roaring index is a pre-stage filter; the SIMD BM25 is a hot inner loop within Frankensearch's lexical arm via an extension point. Coordinate with `frankensearch-core` upstream for the BM25 vectorization hook.
- **Deterministic** — bitmap operations are well-defined; SIMD-scalar results must be bit-identical (we use integer accumulator paths, not floating-point reduction).
- **Cross-platform** — runtime feature detection; never compile-time assumes AVX-512 unless caller opts in.
- **AGENTS.md compliant** — no new forbidden deps; uses `roaring` (no Tokio/no rusqlite/no petgraph), portable SIMD stable since Rust 1.62 on stable for the integer subset we need.

## Acceptance

- `ee search 'topic AND tag:rust AND NOT tag:archived'` against a 100k-memory fixture returns top-K in p50 ≤ 1.5 ms (was ≥ 38 ms). p99 ≤ 6 ms.
- Bit-identical output: SIMD path vs scalar path produces byte-equal `score` arrays for the same input. Verified by `tests/search_simd_parity.rs`.
- Roaring index rebuild on workspace open is bounded: ≤ 200 ms for 100k memories on `mac-m3-pro`.
- `ee search --explain` JSON includes `searchHotPath: { tags: bitmap, scoring: simd_avx512|simd_neon|scalar }` for diagnosability.
- Failure mode: bitmap corruption → degraded `tag_bitmap_unavailable`, repair `ee index rebuild`.

## Test requirements

- Unit: `src/search/tag_bitmaps.rs` ships inline tests for: build_index_empty, build_index_dense, intersection_correctness, negation_correctness, bloom_false_positive_rate_within_budget.
- Unit: `src/search/bm25_simd.rs` ships SIMD-vs-scalar parity tests for at least four input shapes (empty, single-doc, sparse, dense).
- Property: `tests/property_search_simd_parity.rs` — for any (query, corpus) pair, SIMD and scalar agree byte-for-byte.
- Integration: `tests/search_hot_path_integration.rs` against fixture corpus, asserts ranking determinism and explain output shape.
- E2E: `scripts/e2e_overhaul/search_hot_path.sh` exercises `ee search` with bitmap and SIMD on/off, asserts identical top-K with different timings.
- Perf: `benches/search_hot_path.rs` criterion bench; budget pinned in `benches/budgets.toml`.
- Cross-platform: `tests/cross_platform_determinism.rs` (bd-3usjw.25) extended with search-hot-path output hashes.
- Failure-mode fixtures: `tag_bitmap_unavailable.json`, `simd_unavailable_fell_back_to_scalar.json`.

## File surface

- `src/search/tag_bitmaps.rs` (NEW) — Roaring index build, persist, intersect, negate.
- `src/search/bloom_prefilter.rs` (NEW) — counting Bloom filter for negation hints.
- `src/search/bm25_simd.rs` (NEW) — portable SIMD BM25 inner loop + runtime-feature dispatch.
- `src/search/hot_path.rs` (NEW) — coordinator wiring bitmap → Bloom → BM25 → Frankensearch tier.
- `src/core/effect.rs` (EXTENDED) — search effect routes through hot_path when enabled.
- `src/config/mod.rs` (EXTENDED) — `[search.hot_path].tag_bitmaps`, `bloom_prefilter`, `simd_bm25` toggles.
- `docs/adr/00XX-search-hot-path.md` (NEW).
- Possible upstream PR: `frankensearch-core` extension point for vectorized BM25.

## Rejected alternatives

1. Bitmap intersection via `bit-vec` — slower than Roaring on sparse-to-dense mixtures.
2. AVX-512 only (compile-time) — breaks Linux x86_64 musl portability and aarch64.
3. f32 SIMD reductions — non-deterministic across CPUs (associativity differs). Stay integer or fixed-point.
4. Push everything to Frankensearch — that crate owns embedding policy, not lexical-index micro-optimization for our specific tag-cardinality profile.

## Dependencies on other beads

- Independent of other SRR children.
- Synergy with bd-3usjw.25 (cross_platform_determinism harness) — the SIMD-parity test rides that harness.
- Bd-17c65.14.10 (N10 SIMD BM25) overlaps partially — this bead generalizes that one to runtime-detected SIMD with full bitmap + Bloom integration; we should close N10 as 'superseded by SRR4' before starting work, OR merge the two beads.

## Risk

- SIMD code paths are easy to break under refactor → integer-accumulator-only design + bit-identical parity test catches drift.
- Roaring index disk size growth → cap at 5% of DB size; degrade with `tag_bitmap_oversized`.

## Cost of omission

For workspaces with >50k memories and tag-heavy queries, the difference is 'is this tool real-time' vs 'this tool stalls my agent'. SRR4 is what makes `ee` viable at memory-corpus scale.
