title: EE-TST-008: Define per-bead closure evidence dossier and closeout checklist
description:
Define the standard evidence package future agents must produce before closing implementation beads.

Background:
The backlog now contains detailed acceptance criteria and broad testing requirements, but real-world agent implementation still needs a uniform closeout protocol. Without one, future agents can honestly run useful checks yet leave vague close reasons that do not prove what changed, which public contracts were exercised, which artifacts were produced, or which degradations were intentionally skipped. EE should make closure evidence as structured as its memory evidence.

Scope:
- Define a per-bead closure dossier schema or template for implementation work.
- Specify what must be captured for code, docs, schema, test, e2e, fixture, and readiness-gate beads.
- Tie the dossier to the existing test strategy, golden/schema runner, e2e artifact policy, and failure replay artifacts.
- Require future agents to include enough evidence in the close reason or linked artifact summary that another agent can validate the closure without rereading the original markdown plan.
- Keep generated closure artifacts out of commits unless they are intentional golden fixtures or tracked documentation.

Why this improves user outcomes:
EE is designed for agents, and agents need trustworthy handoffs. A closure dossier turns every completed bead into a small audit record: what user behavior changed, how it was verified, what degraded states were covered, where logs live, and what remains intentionally out of scope. That reduces silent feature loss, shallow testing, stdout contract regressions, and hard-to-debug partial implementations.

## Acceptance Criteria

Detailed closure criteria are stored in this bead's structured acceptance_criteria field. Treat those criteria as part of this bead's implementation contract, including comprehensive testing, e2e evidence, and logging requirements.
design:
Recommended design:
- Use a small structured schema such as `closure_dossier.v1` plus a concise human-readable summary. The exact storage path can be implementation-driven, but it should be discoverable from the bead close reason, final comment, or verification artifact directory.
- Required fields should include bead id/title, implementation summary, files changed by category, public commands/contracts affected, unit tests run, e2e/golden/schema/eval fixtures run, stdout/stderr isolation status, redaction status, artifact paths, skipped checks with rationale, degraded/offline cases covered, dependency or readiness-gate impact, and follow-up bead IDs.
- The dossier should be easy for agents to emit during normal work: one closeout checklist, deterministic field names, no prose-only critical data, and no dependence on hidden global state.
- The dossier should be validated by the same verification ecosystem as command outputs: schema checks, golden examples, redaction checks, and failure replay links where appropriate.
- Do not turn this into bureaucratic overhead for trivial documentation beads; define a lightweight profile for docs-only work and a full profile for implementation, public contract, storage, evaluation, and safety-critical beads.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

Acceptance criteria:
- A `closure_dossier.v1` schema or equivalent template is defined with required and optional fields for feature, chore, docs, gate, test-harness, and epic closeouts.
- The template requires explicit evidence for commands run, unit tests, e2e scripts, golden/schema contracts, evaluation/replay fixtures, artifact/log paths, stdout/stderr isolation, redaction status, degraded/offline coverage, and skipped checks with rationale.
- The template includes examples for at least four cases: a small docs-only bead, a CLI feature bead, a storage/indexing bead, and an epic/readiness-gate bead.
- The closeout rules state that generated artifacts stay out of commits unless they are intentional fixtures or tracked docs, while close reasons or final bead comments must include enough summary data to locate and interpret artifacts.
- CI/local verification orchestration and failure triage tasks know how to validate or reference closure dossiers without requiring agents to reread the markdown plan.
- The rules explicitly prevent closing a bead with vague claims such as "tests pass" unless concrete commands, results, and relevant artifact locations are recorded.

Testing and logging requirements:
- Add or update unit tests for core logic introduced or changed by this bead, covering happy path, boundary/empty inputs, invalid inputs, degraded dependencies, deterministic ordering, and idempotency/mutation rules as applicable.
- If the behavior is visible through the CLI, MCP, hook, export, renderer, or evaluation output, add or extend a real-binary e2e, golden, schema, contract, replay, or evaluation fixture that exercises the public surface in an isolated local workspace.
- E2E/logged tests must capture command, cwd/workspace, sanitized environment overrides, elapsed time, exit code, stdout/stderr artifact paths, schema/golden validation status, redaction status, and a concise first-failure diagnosis.
- Stdout assertions must prove stdout contains only machine data; diagnostics, progress, and debugging context must go to stderr or explicit artifacts.
- If no executable test is appropriate for this bead, the close reason or a br comment must explain why and identify the nearest bead that provides coverage.

title: EE-FEEDBACK-RATE-001: Add harmful-feedback rate limiting, protected rules, and asymmetric inversion threshold
description:
Make the harmful-feedback signal robust against accidental and adversarial misuse without weakening its protective effect.

Background:
The README documents that harmful feedback decays trust faster than helpful feedback promotes it (harmful_weight 2.5 in the default config) and that two harmful events can invert a rule into an anti-pattern. H2 adversarial review pointed out that this asymmetry is exactly what an attacker (or a careless agent) needs to weaponise: an agent can mark unrelated rules harmful in bulk and silently invert the trust of the whole procedural layer. F4 failure-mode review flagged that even non-adversarial agents misclick or misroute outcome events under fatigue.

The bead set has feedback infrastructure (Epic: Feedback And Rules) and ee outcome (the README example shows `ee outcome --memory <id> --helpful` and `--harmful`). The trust class enum (EE-260), trauma metadata, and decay scoring all assume harmful events are scarce and high-signal. They are not robust to a fast burst of harmful events from a single source, and there is no protected_rule mechanism for memories the user has explicitly endorsed.

Intended scope:
This bead adds three guards on top of the existing feedback path, not a parallel system:
- Per-source rate limit on harmful outcome events (default: max 5 harmful events per source per hour, configurable). Excess events are recorded in a quarantine table with stable provenance and require a reviewer action before they affect scoring.
- Protected rule mechanism: `ee rule protect <id>` (and a flag on `ee remember` for human_explicit memories) marks a rule as resistant to inversion. Protected rules require harmful_count >= max(2, helpful_count * 2 + 1) before any inversion or auto-disposition, and any attempt is auditable.
- Asymmetric inversion threshold: the simple "two harmful = invert" path becomes a deterministic rule that requires evidence diversity (harmful events must come from at least two distinct sessions or sources) and a non-empty decay window where no helpful event arrived. The exact rule is named in the ADR and pinned by golden tests.

Public surface: `ee rule protect <id> [--unprotect] --json`, `ee outcome quarantine list/release --json`, and a stable degraded code feedback_quarantined when the rate limit fires.

Why this matters:
The harmful-feedback path is the only reliable way the system corrects itself. If it is fragile to bursts or single-source spam, agents will distrust outcome events as a class, and the entire feedback loop collapses.

## Acceptance Criteria

Detailed closure criteria are stored in this bead's structured acceptance_criteria field. Treat those criteria as part of this bead's implementation contract, including harmful-feedback rate limits, protected rules, asymmetric inversion thresholds, quarantine commands, status/why output, adversarial fixtures, and e2e logging requirements.
design:
Recommended design:
- Source identity uses the existing agent identity (Epic: Agent Detection) when available; falls back to (caller_pid, caller_command_hash) otherwise. The same source id rule that powers cass import idempotency (EE-067) is reused.
- Rate-limit state lives in a small FrankenSQLite table (feedback_rate_state) keyed by (source_id, hour_bucket). Cleanup is part of the steward (Epic: Steward) so old buckets do not accumulate.
- Quarantine release is non-destructive by default (release moves the event into the live feedback path; reject moves it into a tombstoned audit row). The user can always replay the quarantine via the support bundle.
- Inversion thresholds are encoded as configuration with documented defaults; do not hardcode 2 distinct sessions or 2 helpful + 1 harmful in code paths. The ADR pins the defaults and the test suite exercises the boundary cases.
- Protected rules surface clearly in `ee why <id>` so agents understand why a known-good rule will not invert.
- Compose with EE-CONC-001 (advisory lock: protect/unprotect is a write op), EE-CURATE-TTL-001 (auto-disposition must respect protected mark), and EE-TRUST-RECON-001 (taxonomy decides which trust classes can ever be protected by default).
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

Acceptance criteria:
- A new feedback_quarantine table records per-source harmful event bursts with: source_id, memory_id, recorded_at, reason, raw_event_hash. Quarantined events do not affect scoring until released.
- Per-source rate limiting is configurable via [feedback].harmful_per_source_per_hour (default 5) and [feedback].harmful_burst_window_seconds (default 3600). Defaults are documented in the README config table.
- Protected rules are marked via a protected boolean on the rule row. The mark is set by `ee rule protect <id> --json`, by `ee remember --protect` for human_explicit memories, and by the curation auto-promote path only with explicit user consent. The mark is auditable and visible in `ee why <id>`.
- Inversion of a non-protected rule requires at least two harmful events from distinct sessions or sources within the decay window with no intervening helpful event from the same set of sources. The deterministic rule is documented in the ADR (links to EE-TRUST-RECON-001) and pinned by a golden test.
- Inversion of a protected rule requires harmful_count >= max(2, helpful_count * 2 + 1) AND a manual `ee curate apply` event AND a non-empty audit comment justifying the inversion. Auto-paths cannot invert protected rules.
- `ee outcome quarantine list --json` is read-only and lists all quarantined events with full provenance. `ee outcome quarantine release <id> --json` releases a single event, recording the action in the audit log; `--reject` discards it; both paths emit stable degraded codes when applicable.
- `ee status --json` includes a feedback_health block: per-source harmful counts in the burst window, quarantine queue depth, protected rule count, last inversion event, and the next deterministic action.

Testing and logging requirements:
- Unit tests cover rate limit math under frozen time (4 events at boundary, 5 at threshold, 6 over), quarantine insertion, deterministic inversion rule (2 same-source vs 2 distinct-source events), and protected rule inversion gate.
- Property tests assert: rate limit is monotonic in time, quarantine never deletes evidence, protected rules are never silently inverted, helpful_count is always non-negative, and the inversion rule is deterministic across process restarts.
- Adversarial fixtures cover: a single source emitting 100 harmful events in 60 seconds (rate-limited), two sources colluding to emit 2+2 harmful events on the same rule (inversion fires), a single source spamming harmful then quietly emitting helpful (must not auto-clear quarantine), and a protected rule receiving a flood of harmful events (no inversion until manual curation).
- Integration tests using the real ee binary register a memory, mark it protected, attempt inversion, verify denial, then unprotect, attempt inversion again, verify success, then check the audit log shape end-to-end.
- E2E logs capture commands, source ids, frozen-time clock anchor, quarantine deltas, and audit log diffs for every transition.
- Stdout assertions prove only machine data leaves stdout for `ee rule protect`, `ee outcome quarantine list/release/reject`, and `ee status --json`.
- Closeout evidence cites the deterministic inversion fixture, the protected rule fixture, the rate-limit boundary fixture, and the adversarial corpus.
notes: Closes the H2 weaponization vector flagged by adversarial review (single-source harmful burst inverts unrelated rules) and the F4 fragility flagged by failure mode (unprotected human_explicit rules can be auto-inverted by misrouted outcome events). Default rate (5/hour) and inversion threshold (2 distinct sources, no intervening helpful) chosen to be conservative; both are configurable.
close_reason: Harmful-feedback rate limiting complete: per-source limits, quarantine table, list/release/reject, distinct-source inversion. 2308 tests pass including quarantine_reject, rate_limit, and distinct_sources fixtures.

title: [PERF] db::insert_pack_record: per-item pack persistence executes many statements
description:
Path: ee context -> src/core/context.rs:408 persist_pack_record -> src/core/context.rs:478 builds pack item inputs -> src/db/mod.rs:7936 insert_pack_record.
Code evidence: src/db/mod.rs:7946 inserts the pack record once, src/db/mod.rs:7965 loops over every pack item and executes one INSERT each, and src/db/mod.rs:7988 loops over every omission and executes one INSERT each.
Suspected complexity: O(i + o) separate DB execute calls per context request, where i is selected items and o is omitted candidates; with 100 candidate_pool this can dominate small-pack latency and creates avoidable write contention.
Suggested fix: wrap pack record/items/omissions in one explicit transaction and add batch insert helpers or multi-row insertion where SQLModel/FrankenSQLite supports it. Preserve stable audit semantics and rollback on partial failure.
Verification plan: benchmark the canonical `ee context "fix failing release workflow" --workspace . --max-tokens 4000 --json` with candidate_pool 100/500 and compare DB execute count, p95 latency, and pack row integrity before/after.

title: Audit baseline infrastructure commands as boring mechanical surfaces
description:
## Background

The audit focused on smart-sounding command families, but `ee` also has many boring infrastructure commands that must remain strictly mechanical: `init`, `remember`, `outcome`, `import`, `index`, `workspace`, `profile`, `db`, `backup`, `restore`, `export`, `eval`, `completion`, and related config/status paths. These are not candidates for skills; they are the substrate that skills and agents depend on.

This bead makes those baseline surfaces explicit so they are not protected only indirectly by the command coverage matrix.

## Acceptance Criteria

See this bead's structured acceptance_criteria field for the detailed completion contract, including unit/static checks, e2e or docs/e2e coverage, detailed logging, and no-feature-loss requirements.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

title: [GAP] ee import cass lacks --since <duration> flag — M3 acceptance + North Star Scenario 3 cannot run as documented
close_reason: Implemented --since duration filtering for ee import cass

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Plan §29 M3 sample: `ee import cass --workspace . --since 90d --json`. Plan North Star Scenario 3 uses the same flag verbatim.

Current src/cli/mod.rs:3296-3312 CassImportArgs has --limit, --database, --dry-run, --no-spans. No --since.

Concrete impact: scenario-level acceptance test for 'Repeated CI failure becomes procedural memory' cannot run as documented; all callers must either accept the default 10-session limit or pass --limit <huge>, which is wasteful and not what the plan promised. The 90d window is the bounded-history contract — without it, every import is implicitly 'all sessions ever' bounded only by --limit, which couples session age to session count incorrectly.

Fix scope (small, isolated):
1. Add --since <duration> to CassImportArgs (clap-parses humantime-style: 90d, 24h, 7d3h)
2. Plumb through to CassImportOptions.since: Option<DateTime<Utc>> (now - duration)
3. import_cass_sessions filters by session.started_at >= since
4. Add --since to dry-run rendering output so users see the window applied
5. Test: fixture cass DB at tests/fixtures/cass/ has sessions across 100+ days; --since 30d returns N sessions, --since 90d returns M, --since omitted returns the default-limit slice as today
6. Document in the help text that --since and --limit AND together (not OR)

Honor the 'no destructive scope creep' principle: --since adds a filter, doesn't remove --limit.

title: Classify every ee command against the mechanical CLI boundary
description:
## Background

Before implementation changes, the project needs a complete command inventory that classifies every command family by responsibility. The audit showed direct LLM/API dependencies are absent, but command names and outputs can still cross the boundary by simulating judgment or returning sample conclusions.

This bead creates the authoritative classification table future work depends on. It must cover `src/cli/mod.rs` command variants and their core handlers, not only the obvious risky modules.

## Classification categories

- Mechanical CLI: deterministic computation over explicit inputs, persisted DB rows, local files, generated indexes, frozen fixtures, hashes, schemas, and graph projections.
- Agent skill: qualitative synthesis, task planning, procedure authoring, causal interpretation, preflight questioning, learning experiment design, or other work that requires intelligence around evidence.
- Mixed: command must be split into a mechanical Rust sub-surface plus a project-local skill workflow.
- Degraded/unavailable: command shape may remain, but must return stable degraded JSON until it can be implemented honestly.

## Audit anchors

Known risky surfaces include lab, causal, learn, procedure, preflight, tripwire, rehearse, certificate/claims, economy, situation/plan, recorder tail/follow, memory revise, and status health. The inventory must still inspect the whole CLI, including commands that currently look safe.
design:
Create a durable markdown or generated report, but do not rely on the old chat audit as the source of truth. Walk from `src/cli/mod.rs` command enums to each handler and core module. For every command, record: command path, handler, core module, current data sources, whether it reads persisted state, whether it emits mock/sample/stub data, whether it gives recommendations, and target disposition.

Prefer a checked-in artifact under project docs only if implementation work for this bead requires it. The bead itself must identify the intended artifact path before implementation.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance criteria

- Inventory covers every CLI command path exposed by `ee --help-json` or the Clap command enum.
- Each command path has a target disposition: keep mechanical, split, move to skill, degrade/unavailable, or retire only if explicitly approved by a later bead.
- Every command currently using mock/sample/stub/simulated data is listed with file and line anchors.
- Every command that emits recommendations, next actions, confidence, causality, risk, procedure, learning, or planning language is reviewed for boundary fit.
- Unit tests or snapshot tests cover the inventory generator if a generator is introduced.
- An e2e script records and logs `ee --help-json`, command path count, unmapped command count, elapsed time, exit code, stdout/stderr paths, command matrix coverage, and first-failure diagnosis.
- The output is self-contained enough that future agents do not need the original audit conversation.

title: [release] GitHub Actions release workflow with cross-platform builds and Sigstore signing
description:
## Background
README claims: The release workflow should detect a version change in Cargo.toml, tag, build cross-platform binaries, sign with Sigstore, and upload to GitHub Releases. No such workflow exists.

## What ships
.github/workflows/release.yml:
1. Trigger: push to main where Cargo.toml [package].version changed.
2. Job 1: tag (extracts new version, creates and pushes tag vX.Y.Z).
3. Job 2: matrix build for the 5 targets in [release] install.sh bead. Each builds via cargo (or rch exec -- cargo when available), produces tar.xz, generates SHA256 (.sha256), signs via cosign (.sigstore.json).
4. Job 3: gh release create with all assets attached + install.sh + install.ps1 copies + auto-generated release notes from CHANGELOG (or git log since last tag).
5. Forbidden-deps audit gate: no release if cargo tree shows any forbidden crate.
6. Vision-coverage gate (post-Wave 0): no release if gap_percentage > 0 unless --allow-gap override label present.
7. Post-release smoke: run install.sh against the just-published release in a clean container.

## Acceptance
- A version bump on main triggers the full pipeline; assets land on the GitHub release.
- Sigstore bundle verifies via cosign verify.
- All 5 platform tarballs install cleanly via install.sh.
- Closure linter passes.

title: F2: Algorithm wrapper conventions — CGSE witnesses + sampling + budget for 15 fnx algorithms
description:
# F2 — Algorithm wrapper conventions (CGSE witnesses + sampling + budget)

## Why this is foundational

The 10 features in this epic will call ~15 different fnx_algorithms functions: personalized_pagerank, hits, katz_centrality, communicability_betweenness, group_betweenness, voterank, louvain_communities, k_truss_rust, onion_layers_rust, articulation_points, transitive_closure, transitive_reduction, dominance_frontiers, immediate_dominators, antichains, all_pairs_lca_rust, voronoi_cells_rust, gomory_hu_tree_rust, min_cost_flow, ego_graph_rust, simrank_similarity_rust, modularity, etc.

Today's two algorithm wrappers (pagerank, betweenness) each independently handle: input validation, CGSE compatibility mode (Strict vs Hardened), result construction, error mapping. There is no shared pattern for: timeouts (large graphs hang Dijkstra-family algorithms), sampling fallbacks (betweenness uses pivot sampling for |V|>500, but no other algorithm does), or witness recording (`fnx_runtime::CgseValue` carries complexity counters but they're not always saved).

If we let each of the 10 features re-invent the wheel, we'll ship 10 inconsistent wrappers and the inevitable bug-fix sweeps will be 10× worse.

## What

Build a single algorithm-wrapper module — `src/graph/algorithms.rs` — that provides:

1. **`run_with_budget<R, F>(name, budget, f) -> Result<R, GraphError>`** — wraps any fnx algorithm call with a soft timeout. If the call exceeds `budget` (default: 250ms foreground, 2s background), return `GraphError::Timeout`. Implementation: spawn a worker thread via asupersync (no tokio), join with timeout. Honor the asupersync Cx pattern.

2. **`run_with_sampling<R, F>(name, |V|, sample_threshold, sample_size, f_exact, f_approx) -> R`** — if |V| < threshold (default 500), call f_exact; else call f_approx with sample_size pivots (default 100). Records sampling choice in CGSE witness. Same idea as beads_viewer's betweenness fallback.

3. **`emit_complexity_witness(name, snapshot_version, params, observed_counters)`** — every algorithm wrapper records a JSON witness with: algorithm name, snapshot content_hash, parameter values, fnx_runtime CGSE counters (path-decision hash, edge-traversal count, etc.), wall-clock elapsed_ms, sampling info if used, and CGSE compatibility mode. Witnesses store in a new table `graph_algorithm_witnesses` (workspace_id, snapshot_id, algorithm, params_json, witness_json, recorded_at).

4. **`with_cgse_mode<R>(mode, f) -> R`** — explicit Strict/Hardened mode toggle, defaulting to Strict (matches existing pagerank wrapper). Some algorithms (e.g., voronoi_cells with non-unique distances) need Hardened to fall through deterministically.

5. **Common error envelope** — every wrapper returns `GraphError` (already exists in src/graph/mod.rs) with typed variants: AlgorithmTimeout, AlgorithmFailed, InvalidInput, SnapshotStale, FnxError(String). No `Result<T, String>` leakage.

## How (key implementation choices)

- **No async runtime change**: Use asupersync (existing). No tokio.
- **Witness writing**: Best-effort, never blocks. If write fails, log and continue.
- **CGSE policies**: Use existing fnx_runtime::CgseValue path-decision hashes. Same tie-break policy as existing pagerank wrapper.
- **Determinism**: Every algorithm wrapper must produce byte-identical outputs across 3 runs against the same snapshot — including witness hashes (modulo wall-clock fields). This is verified by F4.

## Tests

- Unit test: `run_with_budget` returns Timeout when f sleeps past budget.
- Unit test: `run_with_sampling` chooses exact vs approx based on |V|.
- Unit test: `emit_complexity_witness` writes a row and round-trips through JSON.
- E2E: real fnx_algorithms call wrapped, snapshot built, witness emitted, all in <500ms on 100-node fixture.

## Acceptance

- New module `src/graph/algorithms.rs` lands.
- 5 helper functions implemented and tested.
- One existing wrapper (pagerank) refactored to use the new helpers as a proof point — no behavior change.
- New `graph_algorithm_witnesses` table via migration.
- All wrappers in features G1-G10 use this module.

## Dependencies

Blocks: G1-G10 (every feature uses these helpers).
Parent: bd-bife.

## Related code

- `src/graph/mod.rs:refresh_centrality` — current pagerank/betweenness pattern
- `fnx_runtime::CgseValue` — already used; extend to record full counters per algorithm
- ADR 0008 (Graph metrics as derived state)

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel
comments.text:
## Phase 6 refinement notes — metrics cache key + concurrency

1. **Cache key**: Add F2.e (algorithm result cache) — a function-level cache keyed by (algorithm_name, snapshot_content_hash, sorted_params). Cache hit returns the previously computed result; cache miss runs the algorithm. Cache lives in graph_algorithm_witnesses with a 'result_json' column (or a sibling table graph_algorithm_results). Eviction: same as snapshot eviction (RX7).

2. **Cache invalidation**: Snapshot refresh invalidates ALL cached results for that snapshot's graph_type. The witness table records snapshot_id, so invalidation is a single DELETE WHERE snapshot_id < latest.

3. **Concurrency**: Multiple agents calling ee context simultaneously will all want PPR. The wrapper must use a per-(algorithm, snapshot_hash, params) compute-once-share-many lock (think Once<T> in std). Without this, 10 concurrent ee context calls all compute PPR independently, wasting 270ms each.

4. **F2.f**: Hash-stability test. The (algorithm_name, snapshot_content_hash, sorted_params) key must be byte-stable across runs. Sorted_params canonicalization: serialize to deterministic JSON (BTreeMap, no floating-point representation drift). Test: 3 invocations with same logical params (different insertion order) produce the same key.

Add bd-igvt.7 (cache key + concurrency) and bd-igvt.8 (hash stability) subtasks.

comments.text: Round 4 operations pinning. Worker_id assignment: worker_id=blake3(hostname+pid+graph_type)[:16]; worker_expires_at=now+300s; expired locks auto-reclaimable. Log message conventions: tracing! macros, snake_case fields. Standard fields: elapsed_ms (i64), algorithm (str), snapshot_id (i64), graph_type (str), cache_hit (bool), degraded_count (i32). Log levels: TRACE per-iteration; DEBUG per-algorithm-invoke; INFO per-snapshot-refresh; WARN on timeout/sampling/scale; ERROR on algorithm failure returning Err. F2.cache concurrency: compute_or_load returns shared future; concurrent same-key calls share one computation; cache stores result_json once; cache hit deserializes back to typed R; failed deserialization = cache miss + warn. Each wrapper emits one tracing event per invocation (per RX22 telemetry taxonomy).

title: F2.bench: Criterion perf benches for PPR + Louvain + k-truss + Gomory-Hu + HITS
description:
## Why
The 'phased precompute' design principle (foreground ≤250ms, background ≤2s) requires benches that fail when these thresholds are exceeded. Mirror benches/context.rs pattern.

## Bench targets
- benches/graph_ppr.rs (group: graph_ppr) — assert PPR adds ≤30ms p50 on 1k-memory workspace (G1's spec).
- benches/graph_louvain.rs (group: graph_louvain) — Louvain ≤100ms on 1k nodes (G4 budget).
- benches/graph_ktruss.rs (group: graph_ktruss) — k-truss ≤150ms on 10k-edge subgraph (G4 budget).
- benches/graph_gomory_hu.rs (group: graph_gomory_hu) — build ≤5s on 1k nodes, query ≤0.1ms (G6 budget).
- benches/graph_hits.rs (group: graph_hits) — HITS ≤100ms on 1k nodes (G10 budget).

Each bench:
1. Uses the in-process harness (LabRuntime, hash embedder).
2. Seeds 3 scales (10/100/1000 memories).
3. Asserts hard ceiling per scale.
4. Commits baseline JSON under benches/baselines/graph-v0.1.json.

title: F2.cache: Algorithm-result cache keyed by (algorithm, snapshot_hash, params)
description:
## Why
PPR runs on every ee context query. Cold compute is ~30ms; cache hit is <0.5ms. 10 concurrent agents calling ee context independently = 270ms of wasted work / cache thrash.

## Tasks
1. New table: graph_algorithm_results (workspace_id, snapshot_id, algorithm, params_hash, result_json, computed_at, ttl_seconds). PRIMARY KEY (workspace_id, snapshot_id, algorithm, params_hash).
2. F2's wrappers consult cache BEFORE invoking fnx. Cache key = blake3((algorithm, snapshot_content_hash, canonical_serialized_params)).
3. Cache eviction: results older than the most recent snapshot for the same graph_type are deleted (one DELETE per snapshot refresh).
4. Concurrency: per-key Once<T>-style lock prevents 10 agents from computing the same result in parallel.

## Acceptance
- Migration adds graph_algorithm_results table.
- F2's run_with_budget consults cache; cache hit returns immediately.
- Concurrency test: 10 parallel threads request the same algorithm → only ONE actually computes (rest wait).
- 4 unit tests + 1 perf test.

Parent: bd-igvt. Blocked by: F2.c (witnesses table — cache lives alongside).
close_reason: Closed from StormyCove/DarkDuck RCH evidence: graph_algorithm_results cache implementation, DB helpers, per-key serialization, cached-budget skip, and cache-hit perf regression are implemented and focused-verified remotely with no local fallback.

title: [HIGH] hooks: installer follows hook-path symlinks and can overwrite arbitrary targets
description: src/hooks/installer.rs:174-188 classifies existing hooks with path.exists()/read_to_string(), and src/hooks/installer.rs:294-324 writes/chmods target_path with std::fs::write/metadata/set_permissions. All of these follow symlinks. A symlink in the hook directory that points at a marker-bearing file, or a forced install over a symlink, can overwrite and chmod the symlink target outside hook_dir. Fix by using symlink_metadata/lstat, rejecting symlink hook targets, and writing via a temp file plus atomic rename/open options that do not follow symlinks.
close_reason: Fixed: check_existing_hook uses symlink_metadata (lstat), rejects symlinks with Symlink status, write_hook_file checks for symlinks before writing, added tests

title: SECURITY: raw provider tokens bypass memory redaction and can persist unredacted
description: HIGH. ee remember persists prepared.content after validate_remember_policy, but that policy is a substring deny-list (src/core/memory.rs:352, src/core/memory.rs:356, src/core/memory.rs:536). It does not invoke policy::redact_secret_like_content, and SECRET_KEY_PATTERNS only catches contextual key names (src/policy/mod.rs:25, src/policy/mod.rs:454). Raw token formats such as sk-ant-api03-..., sk-proj-..., or ghp_... without labels can be saved as memory content. Curation apply also trusts the same incomplete redactor before updating memory content (src/core/curate.rs:1827, src/core/curate.rs:1843). Impact: a local agent session can permanently store API tokens in the memory DB, search index, context packs, backups, or audit outputs. Expected fix: use a shared detector/redactor for manual memory and curation proposed_content, include provider prefix and AWS env style patterns, and add secret-pattern unit tests.

## Surface
UUIDv7 generation in ee (audit cycle 6, surface 4)

## Finding
ee depends on `uuid = { version = "1", features = ["v7"] }` (Cargo.toml). With uuid 1.10+ the `Uuid::now_v7()` impl uses a per-process atomic counter to break ties at sub-millisecond granularity, so within ONE process, IDs generated in tight bursts are monotonic.

But the monotonicity is bounded by process lifetime:
- Two ee invocations on the same host that both call now_v7() within the same millisecond start independent counters seeded from random bytes. Their IDs may interleave in arbitrary order when sorted.
- Two ee invocations on different hosts (multi-agent swarm across machines, or a backup restore from another host) have no clock-sync guarantee; clock skew of even a few ms can flip ordering.

The id-module doc comment at src/models/id.rs:21 acknowledges 48-bit timestamp + random bytes but does not state the cross-process limitation. AGENTS.md 'Key Dependencies' table lists 'uuid (v7) | Time-ordered IDs' without qualification.

## Existing test
src/models/id.rs:903-912 (`ids_from_now_v7_are_unique_within_a_burst`) only checks UNIQUENESS, not monotonic ordering across calls.

## Why it matters
1. audit_log V033 hash chain orders by insertion sequence — chain order does NOT depend on UUID ordering, so the chain itself is safe. Confirmed: src/core/audit.rs hashes prev_hash + row_payload by insert order.
2. recorder events: src/core/recorder.rs:128 generates run_id and src/core/recorder.rs:303 generates evt_<uuid>. If a downstream tool sorts events by ID for display, sub-ms bursts within one process appear in order, but events from concurrent recorder processes do not.
3. memory IDs: queries that say 'order by id desc' as a proxy for 'newest first' will be slightly wrong at sub-ms scale across processes.
4. Multi-agent swarm scenarios from project memory (active swarm session 2026-05-02) generate IDs across many panes — cross-process ordering matters.

## Severity
LOW because:
- ee almost never sorts by ID for correctness; persisted timestamps (`created_at`, `recorded_at`) provide explicit ordering.
- The hash chain is decoupled from UUID order.
- Within-process monotonicity (the most common case) IS guaranteed by uuid 1.10+.

## Fix options
A) Document the cross-process limitation in src/models/id.rs and AGENTS.md. State explicitly: 'UUIDv7 ordering is monotonic within one process; for cross-process / cross-host ordering use the explicit timestamp columns.'
B) Add a contract test that asserts intra-process burst monotonicity (>1000 IDs strictly ascending) so a future uuid-crate downgrade is caught.
C) For features that genuinely need cross-process monotonicity (none today, but the audit chain is the candidate), add an explicit sequence column populated via a transaction-scoped MAX+1 query.
close_reason: Documented UUIDv7 process-local ordering limits and added in-process monotonic burst contract test

title: [HIGH] recorder_events / audit_log have no append-only DB triggers — only post-hoc hash-chain detection
description:
Cycle-4 reviewer audit (REVIEWER pane). Surface: recorder append-only + audit append-only.

EVIDENCE:
  - grep 'CREATE TRIGGER' over src/db/mod.rs returns ZERO hits — the entire schema has no triggers.
  - V027_RECORDER_STORE (src/db/mod.rs:2611) defines recorder_events with chain hashes (event_hash, previous_event_hash, chain_status) but NO 'BEFORE UPDATE/DELETE … RAISE(ABORT)' guard.
  - V033_AUDIT_HASH_CHAIN similarly relies on row-level hashing without a write-side guard.
  - The Rust API exposes no update_recorder_event() or update_audit_log_row(), so legitimate code paths cannot mutate. But ANY raw SQL call (via DbConnection::execute_raw_for or a future migration script) will silently succeed.

DETECTION-ONLY POSTURE:
  - audit chain: src/core/audit.rs:281 verify_entries() recomputes blake3 over (id, workspace_id, timestamp, actor, action, target_type, target_id, details, surface, mutation_kind, before_hash, after_hash, prev_row_hash) and compares against this_row_hash. The existing tampering test (audit.rs:769 verify_detects_tampered_row) confirms detection works — but only when verify_audit() is invoked. Between mutation and the next verify run, the tampered state is treated as truth by every read path.
  - recorder chain: similar — chain_status='broken' is computed at INSERT time only (recorder.rs:728 RecorderEventChainStatus::for_event). No background re-verification job and no equivalent of verify_audit() for events surfaced via CLI.

CONSEQUENCE: a buggy migration that adds a column with UPDATE-style backfill, or an admin maintenance script, can silently rewrite history without immediately breaking anything user-visible.

FIX:
  Add a defensive migration (V036_APPEND_ONLY_TRIGGERS) with:
    CREATE TRIGGER recorder_events_no_update BEFORE UPDATE ON recorder_events
      BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'recorder_events is append-only'); END;
    CREATE TRIGGER recorder_events_no_delete BEFORE DELETE ON recorder_events
      WHEN OLD.run_id IS NOT NULL  -- still allow ON DELETE CASCADE from recorder_runs
      BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'recorder_events is append-only'); END;
    CREATE TRIGGER audit_log_no_update BEFORE UPDATE ON audit_log
      BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'audit_log is append-only'); END;
    CREATE TRIGGER audit_log_no_delete BEFORE DELETE ON audit_log
      BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'audit_log is append-only'); END;

  (Note: the recorder_events FK has ON DELETE CASCADE from recorder_runs — the BEFORE DELETE trigger needs to allow cascades or be omitted; UPDATE blocking is the high-value half.)

  Then add tests:
    - try UPDATE/DELETE on recorder_events through DbConnection — assert error.
    - regression: verify_audit + recorder chain still pass after migration applied.

PRIORITY rationale: HIGH not CRITICAL because chain hashing already provides detection. The trigger is defense in depth — closes the window where tampering is silent until next verify run.
close_reason: Implemented and evidenced by d3a6064 plus tests/golden/append-only-triggers.snap. V036_APPEND_ONLY_TRIGGERS installs recorder_events_no_update, audit_log_no_update, and audit_log_no_delete; recorder_events DELETE remains allowed by design for recorder_runs cascade and is tracked separately by eidetic_engine_cli-baap. Verified via RCH: cargo test --lib append_only_trigger passed 4/4, and cargo test --lib deleting_recorder_run_still_cascades_to_events passed 1/1. Closure linter surface snapshot exists for implements-surface:append-only-triggers.

title: [CONCURRENCY-TEST] cass import: sequential ledger smoke test misses concurrent lost update
description:
Files: tests/smoke.rs:2910, tests/smoke.rs:3019, src/cass/import.rs:766, src/cass/import.rs:814.
Code path: the existing smoke coverage runs a first import, closes the connection, then runs a second import and checks attempt_count == 2 plus preserved imported totals. That verifies sequential resumption but cannot catch the concurrent read-modify-write interleaving in ensure_running_ledger and complete_ledger.
Hazard: the test suite can pass while two real imports started at the same time lose attempt/import counters or turn one duplicate session into a storage error.
Repro plan: add a new concurrent smoke/integration test using a temporary file DB, a deterministic CASS fixture, and two threads or subprocesses synchronized at import start. Assert both commands exit success, exactly one session is imported, the other is skipped, and the ledger attempt/import counters reflect both callers.

comments.text:
Plan §12.4: 'ee playbook extract --workspace . produces curation_candidates with candidate_type = rule.'

Searched src/cli/mod.rs: no Command::Playbook, no PlaybookCommand. The flow today is curate-only: `ee curate candidates --candidate-type rule` lists pending rule candidates, but nothing produces them from semantic memories.

Concrete impact: the chain Episodic → Semantic → Procedural relies on TWO proposers — consolidator (producing summary candidates, plan §12.3) and extractor (producing rule candidates, §12.4). Searched src/curate/: there is consolidation logic but no rule-extraction proposer. So the procedural-memory tier never grows on its own; agents must hand-write `ee rule add`. North Star Scenario 3 explicitly steps through `ee review session ... --propose` then `ee curate apply` — this works for episodic→semantic but not for semantic→procedural.

Fix scope:
1. Add Command::Playbook with subcommands Extract { workspace, --since, --json }, Show, List
2. fn extract_playbook_candidates: scan memories WHERE level='SEMANTIC' AND state='active' over the window, group by tag/topic, produce candidate rules with specificity score and evidence pointers
3. Each candidate is INSERTed into curation_candidates with candidate_type='rule'
4. Existing `ee curate validate` and `ee curate apply` are reused — no new validator needed (cross-ref §16.4)
5. Test: fixture with 5 semantic memories about 'cargo fmt before release' → ee playbook extract → 1 rule candidate with all 5 as evidence

title: [MEDIUM] upsert_workspace_row TOCTOU race — concurrent ee processes can hit UNIQUE constraint
description:
## Surface
ee workspace registry concurrency (audit cycle 6, surface 2)

## Finding
`src/core/workspace.rs:544-565`:
```rust
fn upsert_workspace_row(conn: &DbConnection, target: &StoredWorkspace) -> crate::db::Result<()> {
    if conn.get_workspace(&target.id)?.is_some() {
        return Ok(());
    }
    if conn.get_workspace_by_path(&target.path)?.is_some() {
        return Ok(());
    }
    let scope = WorkspaceScopeFields { ... };
    conn.insert_workspace_with_scope(&target.id, &CreateWorkspaceInput { ... }, &scope)
}
```

The two existence checks happen OUTSIDE any transaction, then an insert follows. Two concurrent `ee` processes hitting the same registry path with the same workspace path produce a TOCTOU:

- t0: Process A: get_workspace(id_A) -> None
- t1: Process B: get_workspace(id_B) -> None
- t2: Process A: get_workspace_by_path(path) -> None
- t3: Process B: get_workspace_by_path(path) -> None
- t4: Process A: insert(id_A, path) -> OK
- t5: Process B: insert(id_B, path) -> UNIQUE constraint failure on workspaces.path

(Workspace IDs differ because each process generates its own Uuid::now_v7. Path is shared.)

## Why it matters
1. Two ee invocations starting at the same moment from the same shell pipeline can crash the second one with an opaque 'UNIQUE constraint failed' error rather than the intended idempotent no-op.
2. Multi-agent swarms routinely run multiple ee processes per workspace. The probability of collision is small but non-zero.
3. The function is named 'upsert' but is actually 'check-then-insert' — true upsert (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING) would close the race in one statement.

## Repro
Use GNU parallel or a small bash loop to fire two 'ee --workspace <path> workspace alias --as race' invocations against a fresh registry directory; expect occasional UNIQUE constraint failures from the second process.

## Fix options
A) Replace the check-then-insert sequence with INSERT INTO workspaces ... ON CONFLICT(path) DO NOTHING and ON CONFLICT(id) DO NOTHING. SQLite supports compound ON CONFLICT via index-name, or split into two statements wrapped in one transaction.
B) Wrap the whole function in with_transaction (BEGIN IMMEDIATE) — opens a write lock before the first read, so the second process serializes behind the first and sees the row on its second read. with_transaction already exists at src/db/mod.rs:330 and uses BEGIN IMMEDIATE which is correct for this case.
C) Catch the UNIQUE constraint error in upsert_workspace_row and treat it as 'already exists, fine'. Cheapest fix but masks other constraint violations.

Option B is preferred: it requires the smallest diff and aligns with the existing transaction-retry machinery.
close_reason: TOCTOU race eliminated by replacing check-then-insert pattern with atomic INSERT OR IGNORE via upsert_workspace_with_scope. Tests pass. Commit 5b46309.

title: [CONCURRENCY] cass import ledger: read-modify-write counters lose updates
description:
Files: src/cass/import.rs:766, src/cass/import.rs:814, src/db/mod.rs:4291.
Code path: ensure_running_ledger reads the existing ledger by source and writes attempt_count = existing.attempt_count + 1. complete_ledger later re-reads the row and writes imported_session_count/imported_span_count = existing counts + local delta. DbConnection::update_import_ledger overwrites absolute counter values. None of these read-modify-write sequences are enclosed in one transaction or implemented as atomic SQL increments.
Hazard: concurrent imports sharing a source_id can lose attempts and imported count increments. Interleaving: A and B both read attempt_count=1; both update to 2, so two attempts record as one. The same pattern applies to imported_session_count/imported_span_count in complete_ledger.
Repro plan: add a file-backed concurrency test with two connections and a barrier around ensure_running_ledger/complete_ledger. Expected final attempt_count and imported counts equal the sum of both callers. Fix with a single transaction using BEGIN IMMEDIATE plus UPDATE ... SET count = count + ? or route ledger writes through the write owner.

title: [reliability] CASS subprocess stdout/stderr reader threads not joined on timeout
description:
**File:** src/cass/process.rs:260-303

**Defect:** When spawning a CASS subprocess with timeout, two reader threads are spawned for stdout and stderr:
```rust
let stdout_thread = thread::spawn(move || { ... });
let stderr_thread = thread::spawn(move || { ... });
```

On timeout (line 303), the code sleeps and polls `child.try_wait()`, but if the process never exits naturally, the reader threads may block forever on `read_line()` from pipes that are never closed.

**Observable:** On timeout with a hanging CASS process: orphaned threads blocking on I/O, potential resource leak (file descriptors, thread handles).

**Repro:**
1. Configure a CASS binary that hangs indefinitely
2. Run `ee import cass` with timeout
3. Timeout triggers but reader threads don't terminate
4. Thread count increases with repeated attempts

**Fix:** 
1. Kill the child process on timeout (`child.kill()`) before joining threads
2. Or use non-blocking I/O with select/poll
3. Or close pipe handles from the parent side to unblock readers

P1 because this can cause resource exhaustion with repeated timeouts.
close_reason: Reader thread blocking already prevented by existing kill-before-join sequence; added debug logging for kill failures. Sequence: kill() sends SIGKILL, wait() reaps child and closes pipe ends, reader threads get EOF from read_to_end() and return.

title: [idea-wizard] Epic: Deterministic pack-quality sentinel and behavioral drift gates
description:
Background:
Existing work already provides context pack quality metrics, deterministic eval fixtures, pack replay ledgers, pack diff, freshness reporting, and performance gates. What is still missing is a behavioral drift sentinel that answers a sharper question: for canonical agent tasks, did the pack select the evidence we expect, omit the evidence we expect, preserve provenance/redaction/degradation posture, and stay useful under lexical-only or stale-derived-asset conditions?

This epic is plan-space only until current pack replay/freshness work closes. It must build on existing `ee eval`, `ee context`, `ee pack`, pack replay ledgers, and fixture schemas. It must not invent a second evaluator, second retrieval stack, or subjective LLM judge.

Intended UX:
- `ee eval run --pack-quality --json [--scenario <id>]` or an equivalent eval-namespaced read-only surface runs deterministic pack-quality checks.
- The output is a stable `ee.eval.pack_quality_report.v1` response containing fixture IDs, command invocations, expected/actual selected memory IDs, omitted evidence, provenance density, degradation deltas, redaction status, pack hashes, ledger hashes, pass/fail status, and first-failure diagnosis.
- The report is suitable for CI and support-bundle inclusion, but the command itself remains read-only and local-first.

Out of scope:
- No LLM-as-judge scoring.
- No replacement for existing per-pack quality metrics.
- No custom retrieval or ranking algorithm.
- No daemon, web UI, or cloud service.

## Success Criteria

- A deterministic pack-quality sentinel can be run from the eval command family without daemon mode, network access, or hidden mutation.
- Canonical fixture tasks detect selected-memory drift, omitted critical evidence, degradation posture changes, redaction leaks, missing/malformed ledgers, and stale derived assets with stable machine-readable first-failure details.
- Reports reuse existing context/pack/eval/ledger services and include reproduction commands, pack hashes, ledger hashes, fixture IDs, and scenario IDs.
- Contract, golden, unit, and logged no-mock E2E coverage prove stdout discipline, deterministic ordering, redaction safety, and degraded-mode honesty.
- Documentation explains how this sentinel differs from per-pack quality metrics, pack diff, performance benchmarks, and support bundles.

Reconcile the trust class taxonomy across the canonical OPUS plan, the main plan, and the README before any code lands that depends on it.

Background:
The README documents five trust classes (human_explicit, agent_validated, agent_assertion, cass_evidence, legacy_import) with explicit initial confidences. EE-260 ("Add trust class enum and memory fields") is in the bead set as a P1 feature; if it lands without an ADR-level reconciliation, the implementing agent will silently choose one taxonomy and the others will rot.

The bead set has no bead that explicitly resolves this divergence. Multi-agent triangulation flagged it as a high-confidence ambiguity (D2 mode, F4 mode) and as a trust-pipeline correctness risk (H2 adversarial review).

Intended scope:
This bead is a docs/ADR bead. It produces (a) one ADR under docs/adr/ that specifies the canonical trust class set, the canonical initial confidences, the canonical state machine for promotion/demotion/inversion, the audit shape for each transition, and the public schema field name and version; (b) updates to the README and OPUS plan that point to the ADR; (c) a fixture test that asserts the chosen taxonomy round-trips through the future enum without loss; (d) a checklist on EE-260 that requires the ADR to exist before EE-260 can close.

It does not implement the enum or any state machine. It locks the spec.

Why this matters:
Trust class is load-bearing for retrieval scoring, packing priority, prompt-injection defense, redaction policy, audit log shape, MCP schema, and curation. If two implementations diverge in their understanding of "agent_validated", every downstream feature inherits the inconsistency. Resolving it once in plan space costs a few hours; resolving it after twenty downstream beads ship costs a sprint.

## Acceptance Criteria

Detailed closure criteria are stored in this bead's structured acceptance_criteria field. Treat those criteria as part of this bead's implementation contract, including the ADR, fixture, cross-link, and testing requirements.
design:
Recommended design:
- Take the README five-class set as the canonical baseline (human_explicit, agent_validated, agent_assertion, cass_evidence, legacy_import) because it is already user-facing in published documentation. Map any extra classes from the longer plan into either a `trust_class` plus a `trust_subclass` qualifier (recommended) or document them as future-work and reject them in v1.
- Use the README-published initial confidences (0.85, 0.65, 0.50, 0.45, 0.30) as the canonical defaults. Tune per-environment overrides via the existing config layer (see EE-021 config parser, EE-022 config precedence merge). Do not introduce a new config surface in this ADR.
- Define exactly four transition triggers: outcome_helpful, outcome_harmful, validation_passed (e.g. fixture replay confirms rule), validation_contradicted (replay falsifies rule). Each trigger maps to a deterministic delta (helpful: +0.04 utility, no class change unless threshold; harmful: weighted 4x; validation_passed: +0.06 confidence, may promote class with provenance). Numbers come from §18 decay/trauma guard.

title: EE-PRIV-WS-001: Canonicalize workspace paths, enforce symlink isolation, and prove cross-workspace separation
description:
Canonicalize workspace paths, reject symlink confusion, and prove cross-workspace isolation in tests so memory from project A can never silently surface in project B.

Background:
H2 adversarial review and F4 failure-mode analysis flagged that EE keys retrieval and packing on workspace identity. Workspace identity in turn comes from path-derived hashing (see EE-023 workspace detection, EE-026 health, EE-027 check posture, EE-094 agent path scoping). Every modern dev environment has symlinks, bind mounts, and worktrees. If two paths canonicalize differently and EE treats them as different workspaces, the user gets duplicate memories. If two paths canonicalize identically when they should not (e.g. a git worktree pointing at a sibling directory), memory leaks across project boundaries. The bead set has no bead that owns canonicalization, symlink policy, or the cross-workspace leakage test.

Intended scope:
This bead owns the canonicalization contract, the symlink policy, the test fixture that proves isolation, and the diagnostic surface that explains workspace identity to the agent.

Public surface:
- A canonicalization function inside config/workspace that resolves any input path to a stable canonical form (real path resolution, normalization, case handling per platform), is deterministic, and produces a salted hash used as the workspace identity.
- A symlink policy: by default, EE refuses to register a workspace whose canonical path differs from the input path because of a symlink in the chain, unless the user explicitly opts in via `ee init --allow-symlink`. The refusal returns a stable error code and a useful next action.
- `ee workspace identity --json` reports input path, canonical path, salted hash, symlink chain (if any), git root, fork/worktree posture, and the policy decision. Read-only.
- `ee doctor --fix-plan` adds a check that detects ambiguous workspace state (two registered workspaces canonicalize to the same hash) with a non-destructive repair plan.

Why this matters:
A privacy-violating cross-workspace leak would erode trust in EE permanently. The leak is realistic on any developer machine that uses `ln -s`, `git worktree`, or bind mounts. Fixing it after launch costs an emergency advisory; fixing it now costs one bead.

## Acceptance Criteria

Detailed closure criteria are stored in this bead's structured acceptance_criteria field. Treat those criteria as part of this bead's implementation contract, including canonical path semantics, symlink-denial policy, workspace identity schema, doctor fix-plan behavior, cross-workspace isolation tests, adversarial symlink fixtures, and e2e logging requirements.
design:
Recommended design:
- Use std::fs::canonicalize as the base resolver, then layer normalization (Unicode NFC for paths exposed to the user, case-fold for the hash on case-insensitive filesystems, no trailing-slash differences).
- Store the per-installation salt in the user state dir (e.g. ~/.local/share/ee/.salt) with mode 0600. The salt is created on first run and is never written to logs, audit entries, support bundles, or JSONL exports. The redaction policy (privacy bead set) treats the salt as a Secret class.
- Detect symlinks by comparing input path components against the canonical path components. The first divergence flags a symlink and is recorded in symlink_chain. The check is deterministic and does not require re-traversal.
- Worktree and fork detection layer on top by inspecting `.git/worktrees/` (if present) or upstream metadata (already partly addressed by EE-094 agent path scoping). Capture both pieces of information without forcing them.
- The cross-workspace isolation test is the load-bearing artifact. Make it part of the EE-TST-004 walking-skeleton script so any future change that breaks isolation also breaks the walking-skeleton gate.
- Compose with EE-CONC-001 advisory lock: workspace registration is a write op and must take the lock.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

Acceptance criteria:
- The canonicalize_workspace_path function takes an input path and returns Outcome<CanonicalWorkspace> with fields: input_path, canonical_path, salted_hash, symlink_chain (list of links traversed), platform_case_handling (preserve/lower), git_root (option), worktree (option), fork (option). It is deterministic for fixed input + salt.
- The salted hash uses BLAKE3 keyed by a per-installation salt stored under the user state dir; the salt is created once and never rotated automatically. Two distinct installations produce different hashes for the same path.
- The default policy refuses to register a workspace if the canonical path differs from the input path through a symlink. The refusal returns exit code 7 (policy denied) with a stable error code workspace_symlink_blocked and a next action that includes `ee init --allow-symlink` and a doctor command.
- `ee workspace identity --json` is read-only and stable; its schema is versioned (ee.workspace.identity.v<N>); it never mutates state and never registers a workspace.
- `ee doctor` includes a workspace_collision check that flags any two registered workspaces with the same salted hash; the check returns a non-destructive fix-plan that names both workspaces and the next steps to merge or rename them.
- Cross-workspace isolation is proven by an integration test that registers workspaces A and B, writes one memory in A and one in B, then asserts that searching in B never returns A memories under any of: same query text, same tags, same level, same kind, exact memory id (which must be re-key-required across workspaces).

Testing and logging requirements:
- Unit tests cover canonicalization for: simple paths, paths through one symlink, paths through nested symlinks, broken symlinks, paths with mixed case (case-insensitive vs case-sensitive filesystems), paths through bind mounts (Linux), worktree-rooted paths (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`), and unreachable paths (returns a stable error).
- Integration tests using a real ee binary register workspaces under a temp directory, run `ee workspace identity --json` for each, assert the hashes differ, write memories in each, then run cross-workspace search and assert empty results.
- Adversarial tests: a malicious agent supplies a path that resolves to another registered workspace by way of a freshly created symlink; the test asserts policy denial.
- Property tests: for any random valid path, canonicalization is idempotent (canon(canon(p)) == canon(p)) and stable across process restarts within the same installation.
- E2E logs capture inputs, canonicalizations, registered workspaces, attempted leaks, and the audit entries written by `ee workspace identity` (none) and `ee init` (registration audit).
- Stdout assertions prove only machine data leaves stdout for `ee workspace identity --json` and `ee init --json`.
- Closeout evidence cites the cross-workspace isolation test name, the per-platform canonicalization fixtures, and the audit log diff for the policy-denied case.
notes: Closes a privacy attack vector flagged by H2 adversarial review (path confusion via symlinks) and a usability defect flagged by F4 failure mode (worktree paths producing two identities for one project). Cross-workspace isolation is the single biggest privacy promise EE makes; if it leaks, no other guarantee matters.

title: EE-244: Implement job diagnostic output
description:
Source plan item: EE-244 from the `Diagnostics And Evaluation` backlog.

Task: Implement job diagnostic output

Background and intent:
Prove usefulness and repairability through diagnostics, why output, evaluation fixtures, degradation matrices, performance timing, and metric gates.

Why this matters:
This bead contributes to the overarching goal of making `ee` a dependable local memory substrate for coding agents: useful before work, auditable after work, and safe under degraded conditions. The work should be implemented in the smallest coherent slice that fully satisfies the public contract implied by the title.

Dependency context:
Original plan dependencies: EE-200, EE-240. These are also represented as br dependency edges where the referenced bead exists.

Non-negotiable constraints:
Global implementation invariants for this task:
- Keep the CLI local-first, deterministic, and agent-native; stdout is data, stderr is diagnostics.
- Preserve the no-Tokio and no-rusqlite constraint unless a later ADR explicitly changes the architecture.
- Use SQLModel Rust plus FrankenSQLite for durable data; do not introduce a second storage stack.
- Use Asupersync for async edges and cancellation/budget behavior; do not smuggle in a Tokio executor.
- Keep JSON as the canonical public contract. TOON, Markdown, diagrams, and MCP are renderers or adapters over the same domain data.
- Mutating commands need dry-run/idempotency/audit behavior unless the task explicitly says otherwise.
- Add focused tests proportional to risk: unit tests for domain logic, contract/golden tests for public output, and integration/evaluation tests for cross-subsystem behavior.

## Acceptance Criteria

Detailed closure criteria are stored in this bead's structured acceptance_criteria field. Treat those criteria as part of this bead's implementation contract, including the comprehensive testing and logging requirements.
design:

- Prefer the planned crate boundaries from the comprehensive plan: CLI wiring in `ee-cli`, reusable domain/services in `ee-core`, models in `ee-models`, persistence in `ee-db`, output rendering in `ee-output`, and adapters in their own optional crates.

title: Add degraded-honesty contracts for unavailable or not-yet-wired commands
description:
## Background

Many risky surfaces are valuable concepts but currently return sample, stub, mock, or simulated results. Future users are better served by an honest degraded response than by a plausible-looking answer that was not computed from evidence.

This bead creates reusable contracts and test helpers that force not-yet-wired commands to say exactly what is unavailable, what evidence was missing, and what command or bead is needed to make it real.

## Acceptance Criteria

See this bead's structured acceptance_criteria field for the detailed completion contract, including unit/static checks, e2e or docs/e2e coverage, detailed logging, and no-feature-loss requirements.
design: Extend the existing degraded-honesty patterns rather than creating a parallel error system. Public JSON should use stable schema/degradation fields and avoid human-only caveats. Contract tests should detect forbidden phrases and forbidden production data sources such as `generate_sample_*`, `create_mock_*`, `simulate command execution`, and `stub success` in command paths unless explicitly gated to test-only code.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

- There is a reusable degraded response shape for command families whose honest implementation is not ready.
- Unit tests cover degraded response builder behavior, stable code/severity mapping, repair command canonicalization, missing-capability detail payloads, no-style JSON serialization, and deterministic ordering.
- Contract tests fail if production command output contains sample/mock/stub data while reporting success.
- Contract tests fail if a command claims persisted records, verification, replay, causal uplift, procedure validation, or certificate validity without concrete evidence sources.
- Tests cover JSON stdout isolation, degradation code stability, repair text, and no terminal styling in machine output.
- E2E scripts cover unavailable dependency, stale derived asset, missing config, unsupported feature flag, and intentionally-not-yet-wired command cases.
- E2E logs include command, cwd/workspace, sanitized env, elapsed time, exit code, stdout/stderr paths, schema validation, degradation codes, repair command, command-boundary matrix row, side-effect class, and first-failure diagnosis.
- The tests allow deterministic fixtures under `tests/fixtures/` while rejecting those same fixtures in normal workspace command output unless the command is explicitly a fixture/eval command.
close_reason: Degraded-honesty parent contract completed. Evidence: docs/command_classification.md enumerates 21 public degraded command families with code anchors and follow-up beads; src/core/degraded_honesty.rs provides reusable degraded-response, fake-success, repair, severity, and unsupported-evidence validators; tests/degraded_honesty.rs covers the real binary across audit, support, certificate, claim, diag quarantine, rehearse, learn, lab, economy, causal, procedure, situation, plan, eval, review, preflight/tripwire, handoff, daemon, recorder, and demo manifest/artifact paths. Verification: env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR rch exec -- cargo test degraded_honesty --lib passed 19 tests; env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR rch exec -- cargo test --test degraded_honesty passed 25 tests. title: [CONCURRENCY] write owner: durable writes bypass single-writer actor
description:
Files: src/core/write_owner.rs:1, src/core/write_owner.rs:185, src/core/write_owner.rs:290, src/core/memory.rs:312, src/cass/import.rs:373, src/db/mod.rs:214, src/db/mod.rs:570, src/db/mod.rs:597.
Code path: write_owner.rs says all durable writes flow through WriteOwner and exposes WriteHandle::submit(&Cx), but rg shows WriteHandle/WriteOwner are only exported/tested, while production commands call DbConnection::with_transaction and insert/update methods directly. Examples: ee remember writes memory/audit/index job at src/core/memory.rs:312-327; CASS import writes sessions/spans/index jobs at src/cass/import.rs:373-385.
Hazard: concurrent ee invocations can create multiple independent FrankenSQLite writers instead of the FIFO actor promised by ADR-0013. DbConnection::with_transaction starts BEGIN DEFERRED and execute/query helpers do not retry SQLITE_BUSY except at open time, so concurrent write paths can fail with busy/snapshot conflict or partial command failure.
Repro plan: add a file-backed integration test that starts two ee remember or import commands against one DB behind a barrier. Expected: both writes serialize and persist without database is busy; fix by routing production writes through WriteOwner or a single advisory writer gate.
close_reason: Serialized file-backed durable writes with a write-owner gate and contention retry; added two-writer regression test

title: [HIGH] steward: decay budget cancellation happens after durable mutations
description: src/steward/mod.rs:2016-2038 runs run_score_decay_job before recording item/time consumption and checking budget.should_cancel(). A caller can pass --item-limit 0 or an unrealistically small time limit; the sweeper may already update memory scores and mark feedback applied, then the runner reports RunOutcome::Cancelled. Fix by enforcing item/time budgets before mutation, running a preflight/dry-run count before applying, or wrapping the handler in a transaction that rolls back when budget cancellation is reached.

Task: Add forbidden dependency audit for Tokio and `rusqlite`

Background and intent:
Establish the Rust workspace, core crate boundaries, runtime shell, error model, and test harness that every later subsystem depends on. This is the delivery foundation: no feature work should bypass these invariants.

Why this matters:
This bead contributes to the overarching goal of making `ee` a dependable local memory substrate for coding agents: useful before work, auditable after work, and safe under degraded conditions. The work should be implemented in the smallest coherent slice that fully satisfies the public contract implied by the title.

Dependency context:
Original plan dependencies: EE-001. These are also represented as br dependency edges where the referenced bead exists.

Non-negotiable constraints:
Global implementation invariants for this task:
- Keep the CLI local-first, deterministic, and agent-native; stdout is data, stderr is diagnostics.
- Preserve the no-Tokio and no-rusqlite constraint unless a later ADR explicitly changes the architecture.
- Use SQLModel Rust plus FrankenSQLite for durable data; do not introduce a second storage stack.
- Use Asupersync for async edges and cancellation/budget behavior; do not smuggle in a Tokio executor.
- Keep JSON as the canonical public contract. TOON, Markdown, diagrams, and MCP are renderers or adapters over the same domain data.
- Mutating commands need dry-run/idempotency/audit behavior unless the task explicitly says otherwise.
- Add focused tests proportional to risk: unit tests for domain logic, contract/golden tests for public output, and integration/evaluation tests for cross-subsystem behavior.

title: G10: HITS hubs vs authorities — orientation vs grounding query profiles for ee context
description:
# G10 — HITS hubs vs authorities

## Idea (one-liner)

Run HITS on memory_links to compute two scores per memory: **authority** (cited by many good hubs) and **hub** (cites many good authorities). PageRank conflates these; HITS separates them. Use the separation to make `ee context` profile-aware: grounding queries up-weight authorities, orientation queries up-weight hubs.

## Why this matters

Today's `ee context --profile=<name>` is a hand-tuned multiplier table over freshness/confidence/utility. HITS adds a *structurally-derived* axis distinguishing two genuinely different memory roles. Pairs orthogonally with G1's PPR:

- PPR answers: "what's structurally relevant to my query?"
- HITS answers: "of those, which are foundational (authority) vs synthesizing (hub)?"

Together they let `ee context` produce packs that are *either* well-grounded *or* high-synthesis on demand — a capability `ee` does not have today.

## Algorithm

`fnx_algorithms::hits(memory_links_directed)`. Returns two maps: `authority[v]`, `hub[v]`. Iteration cap ~30. Both vectors L2-normalized.

## Pack assembly integration

`ee context --profile=grounding|orientation|balanced|<existing>`:
- `grounding`: rank score = base · (1 + 0.5 · authority[v])
- `orientation`: rank score = base · (1 + 0.5 · hub[v])
- `balanced`: rank score = base · (1 + 0.25 · authority[v] + 0.25 · hub[v])
- Existing profiles unchanged unless `--profile-hits` flag flips them.

## Output shape

`ee why <id> --json` adds:

```jsonc
"hits": {
  "authorityScore": 0.067,
  "hubScore": 0.012,
  "authorityPercentile": 88,
  "hubPercentile": 35,
  "role": "authority"  // authority|hub|both|neither based on percentile thresholds
}
```

`ee insights --section hubs` and `ee insights --section authorities`: top-K each.

## Acceptance

- New module `src/graph/hits.rs` with `compute_hits(graph) -> HitsScores`.
- HITS scores precomputed on snapshot refresh (cached alongside PageRank).
- `ee context --profile={grounding,orientation,balanced}` flag.
- `ee why` shows HITS scores.
- `ee insights` exposes hubs + authorities sections.
- 6 unit tests + 1 e2e + 1 golden.

## Dependencies

Blocked by: F1, F2, F4.
Blocks: nothing.
Parent: bd-bife.

## Notes

- HITS is sensitive to topic drift: a star-shaped subgraph can dominate authority scores. Mitigate by running HITS on the entire memory_links graph (not query-relevant subgraph) and using percentile-of-workspace as the user-facing signal.

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel
comments.text:
## Phase 6 refinement notes — HITS convergence

1. **Disconnected graphs**: HITS power iteration on a disconnected graph converges to the principal eigenvector of the largest component. Other components get scores from their own iteration. Document this behavior.

2. **Convergence threshold**: Iteration cap = 50 (matches PageRank), L2-difference threshold = 1e-6 between successive iterations. If neither hit by iteration 50: emit degraded.hits_convergence_failure (per RX6) AND use the score-vector at iteration 50 anyway (best-effort).

3. **Negative weights**: HITS assumes non-negative weights. The contradicts edges (weight 0 per G1) are correctly handled. Document that other negative-weight scenarios are unsupported and would produce degraded.hits_invalid_weights.

4. **G10.b profile semantics**:
   - grounding: rank += 0.5 × authority
   - orientation: rank += 0.5 × hub
   - balanced: rank += 0.25 × authority + 0.25 × hub
   These are additive boosts (NOT multipliers). Document that grounding+orientation can't be combined — pick one or balanced.

Update G10.a + G10.b accordingly.

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel
comments.text: Round 4 pinning. G10.a unit tests (5 cases): (1) K4 symmetric: authority=hub=uniform 0.25 each. (2) Star graph: hub[center]=1; authority[leaves]>>authority[center]. (3) K_3,3 bipartite-projection: equal within side, sum to 1. (4) 2 disconnected K3 components: scores computed per-component, no cross-contamination. (5) Convergence 50 iters; norm-delta<1e-6; if not reached emit degraded.hits_convergence_failure. G10.b CLI: --profile=grounding boosts authority 0.5x; --profile=orientation boosts hub 0.5x; --profile=balanced 0.25x each. Sparse graph (<50 edges): emit degraded.hits.sparse_graph + recommend disable. G10+G1 interaction: PPR and HITS both cached independently; both invalidate on memory_links snapshot refresh. ee context with --ppr-weight + --profile=grounding: additive boosts compose.

title: G10.consistency: Mathematical-consistency check — HITS principal eigenvector vs PageRank
description:
## Why
HITS authority and PageRank authority are both eigenvector-based but use different propagation rules. For a graph where both should give similar rankings (e.g., balanced reciprocal graph), the rank correlation should be high (>0.7 Spearman). This catches implementation bugs in either wrapper.

## Test
1. Build a fixture: 50 nodes, balanced symmetric edges. Run both pagerank_directed and hits.
2. Compute Spearman rank correlation between PageRank and HITS authority scores.
3. Assert correlation > 0.7 (math says it should approach 1.0 in the symmetric case).

This is a meta-test catching wrapper bugs.

title: EE-DIST-003: Add agent-safe install, update, and install-check workflows
description:
Define and implement agent-safe installation, update, and installation-check behavior for EE.

Background:
Agents need safe non-interactive install/update workflows with dry-run, idempotency, version pinning, and clear recovery paths. Installation must not silently modify unrelated shell profiles, overwrite unknown files, or pull unverified binaries.

Intended public surface:
- `ee install check --json` reports current binary path, version provenance, PATH posture, writable install target, duplicate binaries, and update availability posture when configured.
- Installer script or `ee install plan --json` reports what would be downloaded/copied, verified, and changed.
- `ee update --dry-run --json` reports available version, selected artifact, checksum/signature verification plan, and exact mutations before apply.
- Any mutating install/update path is idempotent, auditable, and refuses unsafe overwrites.

## Acceptance Criteria

Detailed closure criteria are stored in this bead's structured acceptance_criteria field. Treat those criteria as part of this bead's implementation contract, including comprehensive tests and logging requirements.
design: Prefer dry-run/install-plan semantics first. Mutating apply paths must be explicit, idempotent, checksum-verified, and represented in the command-effect manifest. Tests must use temporary install roots only.
acceptance_criteria:

Acceptance criteria:

- Install/update apply, if implemented, refuses unverified artifacts, path traversal, symlink surprises, unknown existing files, target mismatch, downgrade without explicit pin/force semantics, and missing provenance.
- `ee install check --json` detects duplicate `ee` binaries in PATH, stale binary vs workspace schema, unsupported target, missing write permission, and inconsistent feature/channel posture with stable codes and next actions.
- Installer/update behavior never modifies shell profiles, global config, workspace files, or user data without explicit flags and command-effect manifest coverage.
- Public schemas/goldens cover fresh install plan, already-installed idempotent check, update available, pinned version, unsupported target, checksum mismatch, duplicate PATH binaries, permission denied, and offline/no-network configured state.

title: SRR6.35: Withdrawal, tombstone propagation, and peer-cache purge semantics
description:
Implement withdrawal, tombstone propagation, and cache purge semantics for mesh-shared material. Local-first `ee` must remain append-only/audited, but users need a clear way to stop sharing a memory and ask peers to purge cached bodies or mark metadata as withdrawn.

Scope includes: share-withdraw event kind; tombstone vs validity expiry vs peer-cache purge semantics; what remote peers must do with previously cached bodies; how best-effort purge is audited; how unavailable peers receive withdrawal later; and how context/search/why render withdrawn remote material. This is not a guarantee that other machines forget unaudited copies; docs must be honest about that boundary.

Acceptance: event schema support; repository/replay handling; unit tests for tombstone, validity expiry, body purge, and unavailable peer replay; e2e script with two nodes where a shared body is later withdrawn and no longer appears in context except as a provenance/audit tombstone; structured logs for withdrawal_event, purge_requested, purge_applied, peer_unreachable, and residual_metadata_reason.

comments.author: DustyOtter
comments.text: Third polish finding: cache eviction handles disk pressure, but privacy needs a separate withdrawal story. Users must have an honest, audited way to stop future sharing and request peer cache purge.
